7. Click **Save**

zone_min_tls_version_secure.title: Minimum TLS version is set to 1.2 or higher
zone_min_tls_version_secure.description: **Cloudflare zones** are assessed for **minimum TLS version** configuration by checking if the version is set to at least `TLS 1.2` to ensure connections use **secure, modern cryptographic protocols**.
zone_min_tls_version_secure.risk:
Allowing **legacy TLS versions** (1.0, 1.1) exposes connections to known protocol vulnerabilities.
- **Confidentiality**: BEAST, POODLE, and weak cipher suites can be exploited for traffic decryption
- **Compliance**: TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated by PCI-DSS, NIST, and major browsers
- **Integrity**: downgrade attacks can force weaker encryption that is susceptible to tampering

wui.description:
Set **minimum TLS version** to `1.2` or higher.
- **TLS 1.0 and 1.1** are deprecated by all major browsers and contain known vulnerabilities
- Consider setting to `TLS 1.3` for environments with modern client requirements
- Test client compatibility before upgrading minimum version

other.description:
1. Log in to the Cloudflare dashboard and select your account and domain
2. Go to SSL/TLS > Edge Certificates
3. Scroll to Minimum TLS Version
4. Select TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3 from the dropdown
5. Verify that your clients support the selected TLS version

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Set minimum TLS version to 1.2 for secure connections
resource "cloudflare_zone_setting" "min_tls_version" {
  zone_id    = "<ZONE_ID>"
  setting_id = "min_tls_version"
  value      = "1.2" # Critical: blocks legacy TLS 1.0/1.1 connections
}
```

admincenter_users_admins_reduced_license.title: Administrative user has no license or an allowed license (AAD_PREMIUM or AAD_PREMIUM_P2)
admincenter_users_admins_reduced_license.description: Privileged users in Microsoft 365 are evaluated for a **reduced license footprint**: only `AAD_PREMIUM` (P1) or `AAD_PREMIUM_P2` (P2), or no license. Assignments that include productivity app suites indicate excess application entitlements on administrative accounts.
admincenter_users_admins_reduced_license.risk: Productivity licenses on **privileged identities** create mailboxes and collaboration surfaces that widen attack paths. Phishing, malicious content, or rogue OAuth apps can steal credentials/tokens, enabling tenant-wide role misuse, data exfiltration, and configuration tampering-compromising **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

wui.description: Maintain **dedicated admin accounts** with a **least-privilege, reduced-license** model: assign only Microsoft Entra P1/P2 features needed for identity security, or keep them unlicensed for apps. Separate admin from daily-use accounts, enforce **MFA** and just-in-time elevation, and use **privileged access workstations** for administration.

other.description:
1. Sign in to https://admin.microsoft.com
2. Go to Users > Active users
3. Select the affected administrative user
4. Open Licenses and apps
5. To pass the check, do ONE of the following:
   - Unassign all licenses (make the user unlicensed); or
   - Assign only Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 and remove all other licenses
6. Click Save changes

secretsmanager_has_restrictive_resource_.title: Secrets Manager secret has a restrictive resource-based policy
secretsmanager_has_restrictive_resource_.description: **Secrets Manager secrets** are evaluated for **restrictive resource-based policies**: explicit **Deny** for unauthorized principals, **Organization** boundary via `PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:SourceAccount` for service access. Per-principal **NotAction** restrictions are optional (defense-in-depth). Regionalized service principals are supported.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
secretsmanager_has_restrictive_resource_.risk: Without a restrictive resource policy, **any IAM principal** in the account—or even **cross-account entities**—can read, modify, or delete the secret, compromising **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Overly broad policies enable **lateral movement** and **privilege escalation** through exposed credentials.

wui.description:
Apply **deny-by-default** resource policies to every secret:
- Deny all principals except explicitly authorized roles via `StringNotEquals` on `aws:PrincipalArn`
- Deny access from outside the AWS Organization via `aws:PrincipalOrgID`
- Constrain AWS service access with `aws:SourceAccount` (additional restrictive conditions like `ArnLike` are accepted)
- Optionally, restrict each authorized principal to **least-privilege actions** using per-principal `Deny/NotAction` statements (defense-in-depth)

other.description:
1. Open AWS Console > Secrets Manager
2. Select the secret > Overview tab > Resource permissions > Edit permissions
3. Add a **Deny** statement for `Principal: *` with `StringNotEquals` condition listing only authorized `aws:PrincipalArn` values
4. Add a **Deny** statement with `StringNotEquals` on `aws:PrincipalOrgID` to block access from outside your organization
5. For each authorized principal, add a **Deny** with `NotAction` listing only the specific actions they need
6. Save the policy

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::SecretsManager::ResourcePolicy
    Properties:
      SecretId: <example_resource_id>
      ResourcePolicy:  # Critical: deny-by-default with explicit exceptions
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Deny
            Principal: '*'
            Action: '*'
            Resource: '*'
            Condition:
              StringNotEquals:
                aws:PrincipalArn: <AUTHORIZED_ROLE_ARN>
```

secretsmanager_has_restrictive_resource_.notes: This check enforces a strict deny-by-default pattern for Secrets Manager resource policies. It validates four layered controls: (1) an explicit Deny for all unauthorized principals, (2) an organization boundary via PrincipalOrgID, (3) per-principal action restrictions via NotAction (optional, validated only if present), and (4) SourceAccount constraints for AWS service principals (additional restrictive conditions are accepted). Cross-account Allow statements cause the check to fail intentionally to surface expanded trust boundaries for review. Both simple (e.g. appflow.amazonaws.com) and regionalized (e.g. logs.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com) service principals are supported.

githubactions_workflow_security_scan.title: GitHub Actions workflows have no security issues detected by zizmor
githubactions_workflow_security_scan.description: Scan GitHub Actions workflow files for security issues such as template injection, excessive permissions, unpinned actions, and other misconfigurations using the zizmor static analysis tool.
githubactions_workflow_security_scan.risk: Insecure GitHub Actions workflows can lead to supply chain attacks, credential theft, code injection, and unauthorized access to repository secrets.

wui.description: Review your GitHub Actions workflows for security best practices including pinning actions to commit SHAs, using minimal permissions, avoiding template injection, and securing workflow triggers.

other.description: Review and fix the security issues identified by zizmor in your GitHub Actions workflow files.

githubactions_workflow_security_scan.notes: This check requires zizmor to be installed. If zizmor is not available, the check will be skipped gracefully.

gmail_enhanced_pre_delivery_scanning_ena.title: Enhanced pre-delivery message scanning is enabled
gmail_enhanced_pre_delivery_scanning_ena.description: Enhanced pre-delivery message scanning adds additional security checks for messages identified as potentially suspicious. When enabled, Gmail may slightly delay delivery to perform deeper analysis, improving detection of phishing and malware that might otherwise evade standard filters.
gmail_enhanced_pre_delivery_scanning_ena.risk: Without enhanced pre-delivery scanning, some **sophisticated phishing and malware** messages may pass through standard filters and be delivered to users. The additional scanning layer catches threats that the first-pass filters miss, reducing the organization's exposure to **zero-day phishing campaigns** and **targeted attacks**.

wui.description: Enable enhanced pre-delivery message scanning to improve Gmail's ability to detect and block sophisticated phishing and malware before delivery to users.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Gmail**
3. Click **Spam, phishing, and malware**
4. Check **Enhanced pre-delivery message scanning** - Enables improved detection of suspicious content prior to delivery
5. Click **Save**

gmail_untrusted_link_warnings_enabled.title: Warning prompt for clicks on untrusted domain links is enabled
gmail_untrusted_link_warnings_enabled.description: Gmail can display a warning prompt when users click on links to domains that are not trusted. This gives users an opportunity to reconsider before navigating to a potentially malicious website.
gmail_untrusted_link_warnings_enabled.risk: Without untrusted link warnings, users may click on **phishing links** or links to **malware distribution sites** without any warning. This significantly increases the success rate of **social engineering attacks** targeting the organization.

wui.description: Enable warning prompts for clicks on untrusted domain links so users are alerted before navigating to potentially malicious websites from email links.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Gmail**
3. Click **Safety** > **Links and external images**
4. Check **Show warning prompt for any click on links to untrusted domains**
5. Click **Save**

zone_hsts_enabled.title: HSTS is enabled with recommended max-age and includes subdomains
zone_hsts_enabled.description: **Cloudflare zones** are assessed for **HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)** by checking if it is enabled with a `max-age` of at least **6 months** (15768000 seconds) and **includes subdomains** to instruct browsers to always use HTTPS across the entire domain.
zone_hsts_enabled.risk:
Without **HSTS**, browsers may initially connect over HTTP before redirecting to HTTPS.
- **Confidentiality**: creates a window for SSL stripping attacks where attackers downgrade connections to unencrypted HTTP
- **Integrity**: first request can be intercepted and modified before HTTPS redirect
- **Session hijacking**: cookies and credentials may be captured during initial HTTP request

wui.description:
Enable **HSTS** with at least a **6-month max-age** (12 months recommended).
- Verify all resources work over HTTPS before enabling
- Enable **include_subdomains** to protect all subdomains
- Consider **HSTS preloading** for maximum protection against SSL stripping attacks
- Test thoroughly as HSTS cannot be easily disabled once deployed

other.description:
1. Log in to the Cloudflare dashboard and select your account and domain
2. Go to SSL/TLS > Edge Certificates
3. Scroll to HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)
4. Click Enable HSTS
5. Set Max Age Header to at least 6 months
6. Enable Include subdomains and Preload if appropriate
7. Acknowledge the warning and click Save

zone_hsts_enabled.notes: HSTS requires HTTPS to be properly configured. Ensure all resources are accessible via HTTPS before enabling HSTS with a long max-age.

gmail_mail_delegation_disabled.title: Mail delegation is disabled for users
gmail_mail_delegation_disabled.description: Mail delegation allows a delegate to read, send, and delete messages on behalf of another user. When enabled at the user level, this creates a risk that unauthorized individuals could gain access to sensitive email content. Only administrators should be able to manage mailbox delegation.
gmail_mail_delegation_disabled.risk: If users can delegate access to their mailbox, an attacker who compromises one account could silently delegate access to maintain persistent email surveillance. This also increases the risk of **insider threats** and **data exfiltration** through shared mailbox access.

wui.description: Disable mail delegation so that only administrators can manage mailbox access. This prevents users from granting unauthorized access to their email.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Gmail**
3. Click **User Settings** > **Mail delegation**
4. Uncheck **Let users delegate access to their mailbox to other users in the domain**
5. Click **Save**

gmail_pop_imap_access_disabled.title: POP and IMAP access is disabled for all users
gmail_pop_imap_access_disabled.description: POP and IMAP allow users to access Gmail through legacy or third-party email clients that may not support modern authentication mechanisms such as multifactor authentication. Disabling these protocols forces users to access email through approved clients only.
gmail_pop_imap_access_disabled.risk: With POP and IMAP enabled, users can access email through **legacy clients** that rely on simple password authentication, bypassing **multifactor authentication** and other modern security controls. This significantly increases the risk of **credential-based account compromise**.

wui.description: Disable both POP and IMAP access to prevent users from using legacy email clients that bypass modern authentication controls.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Gmail**
3. Click **End User Access** > **POP and IMAP Access**
4. Uncheck **Enable IMAP access for all users**
5. Uncheck **Enable POP access for all users**
6. Click **Save**

gmail_external_image_scanning_enabled.title: Scanning of linked images for malicious content is enabled
gmail_external_image_scanning_enabled.description: Gmail can scan images linked in email messages to detect malicious content. External images can be used to deliver tracking pixels, exploit browser vulnerabilities, or serve as part of phishing campaigns.
gmail_external_image_scanning_enabled.risk: Without external image scanning, attackers can use **linked images to track email opens**, deliver **exploit payloads via image rendering vulnerabilities**, or use images as part of sophisticated **phishing schemes** that mimic legitimate communications.

wui.description: Enable scanning of linked images so that Gmail proactively checks external image resources for malicious content before displaying them to users.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Gmail**
3. Click **Safety** > **Links and external images**
4. Check **Scan linked images**
5. Click **Save**

gmail_comprehensive_mail_storage_enabled.title: Comprehensive mail storage is enabled
gmail_comprehensive_mail_storage_enabled.description: Comprehensive mail storage ensures that a copy of all sent and received messages in the domain, including messages sent or received by non-Gmail mailboxes, is stored in users' Gmail mailboxes. This makes all messages accessible to Google Vault for retention, eDiscovery, and compliance purposes.
gmail_comprehensive_mail_storage_enabled.risk: Without comprehensive mail storage, messages sent through other Google services (Calendar, Drive, etc.) may not be stored in Gmail and therefore **not subject to Vault retention policies**. This creates gaps in **compliance coverage**, **eDiscovery**, and **audit trails** that could violate regulatory requirements.

wui.description: Enable comprehensive mail storage to ensure all email is stored in Gmail mailboxes for Vault retention and eDiscovery compliance.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Gmail**
3. Click **Compliance** > **Comprehensive mail storage**
4. Check **Ensure that a copy of all sent and received mail is stored in associated users' mailboxes**
5. Click **Save**

gmail_auto_forwarding_disabled.title: Automatic forwarding options are disabled
gmail_auto_forwarding_disabled.description: Automatic email forwarding allows users to automatically forward all incoming email to an external address. Disabling this feature prevents unauthorized data exfiltration through email forwarding rules.
gmail_auto_forwarding_disabled.risk: With auto-forwarding enabled, an attacker who gains control of a user account can create **forwarding rules to exfiltrate** all incoming email to an external address. This can persist undetected and provide the attacker with continuous access to sensitive communications even after the account is recovered.

wui.description: Disable automatic email forwarding to prevent users and attackers from setting up rules that exfiltrate email data to external addresses.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Gmail**
3. Click **End User Access** > **Automatic forwarding**
4. Uncheck **Allow users to automatically forward incoming email to another address**
5. Click **Save**

gmail_per_user_outbound_gateway_disabled.title: Per-user outbound gateways are disabled
gmail_per_user_outbound_gateway_disabled.description: A per-user outbound gateway allows users to send mail through an external SMTP server instead of Google's mail servers. Disabling this setting ensures all outbound email is routed through the organization's configured mail infrastructure.
gmail_per_user_outbound_gateway_disabled.risk: With per-user outbound gateways enabled, users can route outbound email through **external SMTP servers**, bypassing organizational **email security controls**, **DLP policies**, and **audit logging**. This creates an unmonitored channel for data exfiltration and policy circumvention.

wui.description: Disable per-user outbound gateways to ensure all outbound email passes through the organization's mail infrastructure where security controls and monitoring are applied.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Gmail**
3. Click **End User Access** > **Allow per-user outbound gateways**
4. Uncheck **Allow users to send mail through an external SMTP server when configuring a "from" address hosted outside your email domain**
5. Click **Save**

storage_ensure_minimum_tls_version_12.title: Storage account minimum TLS version is 1.2
storage_ensure_minimum_tls_version_12.description: **Azure Storage accounts** enforce a `minimum TLS version` of `1.2` for client connections to data services
storage_ensure_minimum_tls_version_12.risk: Allowing TLS `1.0`/`1.1` enables protocol downgrades and exploitation of known flaws (e.g., BEAST), weakening **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Attackers can intercept or modify data in transit and harvest credentials via weakened cipher suites.

wui.description: Set the storage account `minimum TLS version` to at least `1.2` (prefer `1.3` where supported) and disable legacy protocols. Apply **defense in depth** by restricting network access, using **least privilege** credentials, and monitoring handshake failures to identify outdated clients.

other.description:
1. In the Azure Portal, go to Storage accounts and open your account
2. Select Settings > Configuration
3. Set Minimum TLS version to Version 1.2
4. Click Save

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Storage account with minimum TLS 1.2
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<example_location>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"

  min_tls_version = "TLS1_2" # CRITICAL: Enforces minimum TLS 1.2 to pass the check
}
```

storage_ensure_private_endpoints_in_stor.title: Storage account has private endpoint connections
storage_ensure_private_endpoints_in_stor.description: **Azure Storage accounts** are evaluated for the presence of **Private Endpoint** connections. When configured, traffic flows over a VNet private IP via Private Link; when absent, access occurs through the storage account's public endpoint.
storage_ensure_private_endpoints_in_stor.risk:
Relying on the **public endpoint** widens exposure:
- Confidentiality: higher risk of key/SAS compromise and unauthorized reads
- Integrity: abused creds enable writes/deletes
- Availability: subject to DDoS and internet scanning
It can also bypass egress controls, easing covert data exfiltration.

wui.description:
Prefer **Private Endpoints** for storage access and minimize public exposure:
- Limit or disable `Public network access`
- Use private DNS so names resolve to private IPs
- Enforce **least privilege** and **defense in depth** with segmentation and logging
- Monitor access and rotate keys/SAS *as part of routine hygiene*.

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Storage accounts > select your account
2. Under Security + networking, choose Networking > Private endpoint connections
3. Click + Private endpoint > Create
4. Resource type: Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts; Resource: your account; Target subresource: blob
5. Select the Virtual network and Subnet, then Review + create > Create

signon_global_session_policy_network_zon.title: Default Global Session Policy applies a Network Zone condition aligned with the Access Control Policy
signon_global_session_policy_network_zon.description:
Every active Okta **Global Session Policy** must apply the *IF User's IP is* condition, mapped to a **Network Zone**, on its **Priority 1** active rule.

Unlike the idle / lifetime / cookie STIGs, this control does **not** exclude the built-in `Default Rule`. Okta evaluates policies by group assignment. Aligns with **DISA STIG V-279691**.
signon_global_session_policy_network_zon.risk:
When the Global Session Policy does not restrict access by **Network Zone**, every authenticated entity establishes a session regardless of source IP.

- **Stolen credentials** reach the Okta dashboard from any internet-routable address
- **Out-of-band sessions** bypass the organization's Access Control Policy
- **Network anomalies** cannot become deny decisions at sign-on

wui.description:
Configure the **Priority 1** active rule in each Global Session Policy so it:
- Maps the *IF User's IP is* condition to a **Network Zone** aligned with the organization's Access Control Policy
- Uses `In zone` for allow-list zones and `Not in zone` for deny-list zones
- Is enabled (`ACTIVE`) and evaluated before the built-in `Default Rule`, or *is* the `Default Rule` itself

Review group assignments to confirm the rule actually governs the intended users.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the **Okta Admin Console** as a *Super Admin*.
2. Navigate to **Security** > **Networks** and define the **Network Zones** (allow / deny) that match the organization's Access Control Policy.
3. Navigate to **Security** > **Global Session Policy**.
4. Open the **Default Policy** (and repeat for every other active policy).
5. Edit the rule that sits at **Priority 1**, or add a new one and move it to **Priority 1**.
6. Under *Conditions*, set *IF User's IP is* to `In zone` (allow) or `Not in zone` (deny) and select the **Network Zone**.
7. Save the rule.

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "okta_policy_rule_signon" "<example_resource_name>" {
  policy_id          = okta_policy_signon.default.id
  name               = "<example_resource_name>"
  status             = "ACTIVE"
  priority           = 1                               # Critical: rule must sit at Priority 1
  network_connection = "ZONE"                          # Critical: bind the rule to a Network Zone
  network_includes   = [okta_network_zone.allowed.id]  # Critical: zones that reflect the Access Control Policy
}
```

bedrock_guardrails_configured.title: Bedrock has at least one guardrail configured in the audited region
bedrock_guardrails_configured.description:
**Amazon Bedrock guardrails** provide reusable safety policies for filtering harmful or unwanted content in model inputs and outputs.

This evaluation checks whether at least one guardrail exists in each successfully scanned region. It does **not** verify that guardrails are attached to agents or passed on individual model invocation API calls.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Runtime Behavior Analysis
bedrock_guardrails_configured.risk: Without any configured **Bedrock guardrails** in a region, teams lack a native reusable policy object for **content filtering** and **safety controls**. Applications may invoke models without standardized protections against **harmful content**, **prompt injection**, or **sensitive-data exposure** unless equivalent controls are enforced elsewhere.

wui.description:
Create at least one **Bedrock guardrail** in each region where Bedrock is used, then separately ensure those guardrails are attached to relevant agents and invocation paths.
- Configure **content filters** for harmful categories (hate, violence, sexual, misconduct)
- Add **sensitive information filters** and **denied topic policies**
- Apply guardrails at the API call level using `guardrailIdentifier` where supported

other.description:
1. Open the AWS Console and go to Amazon Bedrock
2. Select **Guardrails** from the navigation pane
3. Click **Create guardrail**
4. Configure content filters for harmful categories
5. Set input and output messaging for blocked content
6. Click **Create guardrail**

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
Resources:
  example_resource:
    Type: AWS::Bedrock::Guardrail
    Properties:
      Name: example_resource
      BlockedInputMessaging: "Blocked"
      BlockedOutputsMessaging: "Blocked"
      ContentPolicyConfig:
        FiltersConfig:
          - Type: HATE
            InputStrength: HIGH       # Critical: configures content filtering
            OutputStrength: HIGH
```

bedrock_guardrails_configured.notes: This check validates guardrail existence per successfully scanned region. It does not verify attachment to agents or the use of guardrails on model invocations. Regions where Bedrock guardrails cannot be enumerated are skipped to avoid false failures.

network_flow_log_more_than_90_days.title: Network Watcher has all flow logs enabled with retention set to 0 or at least 90 days
network_flow_log_more_than_90_days.description: **Azure Network Watcher** has **flow logs** enabled for supported targets, such as **virtual networks** and **network security groups**, and configured to retain for at least `90` days (or `0` for unlimited). The evaluation checks that flow logging is enabled and that the retention policy meets the required duration for each configured log.
network_flow_log_more_than_90_days.risk:
Absent or short-retained **flow logs** reduce visibility into IP flows, delaying detection of port scans, brute force, data exfiltration, and lateral movement.

Forensics and accountability degrade, threatening **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

cli.description: az network watcher flow-log create --location <LOCATION> --name <example_flow_log_name> --target-resource-id <example_target_resource_id> --storage-account <example_storage_account_id> --enabled true --retention 90

wui.description: Enable **flow logs** and keep retention `90` days (`0` for unlimited) for supported targets, including **virtual networks** and **network security groups**. Restrict and monitor access to logs, store immutably, and stream to a SIEM to detect anomalies. Apply **defense in depth** and **least privilege**. Prefer **virtual network flow logs** for new deployments as NSG flow logs are being retired.

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Network Watcher > Flow logs
2. Select the relevant flow log or create one for the target resource, such as a virtual network or network security group
3. Set Status to On
4. Set Retention (days) to 0 (unlimited) or at least 90
5. Select a Storage account
6. Click Save or Review + create

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Enable flow logs with retention >= 90 days
resource "azurerm_network_watcher_flow_log" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                 = "<example_resource_name>"
  network_watcher_name = "<example_network_watcher_name>"
  resource_group_name  = "<example_resource_group_name>"
  target_resource_id   = "<example_target_resource_id>"
  storage_account_id   = "<example_storage_account_id>"

  enabled = true

  retention_policy {
    enabled = true
    days    = 90
  }
}
```

network_flow_log_more_than_90_days.notes: Longer retention improves investigation depth but increases storage cost. For new Azure deployments, prefer virtual network flow logs where they satisfy your monitoring requirements because NSG flow logs are on the retirement path.

storage_ensure_soft_delete_is_enabled.title: Storage account has soft delete for containers enabled
storage_ensure_soft_delete_is_enabled.description: **Azure Storage accounts** have **container soft delete** enabled via a retention policy that keeps deleted containers for a set period.
storage_ensure_soft_delete_is_enabled.risk: Without this, container deletions are permanent, reducing **availability** and **integrity**. A compromised user or faulty automation could erase entire datasets, forcing slow restores from backups and extending RTO/RPO, with potential downstream app outages.

cli.description: az storage account blob-service-properties update --resource-group <example_resource_name> --account-name <example_resource_name> --enable-container-delete-retention true --container-delete-retention-days 7

wui.description: Enable **container soft delete** and choose a retention window (`7-365` days) that meets your RPO. Pair with **blob soft delete** and **versioning** for layered recovery. Enforce **least privilege** on delete actions and apply resource **locks** to prevent destructive changes.

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and open <storage account>
2. Under Data management, select Data protection
3. In the Containers section, turn on Soft delete for containers and set Retention (days) to a value (e.g., 7)
4. Click Save

storage_ensure_soft_delete_is_enabled.notes: Additional storage costs may be incurred as snapshots are retained.

signon_global_session_cookies_not_persis.title: Default Global Session Policy has a Priority 1 non-default rule disabling persistent global session cookies
signon_global_session_cookies_not_persis.description:
Every active Okta **Global Session Policy** needs a **Priority 1** rule that is **not** the built-in `Default Rule`, setting *Okta global session cookies persist across browser sessions* to `Disabled`.

Okta evaluates policies by group assignment, so a permissive custom policy can govern users. Aligns with **DISA STIG V-273206 / OKTA-APP-001710**.
signon_global_session_cookies_not_persis.risk:
Persistent global session cookies keep an authenticated Okta session alive across browser restarts.

- **Surviving sessions** outlive the browsing context the user expected
- **Cached authorization decisions** remain in effect after the browser closes
- **Forgotten or shared devices** continue to hold authenticated access until cookies expire on their own

wui.description:
Configure each active **Global Session Policy** so a non-default rule at **Priority 1**:
- Sets *Okta global session cookies persist across browser sessions* to `Disabled`
- Is enabled (`ACTIVE`) and evaluated before the built-in `Default Rule`

Review group assignments to confirm the rule actually governs the intended users.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the **Okta Admin Console** as a *Super Admin*.
2. Navigate to **Security** > **Global Session Policy**.
3. Open the **Default Policy** (and repeat for every other active policy).
4. Add or edit a non-default rule.
5. Move that rule to **Priority 1** so it is evaluated before the built-in `Default Rule`.
6. Set *Okta global session cookies persist across browser sessions* to `Disabled`.
7. Save the rule.

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "okta_policy_rule_signon" "<example_resource_name>" {
  policy_id          = okta_policy_signon.default.id
  name               = "<example_resource_name>"
  status             = "ACTIVE"
  priority           = 1       # Critical: rule must sit at Priority 1 before the Default Rule
  session_persistent = false   # Critical: disable persistent global session cookies
}
```

signon_global_session_lifetime_18h.title: Default Global Session Policy has a Priority 1 non-default rule limiting session lifetime to 18 hours
signon_global_session_lifetime_18h.description:
Every active Okta **Global Session Policy** needs a **Priority 1** rule that is **not** the built-in `Default Rule`, setting *Maximum Okta global session lifetime* to `18` hours or less.

Okta evaluates policies by group assignment, so a permissive custom policy can govern users. Threshold override: `okta_max_session_lifetime_minutes` (minutes). Aligns with **DISA STIG V-273203**.
signon_global_session_lifetime_18h.risk:
Without an enforced session lifetime, an authenticated Okta session can be reused indefinitely without reauthentication.

- **Stolen session material** continues to grant access long after sign-in
- **Authorization changes** (role revocation, group removal) take effect only on the next reauth
- **Token replay** against downstream apps stays viable for the session window

wui.description:
Configure each active **Global Session Policy** so a non-default rule at **Priority 1**:
- Sets *Maximum Okta global session lifetime* to `18` hours or less (`1080` minutes)
- Never sets the lifetime to `0`, which disables the limit
- Is enabled (`ACTIVE`) and evaluated before the built-in `Default Rule`

Review group assignments to confirm the rule actually governs the intended users.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the **Okta Admin Console** as a *Super Admin*.
2. Navigate to **Security** > **Global Session Policy**.
3. Open the **Default Policy** (and repeat for every other active policy).
4. Add or edit a non-default rule.
5. Move that rule to **Priority 1** so it is evaluated before the built-in `Default Rule`.
6. Set *Maximum Okta global session lifetime* to `18` hours or less. Do **not** set it to `0`, which disables the limit.
7. Save the rule.

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "okta_policy_rule_signon" "<example_resource_name>" {
  policy_id          = okta_policy_signon.default.id
  name               = "<example_resource_name>"
  status             = "ACTIVE"
  priority           = 1       # Critical: rule must sit at Priority 1 before the Default Rule
  session_lifetime   = 1080    # Critical: 18 hours in minutes; do not use 0 (disables the limit)
  session_persistent = false   # Critical: avoid persistent global session cookies
}
```

signon_dod_warning_banner_configured.title: Okta sign-in page displays the Standard Mandatory DOD Notice and Consent Banner
signon_dod_warning_banner_configured.description:
Each Okta brand's sign-in page must present the **Standard Mandatory DOD Notice and Consent Banner** (`DTM-08-060`) before granting access.

The check inspects the sign-in page HTML returned by the Okta Management API, using the *customized* page when present and otherwise falling back to the *default* sign-in page.

Aligns with **DISA STIG V-273192 / OKTA-APP-000200**.
signon_dod_warning_banner_configured.risk:
Without the **DOD Notice and Consent Banner**, users are not informed that the system is a U.S. Government information system subject to monitoring.

- **Legal basis** for incident response and prosecution is weakened
- **Alignment** with federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, and standards is broken
- **Implied consent** to monitoring cannot be asserted on connection

wui.description:
Customize the Okta sign-in page for **each brand** to display the **Standard Mandatory DOD Notice and Consent Banner** (`DTM-08-060`) before users authenticate.

Applies only to Okta tenants under **U.S. Department of Defense** scope; non-DOD organizations can mute this check.

other.description:
1. Follow the supplemental *Okta DOD Warning Banner Configuration Guide* shipped with the **DISA Okta IDaaS STIG** package.
2. Sign in to the **Okta Admin Console** as a *Super Admin*.
3. Navigate to **Customizations** > **Brands** and select the brand.
4. Edit the **Sign-in page** customization.
5. Insert the full `DTM-08-060` Standard Mandatory DOD Notice and Consent Banner text into the page content.
6. Publish the customization and verify the banner is presented before sign-in.

signon_dod_warning_banner_configured.notes: Applicable only to Okta tenants under U.S. Department of Defense scope (DISA Okta IDaaS STIG, control V-273192 / OKTA-APP-000200). For non-DOD organizations this check is not applicable and can be muted.

sites_service_disabled.title: Service status for Google Sites is set to off
sites_service_disabled.description: The domain-wide Google Sites configuration has the service **disabled for all users**. Google Sites allows users to create internal and external websites, which may expose sensitive information or create unmanaged content outside the organization's control.
sites_service_disabled.risk: When Google Sites is enabled, users can create websites that may **inadvertently expose internal information** to external parties. These sites can be difficult to track and manage, creating potential **data leakage vectors** outside the organization's standard content management controls.

wui.description: Disable **Google Sites** for all users to reduce the organization's attack surface. If specific users require access, enable it by exception for those users or groups only.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Sites**
3. Click **Service status**
4. Select **OFF for everyone**
5. Click **Save**

additionalservices_external_groups_disab.title: Access to external Google Groups is off for everyone
additionalservices_external_groups_disab.description: The Additional Google services configuration **disables access to external Google Groups** for all users. This setting controls whether users can access groups created outside the organization from their Google Workspace account.
additionalservices_external_groups_disab.risk: When external Google Groups access is enabled, users can access and participate in groups created **outside the organization**, potentially exposing them to **phishing, social engineering, or data leakage** through unmanaged external group communications.

wui.description: Disable access to **external Google Groups** for all users. If specific users require access to external groups, enable it by exception for those users or groups only.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace** > **Additional Google services**
3. Scroll down to **Google Groups**
4. Set it to **OFF for everyone**
5. Click **Save**

additionalservices_external_groups_disab.notes: This check covers the 'Additional Google services > Google Groups' toggle, which is distinct from the 'Groups for Business' sharing settings covered by the groups service checks.

marketplace_apps_access_restricted.title: Users access to Google Workspace Marketplace apps is restricted
marketplace_apps_access_restricted.description: The domain-wide Google Workspace Marketplace configuration **restricts which apps users can install**. Only admin-approved apps from the Marketplace allowlist are permitted, preventing users from installing unvetted third-party applications.
marketplace_apps_access_restricted.risk: Allowing unrestricted Marketplace app installation exposes the organization to **unvetted third-party applications** that may request broad OAuth scopes, potentially gaining access to **sensitive organizational data** including emails, documents, and calendar events without proper security review.

wui.description: Restrict **Marketplace app installation** to only **admin-approved apps** to prevent users from installing unvetted third-party applications that could access sensitive organizational data.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Apps** > **Google Workspace Marketplace apps**
3. Click **Settings**
4. Under **Manage Google Workspace Marketplace allowlist access**, select **Allow users to install and run only selected apps from the Marketplace**
5. Click **Save**

storage_blob_public_access_level_is_disa.title: Storage account has 'Allow Blob Anonymous Access' disabled
storage_blob_public_access_level_is_disa.description: **Azure Storage accounts** with **blob anonymous (public) access** disabled prevent containers or blobs from being set to a public access level. Setting `allowBlobPublicAccess` to `false` enforces no anonymous reads across the account. This is independent from the account's 'Public Network Access' setting, which is evaluated by storage_account_public_network_access_disabled.
storage_blob_public_access_level_is_disa.risk:
Allowing public access permits unauthenticated users to read blob data or enumerate container contents when any container is made public, compromising confidentiality.

Exposed objects can be scraped at scale, enabling data exfiltration and intelligence gathering without audit attribution.

wui.description: Disable **blob public access** at the account and enforce authenticated access based on **least privilege**. Prefer **private endpoints** or restricted networks, use short-lived `SAS` or federated identities, and apply **RBAC** with container-level permissions. Monitor access and review exposure regularly.

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Storage accounts and select the target account
2. Under Settings, open Configuration
3. Set "Allow Blob public access" to Disabled
4. Click Save

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                     = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name      = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                 = "<example_location>"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"
  allow_blob_public_access = false # Critical: disables anonymous/public blob access
}
```

storage_blob_public_access_level_is_disa.notes: This check evaluates the 'Allow Blob Anonymous Access' (allowBlobPublicAccess) setting. The account's 'Public Network Access' (publicNetworkAccess) setting is evaluated by storage_account_public_network_access_disabled.

storage_smb_channel_encryption_with_secu.title: Storage account uses AES-256-GCM for SMB channel encryption on file shares
storage_smb_channel_encryption_with_secu.description:
**Azure Storage file shares (SMB)** are evaluated for **SMB channel encryption** and whether the allowed ciphers include the recommended `AES-256-GCM`.

This identifies if encryption is configured and a secure algorithm is present in the SMB settings for file shares within the storage account.
storage_smb_channel_encryption_with_secu.risk: Missing or weak SMB channel encryption undermines **confidentiality** and **integrity**. On-path attackers could read sensitive files, capture hashes, or modify data in transit. Allowing legacy ciphers increases downgrade risks and can facilitate **lateral movement**, eroding trust boundaries across networks.

cli.description: az storage account file-service-properties update --resource-group <resource-group> --account-name <storage-account> --channel-encryption AES-256-GCM

wui.description:
Enforce **defense in depth** by restricting SMB channel encryption to `AES-256-GCM` on SMB `3.1.1`, removing weaker options.

- Prefer private access (private endpoints/VPN)
- Require secure transfer and modern TLS
- Apply **least privilege** on shares
- Validate client support and monitor connections during rollout

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, open your storage account
2. Go to Data storage > File shares
3. Under File share settings, click Security
4. Select Custom
5. Under SMB channel encryption, select AES-256-GCM
6. Click Save

storage_smb_channel_encryption_with_secu.notes: This check passes only if every SMB channel encryption algorithm allowed on the file shares is in the recommended list, which is configurable via azure.recommended_smb_channel_encryption_algorithms and defaults to AES-256-GCM only, as required by CIS.

storage_account_public_network_access_di.title: Storage account has 'Public Network Access' disabled
storage_account_public_network_access_di.description: **Azure Storage accounts** with **public network access** disabled cannot be reached from public networks. Setting `publicNetworkAccess` to `Disabled` overrides the public access settings of individual containers and forces access through private endpoints or trusted services. This is independent from the 'Allow Blob Anonymous Access' setting.
storage_account_public_network_access_di.risk:
Leaving **public network access** enabled exposes the storage account endpoints to the **public Internet**, widening the attack surface and undermining **defense in depth**.

This increases the risk of **unauthorized access**, **data exfiltration**, and reconnaissance against the account, especially when combined with weak network rules or overly permissive access policies.

wui.description: Disable **public network access** on the storage account and reach it through **private endpoints** or trusted Azure services only. Combine this with **least privilege** RBAC, short-lived `SAS` tokens, and network restrictions. Validate client connectivity before disabling public access in production.

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Storage accounts and select the target account
2. Under Security + networking, click Networking
3. Set Public network access to Disabled
4. Click Save

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                          = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name           = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                      = "<example_location>"
  account_tier                  = "Standard"
  account_replication_type      = "LRS"
  public_network_access_enabled = false # Critical: disables public network access
}
```

storage_account_public_network_access_di.notes: This check evaluates the storage account publicNetworkAccess property. It is independent from the 'Allow Blob Anonymous Access' setting evaluated by storage_blob_public_access_level_is_disabled.

ec2_instance_with_outdated_ami.title: EC2 instance uses a non-deprecated Amazon AMI
ec2_instance_with_outdated_ami.description: **EC2 instances** launched from **Amazon-owned AMIs** are evaluated for the AMI's `DeprecationTime`; instances tied to images with a deprecation date in the past are reported as using **deprecated AMIs**.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
ec2_instance_with_outdated_ami.risk:
Running on a **deprecated AMI** undermines security and availability:
- Missing patches enable exploitation of known CVEs (confidentiality/integrity)
- Unsupported components hinder hardening and forensics
- AMI removal from catalogs complicates scale-out and recovery (availability)

wui.description: Adopt **non-deprecated, maintained AMIs** and perform rolling replacements of affected instances. Standardize on hardened golden images with **regular AMI rotation** and `DeprecationTime` monitoring. Update launch templates/ASGs to reference current images. Automate patching via an image pipeline and apply **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. In the EC2 console, go to AMIs
2. Set Owner to "Amazon" and ensure deprecated AMIs are not included; copy the AMI ID
3. If using an Auto Scaling Group:
   - Launch templates > select the one in use > Create new version with Image ID set to the copied AMI and set it as default
   - Auto Scaling Groups > select the group > Start instance refresh
4. If it is a standalone instance:
   - Launch a new instance using the copied Amazon AMI
   - Move workloads and terminate the old instance

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# Use a non-deprecated Amazon AMI for instances launched via this template
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::EC2::LaunchTemplate
    Properties:
      LaunchTemplateData:
        ImageId: "<non_deprecated_amazon_ami_id>"  # Critical: Amazon-owned AMI with no DeprecationTime
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# EC2 instance using a non-deprecated Amazon AMI
resource "aws_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  ami           = "<non_deprecated_amazon_ami_id>"  # Critical: Amazon-owned AMI with no DeprecationTime
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
}
```

aks_cluster_rbac_enabled.title: AKS cluster has RBAC enabled
aks_cluster_rbac_enabled.description:
**AKS clusters** with **Kubernetes RBAC** enforce authorization through roles and bindings mapped to identities and groups.

This evaluates whether the cluster has RBAC enabled to control access to namespaces and cluster-wide resources.
aks_cluster_rbac_enabled.risk: Without **Kubernetes RBAC**, authorization becomes overly broad, weakening **least privilege**. Compromised credentials could read secrets, alter workloads, or delete services, impacting **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and **availability**, and enabling lateral movement across the cluster.

wui.description:
Enable **Kubernetes RBAC** and design permissions with **least privilege**: scope roles to namespaces, grant access via groups, apply deny-by-default, and separate duties for admins and operators.

Integrate with **Microsoft Entra ID** and review/audit role bindings to maintain **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. In Azure portal, go to Kubernetes services > Create (or edit your deployment template)
2. On the Authentication tab, set Kubernetes RBAC to Enabled
3. Review + Create to deploy (re-create the cluster if the setting can't be changed on an existing one)

aks_clusters_created_with_private_nodes.title: AKS cluster nodes do not have public IP addresses
aks_clusters_created_with_private_nodes.description: **AKS agent pools** use only private addressing, with node public IP assignment disabled (`enableNodePublicIP=false`). Clusters where any pool assigns a public IP to nodes are identified.
aks_clusters_created_with_private_nodes.risk: **Public node IPs** expose worker VMs to Internet scanning and exploit attempts against OS or kubelet services. Successful compromise can lead to stolen secrets and images (**confidentiality**), workload tampering (**integrity**), and node/resource exhaustion via DDoS or cryptomining (**availability**).

wui.description: Disable **public node IPs** on all agent pools (`enableNodePublicIP=false`) and route egress via a **NAT gateway** or **Azure Firewall**. Apply **least privilege** with NSGs blocking Internet ingress, use **private endpoints** and **bastion/VPN** for admin access, and adopt **defense in depth** with continuous hardening and monitoring.

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Kubernetes services > <your AKS cluster> > Node pools
2. For any node pool showing Node public IP: Enabled, click Add node pool
3. Create the new pool with the same size/count; set Node public IP to Disabled (or uncheck Enable node public IP)
4. Wait until the new pool is Ready
5. If replacing a system pool, set the new pool to Mode: System (or Set as default system pool)
6. Delete the old node pool(s) that had Node public IP enabled
7. Verify all node pools show Node public IP: Disabled

image_DS-0014.title: RUN using 'wget' and 'curl'
image_DS-0014.description: Avoid using both 'wget' and 'curl' since these tools have the same effect.

wui.description: Pick one util, either 'wget' or 'curl'

codepipeline_project_repo_private.title: CodePipeline pipeline should use private repository source with authenticated connection
codepipeline_project_repo_private.description: **CodePipeline pipeline** should configure its **source stage** to use a **private repository** with authenticated connection rather than a public GitHub or GitLab repository. This ensures deployment configurations, build artifacts, and CI/CD logic remain protected from unauthorized access.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
codepipeline_project_repo_private.risk: Using **public repositories** as pipeline sources exposes deployment configurations and CI/CD workflows to the internet, increasing risk of **supply chain attacks**, **credential exposure**, and **intellectual property theft**. Adversaries can inject malicious code or leverage exposed secrets to compromise production systems.

cli.description:
aws codestar-connections create-connection --provider-type GitHub --connection-name my-github-connection
aws codepipeline update-pipeline --pipeline file://pipeline-config.json

wui.description:
Configure CodePipeline source stages to use **private repositories** with **AWS CodeStar Connections** for GitHub or GitLab.

Apply **least privilege** to connection permissions, enable **branch protection**, require **code review**, use **signed commits**, and monitor pipeline execution logs. Consider **AWS CodeCommit** for fully managed private Git hosting with native IAM integration.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, navigate to **Developer Tools** → **Connections**
2. Click **Create connection**
3. Choose provider (GitHub or GitLab) and click **Connect**
4. Authorize AWS to access your private repositories
5. Navigate to **CodePipeline** → **Pipelines** and select your pipeline
6. Click **Edit**
7. In the **Source** stage, click **Edit action**
8. Change **Action provider** to **GitHub (Version 2)** or **GitLab**
9. Select **Connection** and choose the connection created in step 4
10. Configure **Repository name** (private repo) and **Branch name**
11. Click **Done** and **Save** the pipeline

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Configure pipeline with private repository via CodeStar Connection
Resources:
  MyConnection:
    Type: AWS::CodeStarConnections::Connection
    Properties:
      ConnectionName: my-github-connection
      ProviderType: GitHub  # or GitLab

  MyPipeline:
    Type: AWS::CodePipeline::Pipeline
    Properties:
      Stages:
        - Name: Source
          Actions:
            - Name: SourceAction
              ActionTypeId:
                Category: Source
                Owner: AWS
                Provider: CodeStarSourceConnection
                Version: 1
              Configuration:
                ConnectionArn: !GetAtt MyConnection.ConnectionArn
                FullRepositoryId: myorg/myrepo  # Private repository
                BranchName: main
```

codepipeline_project_repo_private.notes: This check evaluates CodePipeline source actions that use GitHub or GitLab providers. It detects public repositories by checking repository visibility settings via CodeStar Connections API.

directory_super_admin_only_admin_roles.title: All super admin accounts are used only for super admin activities
directory_super_admin_only_admin_roles.description: Super admin accounts do not also hold **additional admin roles** such as Groups Admin, User Management Admin, etc. Each super administrator has a separate, non-admin account for daily activities, following the **principle of least privilege**.
directory_super_admin_only_admin_roles.risk: A super admin account that also holds additional admin roles increases the **attack surface** for phishing and credential theft. Compromising a single dual-role account grants full administrative access, bypassing **separation of duties** and enabling unauthorized changes to users, billing, and security settings.

wui.description: Apply the principle of separation of duties by maintaining dedicated super admin accounts exclusively for privileged tasks. Daily administrative activities should be performed from separate accounts with only the delegated roles required.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Google **Admin console** at https://admin.google.com
2. Navigate to **Directory** > **Users**
3. Click on the super admin user who also has additional admin roles
4. Click **Admin roles and privileges**
5. Remove the additional admin roles from the super admin account
6. Create a separate account for daily admin tasks

apigateway_restapi_public_with_authorize.title: API Gateway REST API with a public endpoint has an authorizer configured
apigateway_restapi_public_with_authorize.description:
**API Gateway REST APIs** exposed to the Internet are evaluated for an attached **authorizer** that enforces caller identity (Lambda authorizer or Cognito user pool) on method invocations.

Focus is on whether public endpoints require authenticated requests rather than accepting anonymous calls.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Network Reachability
apigateway_restapi_public_with_authorize.risk:
Without an **authorizer** on a public API, anonymous callers can:
- Read or alter data (confidentiality/integrity)
- Trigger backend actions, impacting systems
- Abuse traffic, degrading availability and inflating costs

Endpoint enumeration also enables broader discovery and lateral movement.

wui.description:
Enforce **authentication** on all Internet-facing APIs by attaching an **authorizer** (Cognito user pool or Lambda) that validates tokens and scopes.

Apply defense in depth:
- Restrictive resource policies and IP controls
- WAF, throttling, quotas, rate limits
- Least-privilege backend access and comprehensive logging

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, open API Gateway and select your REST API
2. In the left pane, click Authorizers > Create authorizer
3. Choose Lambda (TOKEN) or Cognito User Pool
4. For Lambda: select the function and set Identity source to method.request.header.Authorization; for Cognito: select the user pool
5. Click Create authorizer to add it to the API

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Create a minimal Lambda TOKEN authorizer for a public REST API
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::ApiGateway::Authorizer
    Properties:
      Name: <example_resource_name>
      RestApiId: <example_resource_id>
      Type: TOKEN  # Critical: adds an authorizer to the REST API
      IdentitySource: method.request.header.Authorization  # Critical: header to read token from
      AuthorizerUri: arn:aws:apigateway:<region>:lambda:path/2015-03-31/functions/arn:aws:lambda:<region>:<account-id>:function/<example_resource_name>/invocations  # Critical: Lambda authorizer function URI
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: Minimal Lambda TOKEN authorizer for API Gateway REST API
resource "aws_api_gateway_authorizer" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name            = "<example_resource_name>"
  rest_api_id     = "<example_resource_id>"
  type            = "TOKEN"  # Critical: enables a Lambda authorizer on the REST API
  identity_source = "method.request.header.Authorization"  # Critical: header to read token
  authorizer_uri  = "arn:aws:apigateway:<region>:lambda:path/2015-03-31/functions/arn:aws:lambda:<region>:<account-id>:function/<example_resource_name>/invocations"  # Critical: Lambda authorizer function URI
}
```

apigateway_restapi_tracing_enabled.title: API Gateway REST API stage has X-Ray tracing enabled
apigateway_restapi_tracing_enabled.description: **API Gateway REST API stages** have **AWS X-Ray active tracing** enabled to sample incoming requests and produce distributed traces across connected services.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Runtime Behavior Analysis
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
apigateway_restapi_tracing_enabled.risk:
Without X-Ray tracing, you lose end-to-end visibility, hindering detection of timeouts, errors, and anomalous latency.

This delays incident response and root-cause analysis, increasing MTTR and risking partial outages (availability) and undetected integration failures (integrity).

wui.description:
Enable **X-Ray active tracing** on all API Gateway stages and propagate trace context through downstream services.

Use prudent sampling, correlate traces with logs/metrics, and alert on errors/latency. Apply **least privilege** to X-Ray access and use **defense in depth** for observability.

other.description:
1. Open the AWS Console and go to API Gateway
2. Select your REST API and choose Stages
3. Select the target stage
4. Open the Logs/Tracing tab, check Enable X-Ray Tracing
5. Click Save

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable X-Ray tracing on an API Gateway REST API stage
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::ApiGateway::Stage
    Properties:
      RestApiId: <example_resource_id>
      DeploymentId: <example_resource_id>
      StageName: <example_resource_name>
      TracingEnabled: true  # Critical: enables AWS X-Ray tracing for this stage
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Enable X-Ray tracing on an API Gateway REST API stage
resource "aws_api_gateway_stage" "example" {
  rest_api_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  deployment_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  stage_name  = "<example_resource_name>"
  xray_tracing_enabled = true  # Critical: enables AWS X-Ray tracing for this stage
}
```

apim_threat_detection_llm_jacking.title: No potential LLM Jacking attacks detected across all Azure API Management instances
apim_threat_detection_llm_jacking.description: **API Management** diagnostic logs in Log Analytics are analyzed for **LLM-related operations**. Requests are grouped by caller IP, the number of distinct monitored actions (e.g., `ChatCompletions_Create`, `ImageGenerations_Create`) within a configurable `minutes` window is measured, and that ratio is compared to a `threshold` to surface anomalous multi-action patterns.
apim_threat_detection_llm_jacking.risk:
Concentrated LLM activity from one IP indicates **automation or leaked credentials**.
- **Availability/cost**: rapid token burn and quota exhaustion
- **Confidentiality**: exposure of prompts/completions and model details
- **Integrity**: abuse of deployment/model actions enabling unauthorized changes or mass content generation

wui.description:
Adopt **defense in depth** for LLM APIs:
- Enforce **least privilege**; isolate management from inference
- Prefer **managed identities** over keys; rotate secrets
- Apply **quotas**, rate limiting, and IP allowlisting; use private access
- Alert on anomalous action diversity; review logs

*Tune `threshold` and `minutes` for your environment.*

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, open your API Management instance
2. Go to APIs > All APIs
3. Click Policies (Inbound processing)
4. Add a when block to block the offending IP:
   - Condition: @(context.Request.IpAddress == "<OFFENDING_IP>")
   - Action: return-response with status 403 Forbidden
5. Save the policy
6. Re-run the scan after the detection window elapses to confirm PASS

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Global APIM policy that blocks a specific IP
resource "azurerm_api_management_policy" "<example_resource_name>" {
  api_management_id = "<example_resource_id>"

  # Critical: Policy XML that blocks the offending IP by returning 403
  xml_content = <<XML
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <base />
    <choose>
      <!-- Critical: Block offending IP to stop LLM jacking -->
      <when condition="@(context.Request.IpAddress == \"<OFFENDING_IP>\")">
        <return-response>
          <set-status code="403" reason="Forbidden" />
        </return-response>
      </when>
    </choose>
  </inbound>
  <backend><base /></backend>
  <outbound><base /></outbound>
  <on-error><base /></on-error>
</policies>
XML
}
```

apim_threat_detection_llm_jacking.notes: This check requires: 1. APIM diagnostic logging to be enabled and configured to send logs to Log Analytics workspace 2. Log Analytics workspace ID and key to be configured in the audit configuration 3. Appropriate permissions to query Log Analytics workspace

apikeys_key_rotated_in_90_days.title: API key was created within the last 90 days
apikeys_key_rotated_in_90_days.description: **Google Cloud API keys** are evaluated for **rotation age** using their `creation_time`. Keys created within the last `90` days are treated as recently rotated; keys older than `90` days are treated as overdue.
apikeys_key_rotated_in_90_days.risk: Stale, long-lived **API keys** are **bearer tokens** without IAM context. If exposed, attackers can invoke allowed APIs, enabling data exfiltration (**confidentiality**), unauthorized changes (**integrity**), and quota/billing abuse or disruption (**availability**). Lack of rotation prolongs misuse.

wui.description: Rotate API keys at least every `90` days. Prefer **service accounts** or OAuth with short-lived credentials. Enforce **API** and **application/IP restrictions**. Store keys in a **secrets manager**, avoid client-side embedding, and monitor usage. Apply **least privilege** and **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. In the Google Cloud Console, go to APIs & Services > Credentials
2. Under API keys, click the key older than 90 days
3. Click Rotate key, then click Create to generate the new key
4. Copy the new key string and update your applications to use it
5. In the Previous key section, click Delete the previous key
6. Repeat for any remaining API keys older than 90 days until only keys created within 90 days remain

apigateway_restapi_waf_acl_attached.title: API Gateway stage has a WAF Web ACL attached
apigateway_restapi_waf_acl_attached.description: **Amazon API Gateway (REST API)** stages are assessed for an associated **AWS WAF web ACL**. The finding reflects whether a `web ACL` is linked at the stage level.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
apigateway_restapi_waf_acl_attached.risk:
Absent a **WAF web ACL**, APIs are exposed to application-layer threats that impact CIA:
- Confidentiality: data exfiltration via injection
- Integrity: parameter tampering and path traversal
- Availability: L7 floods, bot abuse, resource exhaustion
*Public endpoints face heightened risk.*

wui.description:
Attach an **AWS WAF web ACL** to each exposed stage and apply **defense in depth**:
- Use managed rule groups and tailored allow/deny lists
- Apply rate limiting to throttle abuse
- Enforce least-privilege network exposure
- Continuously tune rules using logs and metrics
*Validate changes to reduce false positives.*

other.description:
1. Open the AWS Console and go to WAF & Shield
2. Select Web ACLs (Scope: Regional), choose your Web ACL
3. Click Add AWS resource
4. Select API Gateway, choose the REST API and the specific Stage
5. Click Add/Associate to attach the Web ACL

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Attach a WAFv2 Web ACL to an API Gateway REST API stage
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::WAFv2::WebACLAssociation
    Properties:
      ResourceArn: arn:aws:apigateway:<example_region>::/restapis/<example_resource_id>/stages/<example_stage_name>  # CRITICAL: target API Gateway stage
      WebACLArn: <example_resource_arn>  # CRITICAL: Web ACL to attach
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Attach a WAFv2 Web ACL to an API Gateway REST API stage
resource "aws_wafv2_web_acl_association" "<example_resource_name>" {
  resource_arn = "arn:aws:apigateway:<example_region>::/restapis/<example_resource_id>/stages/<example_stage_name>" # CRITICAL: target API Gateway stage
  web_acl_arn  = "<example_resource_arn>" # CRITICAL: Web ACL to attach
}
```

compliances.name: AWS Well Architected Framework Security Pillar

clusters_authentication_enabled.title: Cluster has authentication enabled
clusters_authentication_enabled.description:
**MongoDB Atlas clusters** enforce **database authentication** for client connections (`authEnabled`).

Identifies clusters where authentication is not required for access.
clusters_authentication_enabled.risk: Without authentication, anyone with network reach can access the database, compromising **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Attackers can exfiltrate data, modify or delete records, and create backdoor users, leading to outages and data loss that impact **availability**.

wui.description:
Enable and enforce **database authentication** on all clusters.
- Prefer strong methods (X.509, OIDC, AWS IAM) over static passwords
- Grant **least privilege** roles and avoid shared accounts
- Rotate credentials/keys
- Combine with IP access lists or private endpoints for **defense in depth**

other.description:
1. In the Atlas UI, open your project and go to Security > Database Access
2. Click Add New Database User
3. Select Username/Password, enter a username and password
4. Assign a role (e.g., readWriteAnyDatabase on admin)
5. Click Add User to save

This creates a database user, enabling authentication for the cluster

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Create a MongoDB Atlas database user to enable authentication
resource "mongodbatlas_database_user" "example_resource_name" {
  project_id         = "<example_resource_id>"
  username           = "<example_resource_name>"
  password           = "<PASSWORD>"
  auth_database_name = "admin"  # Critical: SCRAM user on admin enables DB auth

  roles {                         # Minimal role assignment required to create the user
    role_name     = "readWriteAnyDatabase"
    database_name = "admin"
  }
}
```

clusters_backup_enabled.title: Cluster has backup enabled
clusters_backup_enabled.description: **MongoDB Atlas clusters** have **automated backups** enabled (`cloudBackup`/`backup_enabled`) to generate snapshots and support restore operations
clusters_backup_enabled.risk: Without **backups**, deleted or corrupted records are irrecoverable, undermining **integrity**. Failures or bad deployments can cause prolonged **unavailability** with no restore path. Lacking **point-in-time recovery** prevents precise rollbacks, amplifying the blast radius of mistakes or ransomware.

wui.description: Enable **Cloud Backups** on all production clusters and define backup schedules and retention that meet business **RPO/RTO**. For critical data, enable **point-in-time recovery**. Apply **least privilege** and **separation of duties** to backup access, protect against deletion with policy, monitor backup health, and perform regular test restores.

other.description:
1. Sign in to MongoDB Atlas and open your project
2. Go to Database > Clusters
3. For the target cluster, click the three dots (...) > Edit Configuration
4. Under Additional Settings, toggle Cloud Backup to On
5. Click Save Changes

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "mongodbatlas_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  project_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  name       = "<example_resource_name>"

  cloud_backup = true  # Critical: enables Cloud Backups so the check passes
}
```

clusters_encryption_at_rest_enabled.title: Cluster has encryption at rest enabled with a supported provider or EBS volume encryption
clusters_encryption_at_rest_enabled.description: **MongoDB Atlas clusters** are evaluated for **encryption at rest**. The check looks for a supported encryption provider configured (not `NONE`) or storage-level encryption enabled (e.g., `encryptEBSVolume=true`). Unsupported providers or explicit disablement are highlighted.
clusters_encryption_at_rest_enabled.risk: Absent or misconfigured at-rest encryption allows disks and snapshots to be read if storage, backups, or images are accessed by attackers or insiders. This exposes sensitive records, erodes **confidentiality**, and enables quiet **data exfiltration** after host or control-plane compromise.

wui.description: Enable **encryption at rest** with a supported provider and prefer **customer-managed keys** to control lifecycle and access. Apply least-privilege to key usage, restrict KMS connectivity, and monitor key health and rotation. If using AWS, also ensure volumes are encrypted. This enforces defense-in-depth and data confidentiality.

other.description:
1. In Atlas, go to Security > Advanced
2. Toggle "Encryption at Rest using your Key Management" to On and enter your provider details (AWS KMS/Azure Key Vault/GCP KMS)
3. Save
4. Go to Database > Clusters, open the menu for <example_resource_name> and click Edit Configuration
5. Expand Additional Settings and set "Manage your own encryption keys" to Yes
6. Review Changes > Apply Changes

GCP-0076.title: Google Compute Subnetwork Logging Disabled
GCP-0076.description: Flow logs for subnets should be enabled to capture network traffic details for security analysis.

wui.description: Enable VPC Flow Logs for subnets.

other.description: Flow logs for subnets should be enabled to capture network traffic details for security analysis.

networking_security_group_allows_rdp_fro.title: Security groups do not allow RDP from the Internet
networking_security_group_allows_rdp_fro.description: **OpenStack security groups** are evaluated to verify that RDP (port 3389) is **not exposed to the Internet** (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0). Security groups act as virtual firewalls controlling Windows instance traffic. Unrestricted RDP access violates least privilege and creates significant attack surface. Best practices recommend restricting RDP to **known IP ranges**, **RD Gateway**, or **VPN**.
networking_security_group_allows_rdp_fro.risk: Unrestricted RDP exposes Windows instances to brute-force attacks, password spraying, and RDP vulnerabilities (BlueKeep, DejaBlue). Compromised sessions enable ransomware deployment, credential theft, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. Successful compromise leads to domain controller access, Active Directory enumeration, and organization-wide data exfiltration.

wui.description: Restrict RDP access to known IP ranges using Remote Desktop Gateway or VPN instead of allowing 0.0.0.0/0. Enable Network Level Authentication (NLA) and implement multi-factor authentication for all RDP sessions. Deploy LAPS for unique local administrator passwords and patch Windows systems regularly to address RDP vulnerabilities.

other.description:
1. Navigate to Network > Security Groups
2. Locate the security group with unrestricted RDP access
3. Click Manage Rules
4. Delete RDP rules with Remote 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0
5. Click Add Rule and create a new RDP rule
6. Set Remote to CIDR with your trusted IP (e.g., 198.51.100.50/32)
7. Save changes and verify connectivity

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: restrict RDP to known IP ranges, never 0.0.0.0/0

resource "openstack_networking_secgroup_v2" "windows_servers" {
  name        = "windows-servers-sg"
  description = "Security group for Windows application servers"
}

# GOOD: RDP restricted to corporate VPN IP range
resource "openstack_networking_secgroup_rule_v2" "rdp_from_vpn" {
  direction         = "ingress"
  ethertype         = "IPv4"
  protocol          = "tcp"
  port_range_min    = 3389
  port_range_max    = 3389
  remote_ip_prefix  = "10.8.0.0/24"  # VPN gateway range
  security_group_id = openstack_networking_secgroup_v2.windows_servers.id
}

# GOOD: RDP from RD Gateway security group (reference-based rule)
resource "openstack_networking_secgroup_rule_v2" "rdp_from_rd_gateway" {
  direction         = "ingress"
  ethertype         = "IPv4"
  protocol          = "tcp"
  port_range_min    = 3389
  port_range_max    = 3389
  remote_group_id   = openstack_networking_secgroup_v2.rd_gateway.id  # Reference
  security_group_id = openstack_networking_secgroup_v2.windows_servers.id
}

# Remote Desktop Gateway security group (least privilege)
resource "openstack_networking_secgroup_v2" "rd_gateway" {
  name        = "rd-gateway-sg"
  description = "Security group for Remote Desktop Gateway"
}

# RD Gateway accepts RDP from corporate network only
resource "openstack_networking_secgroup_rule_v2" "rd_gateway_rdp" {
  direction         = "ingress"
  ethertype         = "IPv4"
  protocol          = "tcp"
  port_range_min    = 3389
  port_range_max    = 3389
  remote_ip_prefix  = var.corporate_cidr  # e.g., 198.51.100.0/24
  security_group_id = openstack_networking_secgroup_v2.rd_gateway.id
}

# RD Gateway also needs HTTPS for external RDG clients
resource "openstack_networking_secgroup_rule_v2" "rd_gateway_https" {
  direction         = "ingress"
  ethertype         = "IPv4"
  protocol          = "tcp"
  port_range_min    = 443
  port_range_max    = 443
  remote_ip_prefix  = var.corporate_cidr  # Restrict to corporate IPs
  security_group_id = openstack_networking_secgroup_v2.rd_gateway.id
}

# BAD: Never do this - RDP from anywhere (0.0.0.0/0)
# resource "openstack_networking_secgroup_rule_v2" "rdp_from_anywhere" {
#   direction         = "ingress"
#   ethertype         = "IPv4"
#   protocol          = "tcp"
#   port_range_min    = 3389
#   port_range_max    = 3389
#   remote_ip_prefix  = "0.0.0.0/0"  # DANGEROUS - DO NOT USE
#   security_group_id = openstack_networking_secgroup_v2.windows_servers.id
# }
```

networking_security_group_allows_rdp_fro.notes: This check flags security groups with RDP (port 3389) ingress rules allowing 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. Some architectures legitimately require public RDP access (bastion hosts, RD Gateway, jump servers). Review findings in context of your Windows infrastructure. Rules allowing RDP from specific IPs (e.g., 198.51.100.0/24) or from other security groups (remote_group_id) are not flagged. IPv6 rules (::/0) are also checked. Port ranges that include port 3389 (e.g., 3000-4000) will trigger this check.

blockstorage_volume_multiattach_disabled.title: Block storage volumes do not have multi-attach enabled
blockstorage_volume_multiattach_disabled.description: **OpenStack block storage volumes** are evaluated to verify that **multi-attach** is not enabled. Multi-attach allows a volume to be attached to multiple instances simultaneously, increasing the attack surface and potentially leading to data corruption or unauthorized access from compromised instances.
blockstorage_volume_multiattach_disabled.risk: Multi-attach volumes can be accessed by multiple instances simultaneously, increasing the blast radius if any attached instance is compromised. Data corruption may occur if applications do not implement proper cluster-aware file systems. Unauthorized modifications from one instance can affect all other attached instances.

wui.description: Disable multi-attach on volumes unless specifically required for clustered applications. When multi-attach is necessary, ensure cluster-aware file systems are used and implement strict access controls. Review multi-attach volumes regularly to verify continued business justification.

other.description:
1. Identify volumes with multi-attach enabled
2. Evaluate if multi-attach is truly required for the workload
3. For volumes that do not require multi-attach, migrate data to a new volume without multi-attach
4. Ensure multi-attach volumes use cluster-aware file systems (e.g., GFS2, OCFS2)

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "openstack_blockstorage_volume_v3" "single_attach" {
  name        = "single-attach-volume"
  size        = 10
  multiattach = false
}
```
