2. Set Deployment type to Multi-AZ
3. Select two Subnets in different Availability Zones
4. Set minimal required capacity/throughput and Create
5. Migrate data to the new file system and repoint clients to its DNS name
6. Delete the old Single-AZ file system

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Create FSx for Windows File Server with Multi-AZ
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::FSx::FileSystem
    Properties:
      FileSystemType: WINDOWS
      StorageCapacity: 32
      SubnetIds:
        - <example_subnet_id_1>  # CRITICAL: two subnets -> Multi-AZ across AZs
        - <example_subnet_id_2>  # CRITICAL: two subnets -> Multi-AZ across AZs
      WindowsConfiguration:
        ThroughputCapacity: 8
        DeploymentType: MULTI_AZ_1  # CRITICAL: enables Multi-AZ deployment
        PreferredSubnetId: <example_subnet_id_1>
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: FSx for Windows File Server configured for Multi-AZ
resource "aws_fsx_windows_file_system" "<example_resource_name>" {
  storage_capacity    = 32
  subnet_ids          = ["<example_subnet_id_1>", "<example_subnet_id_2>"] # CRITICAL: two subnets in different AZs
  throughput_capacity = 8
  deployment_type     = "MULTI_AZ_1"                                      # CRITICAL: enables Multi-AZ deployment
  preferred_subnet_id = "<example_subnet_id_1>"
}
```

glue_data_catalogs_not_publicly_accessib.title: Glue Data Catalog is not publicly accessible via its resource policy
glue_data_catalogs_not_publicly_accessib.description:
**AWS Glue Data Catalog** resource policies are assessed for configurations that expose the catalog to anyone, such as `Principal: *`, broad resource scopes, or permissive conditions.

The finding highlights catalogs made public through overly permissive resource-based access.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Network Reachability
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
glue_data_catalogs_not_publicly_accessib.risk: Public catalog access lets unauthorized actors enumerate schemas, S3 locations, and connection metadata, weakening **confidentiality**. If writes are exposed, attackers can alter databases/tables, corrupt lineage, and disrupt jobs and queries, harming **integrity** and **availability**, and enabling lateral movement to data stores.

wui.description:
Enforce **least privilege** on catalog resource policies:
- Avoid `Principal: *` and wildcards
- Grant only required actions to explicit principals
- Prefer identity-based access or Lake Formation for sharing
- Limit scope with precise ARNs/conditions and monitor changes for **defense in depth**

other.description:
1. Sign in to the AWS Console and open the Glue service
2. In the left menu, click Settings
3. Under Data catalog settings > Permissions, click Edit resource policy
4. Remove any statement that has Principal set to * (public) or AWS: "*"; or delete the entire policy
5. Click Save

events_rule_cloudguard_problems.title: Event rule monitoring Cloud Guard problems has notification actions configured
events_rule_cloudguard_problems.description: **OCI Events rules** subscribe to **Cloud Guard problem lifecycle events**-`com.oraclecloud.cloudguard.problemdetected`, `com.oraclecloud.cloudguard.problemdismissed`, and `com.oraclecloud.cloudguard.problemremediated`-and include **notification actions**. *When Cloud Guard sets a reporting region, rules are expected in that region.*
events_rule_cloudguard_problems.risk: Without notifications for Cloud Guard problems, incidents can go unseen, delaying response. Ongoing issues can erode **confidentiality** via data exfiltration, threaten **integrity** through unremediated changes, and impact **availability** by allowing attacks to persist. Silent failures of automated remediation may also go unnoticed.

wui.description: Implement **event-driven alerts** for Cloud Guard problem lifecycle events and route them to trusted **notification channels** and your **SOC/SIEM**. Enforce **least privilege** on publish/subscribe, align rules with the **reporting region**, and use **severity-based filtering** to prioritize response within a **defense-in-depth** approach.

other.description:
1. In the OCI Console, go to Menu > Application Integration > Events Service > Rules
2. Click Create Rule and select the Compartment; switch to the Cloud Guard reporting Region
3. In Conditions, add event types: com.oraclecloud.cloudguard.problemdetected, com.oraclecloud.cloudguard.problemdismissed, com.oraclecloud.cloudguard.problemremediated
4. Under Actions, add Notifications and select the desired Topic
5. Ensure the rule is Enabled and click Create

apiserver_disable_profiling.title: API server pod has profiling disabled (--profiling=false)
apiserver_disable_profiling.description: **Kubernetes API server** runtime profiling is controlled by the `--profiling` flag. The evaluation inspects API server container arguments to confirm `--profiling=false` and that profiling endpoints (such as `/debug/pprof`) are not enabled.
apiserver_disable_profiling.risk: With profiling enabled, `/debug/pprof` exposes stack traces, heap data, and request details that can leak secrets and topology, degrading **confidentiality**. Heavy profiling queries can exhaust CPU and memory, threatening **availability**. Insight into code paths and timings can aid exploitation, affecting **integrity** of the control plane.

wui.description:
Keep API server profiling disabled by default. *If diagnostics are required*, enable it briefly in a controlled, isolated environment.

Apply **least privilege** to debug access, restrict exposure via network controls, and audit usage. Use **defense in depth** and separation of duties for any profiling enablement.

other.description:
1. SSH to the control plane node
2. Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. In spec.containers[0].command, add: `--profiling=false`
4. Save the file; the kubelet will restart the API server automatically
5. Verify the flag is active: `ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -- '--profiling=false'`

apiserver_disable_profiling.notes: Profiling is enabled by default in Kubernetes. Disabling it when not needed helps in securing the cluster.

aks_clusters_public_access_disabled.title: AKS cluster has a private endpoint and node public access is disabled
aks_clusters_public_access_disabled.description:
**AKS clusters** expose a **private control plane FQDN** and agent pools have `enable_node_public_ip=false`.

The evaluation focuses on the presence of a private FQDN and the absence of public IPs on nodes.
aks_clusters_public_access_disabled.risk:
Exposed node IPs or a publicly reachable API increase attack surface, impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity**.
- Internet scans reach kubelet, NodePort, or management agents
- Exploits enable RCE and **lateral movement**
- Metadata/secret theft leads to **credential compromise**

**Availability** is at risk from DDoS on exposed endpoints.

wui.description:
Adopt **private clusters** and eliminate node public IPs:
- Set `enable_node_public_ip=false` on all pools
- Use **Private Link** or peered VNets with VPN/ExpressRoute for admin access
- If public API is unavoidable, restrict with IP ranges and strong auth
- Enforce NSGs/firewalls and **least privilege** for layered defense

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Azure Kubernetes Service and select your cluster
2. Go to Networking > API server access
3. Set Private cluster to Enabled and click Save
4. Go to Node pools, open each pool, select Networking, set Public IP per node to Disabled, and Save
5. Repeat step 4 for all node pools

apiserver_encryption_provider_config_set.title: API server pod has the --encryption-provider-config argument set
apiserver_encryption_provider_config_set.description: **Kubernetes API server** pods include `--encryption-provider-config`, supplying an EncryptionConfiguration to apply **encryption at rest** to selected API resources stored in etcd.
apiserver_encryption_provider_config_set.risk: Absent an encryption provider, **Secrets and credentials** are stored in plaintext in etcd and backups. Access to etcd, control plane disks, or snapshots can expose keys and tokens, enabling unauthorized API calls and lateral movement, compromising **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

wui.description: Enable **encryption at rest** with an `EncryptionConfiguration` and run with `--encryption-provider-config` using a non-`identity` provider (prefer `kms v2`). Apply **least privilege** to key/KMS access, rotate keys, restrict config file access, keep settings consistent across API servers, and re-encrypt existing objects.

other.description:
1. SSH to each control-plane node
2. Create the encryption config file at /etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml:
   ```yaml
   apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
   kind: EncryptionConfiguration
   resources:
   - resources: ["secrets"]
     providers:
     - aescbc:
         keys:
         - name: key1
           secret: <BASE64_32_BYTE_KEY>
     - identity: {}
   ```
3. Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml and:
   - Add the flag under the kube-apiserver container command:
     ```
     - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml
     ```
   - Mount the config path:
     ```yaml
     volumeMounts:
     - name: enc
       mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/enc
       readOnly: true
     ...
     volumes:
     - name: enc
       hostPath:
         path: /etc/kubernetes/enc
         type: DirectoryOrCreate
     ```
   Save the file; the kubelet will restart the API server.
4. Repeat on all control-plane nodes.

apiserver_encryption_provider_config_set.notes: Ensure that the EncryptionConfig file is correctly configured and securely stored.

guardduty_no_high_severity_findings.title: GuardDuty detector has no high severity findings
guardduty_no_high_severity_findings.description: **GuardDuty detectors** are evaluated for the presence of **High-severity findings**. This surfaces whether any detector currently has findings labeled `High` by GuardDuty.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Runtime Behavior Analysis
guardduty_no_high_severity_findings.risk:
Unresolved **High findings** often signal active compromise, enabling:
- Data exfiltration and unauthorized access (confidentiality)
- Privilege escalation and tampering (integrity)
- Disruption via malware/crypto-mining (availability)

Attackers can pivot laterally and persist if not contained.

wui.description:
Treat **High findings** as incidents.

- Prioritize triage and containment; isolate affected resources, rotate secrets
- Automate alerting and response with playbooks; integrate into IR
- Enforce **least privilege**, network segmentation, and hardened baselines
- Continuously tune detections and remove unused access to prevent recurrence

other.description:
1. Sign in to the AWS console and open Amazon GuardDuty
2. Use the Region selector to choose a Region where GuardDuty is enabled
3. Go to Findings and filter: Severity = High (7-8.9), Archived status = Not archived
4. Select all results, click Actions > Archive
5. Repeat steps 2-4 for every Region with GuardDuty enabled
6. Confirm there are 0 active High severity findings in each Region

compliances.name: AWS Well Architected Framework Security Pillar

iam_group_administrator_access_policy.title: IAM group does not have AdministratorAccess policy attached
iam_group_administrator_access_policy.description:
**IAM groups** are assessed for the AWS-managed `AdministratorAccess` policy attachment.

The finding reports any group that has this policy among its attached permissions.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
iam_group_administrator_access_policy.risk:
Group-wide `AdministratorAccess` gives all members unrestricted control. A stolen or misused account can:
- Read/exfiltrate sensitive data (C)
- Modify or delete resources and configs (I/A)
- Disable logging and weaken defenses, enabling persistence and lateral movement

wui.description: Remove `AdministratorAccess` from groups. Apply **least privilege** with task-scoped, customer-managed policies and **separation of duties**. Use roles for admin tasks with MFA, time-bound elevation, and auditing. Regularly review group membership and permissions; prefer **defense-in-depth** guardrails.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to IAM > User groups
2. Select the target group (<groupname>)
3. Open the Permissions tab > Attached policies
4. Select the policy AdministratorAccess and click Detach
5. Confirm to remove the policy

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: IAM group without AdministratorAccess attached
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Group
    Properties:
      GroupName: <example_resource_name>
      ManagedPolicyArns: []  # Critical: empty list ensures AdministratorAccess is NOT attached to the group
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# IAM group with no AdministratorAccess attachment
resource "aws_iam_group" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name = "<example_resource_name>"
  # Critical: do NOT create any aws_iam_group_policy_attachment with
  # policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess" for this group
}
```

apiserver_etcd_cafile_set.title: API server pod has the --etcd-cafile argument set
apiserver_etcd_cafile_set.description:
**Kubernetes API server** uses an **etcd CA file** via `--etcd-cafile` to verify etcd's TLS certificate.

This evaluates whether API server containers specify that CA file, anchoring TLS trust for etcd connections.
apiserver_etcd_cafile_set.risk:
Without a validated **etcd CA**, the API server may accept rogue or intercepted endpoints, undermining:
- **Confidentiality**: exposure of cluster data in transit
- **Integrity**: tampering with Kubernetes state in etcd
- **Availability**: control plane disruption via malicious etcd responses

wui.description:
Anchor etcd connections in **mutual TLS**: provide a trusted CA (`--etcd-cafile`) and unique client credentials, rotate keys, and prefer strong ciphers.

Apply **least privilege** and **network segmentation** so only API servers can reach etcd; disable plaintext or unauthenticated access.

other.description:
1. SSH to the control plane node running kube-apiserver
2. Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. In spec.containers[0].command, add the flag line:
   ```
   - --etcd-cafile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt
   ```
4. Save the file; the kubelet will restart the API server automatically

apiserver_etcd_cafile_set.notes: It is crucial to manage and rotate the CA file securely as part of your cluster's security practices.

apiserver_etcd_tls_config.title: API server pod has --etcd-certfile and --etcd-keyfile configured for etcd TLS
apiserver_etcd_tls_config.description:
**Kubernetes API server** uses **TLS** for its etcd client connection, signaled by `--etcd-certfile` and `--etcd-keyfile` in the API server pod arguments.

This evaluates whether client-certificate authentication is configured between the API server and etcd.
apiserver_etcd_tls_config.risk: Without **TLS and client certs**, API server-etcd traffic can be **intercepted or altered**, compromising **confidentiality** (Secrets, tokens), **integrity** (state tampering), and **availability** (control-plane instability). Attackers could perform MITM, exfiltrate data, or inject state to seize cluster control.

wui.description: Enforce **mutual TLS** between API server and etcd with trusted CAs and unique client certificates. Restrict etcd network access to control-plane nodes, rotate keys, and monitor certificate expiry. Apply **least privilege** and **defense in depth** using private networking and firewall policies.

other.description:
1. SSH to each control plane node
2. Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. In spec.containers[0].command add:
   - --etcd-certfile=<path/to/client-certificate-file>
   - --etcd-keyfile=<path/to/client-key-file>
4. Save the file; the kubelet will restart the API server with the new flags

apiserver_etcd_tls_config.notes: TLS encryption for etcd is not enabled by default and should be explicitly configured.

apiserver_event_rate_limit.title: API server pod has the EventRateLimit admission control plugin enabled
apiserver_event_rate_limit.description: **Kubernetes API server** includes `EventRateLimit` among its enabled admission plugins, applying rate controls to Kubernetes `Event` objects during admission
apiserver_event_rate_limit.risk: Without **event rate limiting**, bursts of Event writes from noisy or hostile workloads can overwhelm the API server, degrading **availability**. This leads to API timeouts, slow or stalled controller reconciliations, and amplifies **DoS** against control-plane endpoints.

wui.description:
Use the `EventRateLimit` admission plugin with conservative, workload-aware thresholds (global, per-namespace, per-user) to cap Event throughput.

Apply **defense in depth**: monitor Event volume, alert on spikes, tame noisy emitters, and uphold **least privilege** to preserve API capacity.

other.description:
1. SSH to the control-plane node and edit the API server static pod manifest:
   - File: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
2. In the kube-apiserver container args/command list, ensure EventRateLimit is enabled:
   - If the flag exists, append EventRateLimit to the list:
     --enable-admission-plugins=... ,EventRateLimit
   - If missing, add it:
     --enable-admission-plugins=EventRateLimit
3. Save the file. The kubelet will restart the API server automatically and the check will pass.

apiserver_event_rate_limit.notes: Tuning EventRateLimit requires careful consideration of the specific requirements of your environment.

apiserver_kubelet_cert_auth.title: API server pod has --kubelet-certificate-authority configured
apiserver_kubelet_cert_auth.description: **Kubernetes API server** is configured with a **kubelet certificate authority** via `--kubelet-certificate-authority` so it can validate kubelet serving certificates during APIkubelet TLS connections.
apiserver_kubelet_cert_auth.risk: Without a trusted kubelet CA, the API server can't verify kubelet identities, weakening TLS and enabling **man-in-the-middle** on control planenode traffic. Attackers could read logs/exec streams (**Confidentiality**), tamper with responses or commands (**Integrity**), and disrupt node management (**Availability**).

wui.description: Enforce **mutual TLS** for API server-kubelet communication. Provide a trusted CA using `--kubelet-certificate-authority`, issue certs from controlled PKI, rotate keys, and limit client credentials per *least privilege*. Prefer private networking and layered controls for **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. SSH to the control-plane node
2. Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. In containers[].command, add: --kubelet-certificate-authority=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
4. Save the file; the kubelet will restart the API server automatically
5. Verify the flag is present in the manifest and the apiserver pod is Running in kube-system

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# kube-apiserver Pod with kubelet CA configured
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: <example_resource_name>
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:
  - name: kube-apiserver
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.27.0
    command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --kubelet-certificate-authority=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt  # Critical: verifies kubelet certs using this CA to secure apiserver<->kubelet
```

apiserver_kubelet_cert_auth.notes: By default, the kube-apiserver does not verify kubelet certificates. Enabling this setting enhances the security of master-node communications.

apiserver_namespace_lifecycle_plugin.title: API server pod has NamespaceLifecycle admission control plugin enabled
apiserver_namespace_lifecycle_plugin.description: **Kubernetes API server** has the `NamespaceLifecycle` admission controller active and not disabled, enforcing namespace lifecycle rules by rejecting objects targeting **non-existent** or **terminating** namespaces and protecting system namespaces from deletion.
apiserver_namespace_lifecycle_plugin.risk:
Without `NamespaceLifecycle`, resources can be created in namespaces being removed or that never existed, causing inconsistent state and controller errors.

This degrades **integrity** and **availability**, leaving orphaned objects, delaying cleanup, and potentially preserving access via leftover service accounts or policies.

wui.description: Ensure `NamespaceLifecycle` remains enabled to enforce namespace governance. Apply **least privilege** for namespace creation/deletion, and use **separation of duties** for approvals. Monitor deletions and remediate stuck finalizers so cleanup completes. Combine with RBAC and audit logs for **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. SSH to the control plane node.
2. Edit the API server manifest: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. In spec.containers[0].command, ensure NamespaceLifecycle is enabled and not disabled:
   ```yaml
   # Critical: enable NamespaceLifecycle plugin
   - --enable-admission-plugins=NamespaceLifecycle
   # If this flag exists with a list, append ,NamespaceLifecycle to it
   # Ensure NamespaceLifecycle is NOT present in:
   # - --disable-admission-plugins=...
   ```
4. Save the file; the kubelet will restart the API server automatically.
5. Verify the setting is present in the running pod spec:
   ```
   kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].command}' | grep NamespaceLifecycle
   ```

apiserver_namespace_lifecycle_plugin.notes: NamespaceLifecycle plugin is usually enabled by default, ensuring proper management of namespace creation and termination.

apiserver_no_always_admit_plugin.title: API server pod does not have the AlwaysAdmit admission control plugin enabled
apiserver_no_always_admit_plugin.description:
**Kubernetes API server** configuration is inspected for the `AlwaysAdmit` admission plugin in `--enable-admission-plugins`.

If `AlwaysAdmit` is configured, the server accepts all admission requests without running other admission controllers.
apiserver_no_always_admit_plugin.risk:
With **AlwaysAdmit**, admission policies don't run after authN/Z, weakening CIA:
- Bypass of controls enables privileged or unsafe workloads (confidentiality, integrity)
- Quotas/limits can be ignored, causing resource exhaustion (availability)
- Misconfigurations persist, enabling escalation and lateral movement

wui.description:
Exclude `AlwaysAdmit` from API server settings. Use a **deny-by-default** admission posture and enable only necessary controllers to enforce policy and limits (e.g., PodSecurity, ResourceQuota, LimitRanger).

Apply **least privilege**, regularly review admission configuration, and audit API activity to detect drift.

other.description:
1. SSH to a control plane node
2. Edit the static pod manifest: sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. In spec.containers[].command, locate the flag --enable-admission-plugins=...
4. Remove "AlwaysAdmit" from the comma-separated list (if it is the only value, remove the entire flag)
5. Save the file; the kubelet will restart the API server automatically
6. Verify it's gone: kubectl -n kube-system describe pod <example_apiserver_pod> | grep -- --enable-admission-plugins (ensure AlwaysAdmit is not present)

apiserver_no_always_admit_plugin.notes: AlwaysAdmit is deprecated and should not be used. Ensure it is removed from the API server configuration.

apiserver_node_restriction_plugin.title: API server pod has NodeRestriction admission control plugin enabled
apiserver_node_restriction_plugin.description:
**Kubernetes API server** has the **NodeRestriction** admission controller enabled via `--enable-admission-plugins`.

This setting confines kubelets to modify only their own `Node` object and bound `Pod` objects.
apiserver_node_restriction_plugin.risk:
Without **NodeRestriction**, a compromised or misconfigured kubelet could alter other nodes or pods, change critical labels/taints, or delete node objects.

This enables lateral movement and workload hijacking, impacting **integrity** and **availability** of the cluster.

wui.description:
Enable the **NodeRestriction** admission controller to enforce **least privilege** for kubelets.

Pair it with **Node** and **RBAC** authorization, strong kubelet identity, and audit monitoring for defense-in-depth. Regularly rotate credentials and limit kubelet access to only its node.

other.description:
1. SSH to the control plane node running the API server
2. Edit the static pod manifest: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. Under spec > containers[0] > command, ensure this flag is present and includes NodeRestriction (add it if missing):
   - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction
   If the flag already exists with other plugins, append ,NodeRestriction to the comma-separated list
4. Save the file; the kubelet will automatically restart the API server

apiserver_node_restriction_plugin.notes: NodeRestriction is critical in clusters where kubelets need restricted access to Node and Pod objects they manage.

cloudsql_instance_postgres_log_min_durat.title: Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instance has the log_min_duration_statement flag set to -1
cloudsql_instance_postgres_log_min_durat.description: **Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL** evaluates whether `log_min_duration_statement` is set to `-1`, disabling **statement duration logging**.
cloudsql_instance_postgres_log_min_durat.risk: When duration-based statement logging is enabled, logs can capture full SQL with literals, exposing **confidential data** in log stores. Adversaries or over-privileged users could harvest secrets/PII, profile schemas, and support **lateral movement**. Heavy logging can also raise costs and impact availability under load.

wui.description: Keep `log_min_duration_statement` at `-1` in production to avoid writing sensitive query text to logs. Apply **least privilege** to log access, enforce **data minimization** with redaction and short retention. *If troubleshooting is required*, enable narrowly and temporarily, prefer non-prod, and monitor access.

other.description:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to SQL > Instances
2. Select your PostgreSQL instance
3. Click Edit
4. In Database flags, add or edit log_min_duration_statement and set it to -1
5. Click Save (the instance may restart)

apiserver_request_timeout_set.title: API server pod has --request-timeout configured
apiserver_request_timeout_set.description:
**Kubernetes API server** has a global request timeout configured via `--request-timeout`.

The presence of that flag on API server containers is assessed.
apiserver_request_timeout_set.risk: Without a defined, appropriate timeout, requests can linger and tie up handlers, reducing **availability**. Attackers can perform slowloris-style holds or heavy reads to cause **resource exhaustion** and backlog growth. Overly short timeouts can cut valid calls, disrupting controllers and clients.

wui.description: Set `--request-timeout` to a bounded value aligned to typical non-watch calls; *when needed*, tune `--min-request-timeout` for watches. Combine with **priority and fairness**, rate limiting, and load testing to prevent starvation. Monitor latency and errors to adjust. Apply **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. SSH to each control-plane node
2. Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. In the kube-apiserver container's command list, add:
   ```yaml
   - --request-timeout=300s
   ```
4. Save the file; the kubelet will automatically restart the API server
5. Repeat on all control-plane nodes

apiserver_request_timeout_set.notes: The default timeout is set to 60 seconds. Adjust according to the specific requirements and constraints of your Kubernetes environment.

compute_instance_group_load_balancer_att.title: Managed Instance Group is attached to a load balancer
compute_instance_group_load_balancer_att.description: Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) should be attached to load balancers via backend services to enable traffic distribution across instances. Load balancers provide health checking, autoscaling integration, and high availability features that are essential for production workloads.
compute_instance_group_load_balancer_att.risk:
Without load balancer attachment, MIGs cannot distribute traffic evenly across instances, which impacts:

- **Application availability** - No automatic failover when instances become unhealthy
- **Scalability** - Autoscaling benefits are limited without proper traffic distribution
- **Performance** - Uneven load distribution can cause hotspots and degraded user experience

wui.description: Attach Managed Instance Groups to load balancers using backend services to enable traffic distribution, health checking, and seamless autoscaling. This ensures high availability and optimal performance for production workloads.

other.description:
1. Navigate to Network Services > Load balancing
2. Create or edit an HTTP(S) load balancer
3. Configure the backend service
4. Select the target MIG from the instance group dropdown
5. Configure port and balancing mode
6. Complete the load balancer setup

apiserver_service_account_key_file_set.title: API server pod has --service-account-key-file configured
apiserver_service_account_key_file_set.description:
**Kubernetes API server** uses `--service-account-key-file` to supply the public key(s) for validating **service account tokens**.

Detection looks for API server containers that lack this flag.
apiserver_service_account_key_file_set.risk: Without a dedicated key file, token validation can fall back to the API server's TLS key, eroding **separation of duties**. Compromise or rotation of that key can enable **token forgery** (confidentiality/integrity) or invalidate tokens, disrupting workloads (**availability**).

wui.description:
Use a dedicated key pair for **service accounts**:
- Configure `--service-account-key-file` with public keys for validation
- Keep signing and serving keys separate (*least privilege*)
- Enforce scheduled key rotation and maintain multiple active keys for **defense in depth**

other.description:
1. SSH to the control plane node.
2. Edit the API server static pod manifest:
   sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
3. In spec.containers[0].command add this line:
   ```
   - --service-account-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/sa.pub
   ```
4. Save the file; the kubelet will restart the API server automatically.

apiserver_service_account_key_file_set.notes: Ensure the public key used is securely managed and rotated in accordance with your organization's security policy.

app_client_certificates_on.title: Web app requires incoming client certificates
app_client_certificates_on.description: **Azure App Service apps** enforce **mutual TLS** when `client certificate mode` is set to `Required`, meaning every inbound request must present a valid client certificate that the app can validate.
app_client_certificates_on.risk: Without **mTLS**, clients aren't cryptographically authenticated at the transport layer. Adversaries can reach endpoints using spoofed sources or stolen tokens, leading to unauthorized data access (confidentiality), request tampering (integrity), and automated abuse that degrades service (availability).

wui.description:
Set `client certificate mode` to `Required` and validate client certs in application logic (issuer, validity, revocation).

Enforce HTTPS only, avoid broad exclusion paths, and manage certs via a trusted CA with rotation and revocation. Apply **least privilege** and **zero trust**, layering with private access or IP restrictions *as needed*.

other.description:
1. Open Azure Portal and go to App Services
2. Select your web app
3. Go to Configuration > General settings
4. Under Client certificate mode, select Required
5. Click Save

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Require client certificates for the App Service (use azurerm_linux_web_app or azurerm_windows_web_app)
resource "azurerm_linux_web_app" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<example_location>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  service_plan_id     = "<example_resource_id>"

  client_certificate_enabled = true      # Critical: enables mutual TLS
  client_certificate_mode    = "Required" # Critical: enforces client certs (passes the check)

  site_config {}
}
```

app_client_certificates_on.notes: Utilizing and maintaining client certificates will require additional work to obtain and manage replacement and key rotation.

app_ensure_auth_is_set_up.title: App Service app has App Service Authentication enabled
app_ensure_auth_is_set_up.description:
**Azure App Service** can enforce built-in **Authentication/Authorization** (Easy Auth) so requests are authenticated by a provider before reaching app code.

This evaluates whether platform auth is enabled for the app and an identity provider is configured.
app_ensure_auth_is_set_up.risk: Without platform **authentication**, apps may accept **anonymous requests**, enabling unauthorized access to APIs and data. Attackers can enumerate endpoints and bypass weak app checks, risking data exposure (C), unauthorized changes (I), and automated abuse impacting availability (A).

wui.description: Enable App Service **Authentication/Authorization** and set `Require authentication` for unauthenticated requests. Use **Microsoft Entra** or a trusted IdP, restrict tenants/audiences, enforce HTTPS, and apply **least privilege** with role/claim checks and Conditional Access for defense-in-depth. Avoid `Allow anonymous requests`.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Azure Portal and go to App Services
2. Select <APP_NAME> and open Authentication
3. Click Add identity provider, choose Microsoft, and click Add
4. Save changes

This enables App Service Authentication for the app

app_ensure_auth_is_set_up.notes: This is only required for App Services which require authentication. Enabling on site like a marketing or support website will prevent unauthenticated access which would be undesirable. Adding Authentication requirement will increase cost of App Service and require additional security components to facilitate the authentication

iam_policy_no_wildcard_marketplace_subsc.title: Custom IAM policy does not allow 'aws-marketplace:Subscribe' on all resources
iam_policy_no_wildcard_marketplace_subsc.description: **Customer-managed IAM policies** are examined for statements that grant `aws-marketplace:Subscribe` on all resources (`*`). This action controls the ability to subscribe to AWS Marketplace products, including **Amazon Bedrock foundation models**, and should be scoped to specific product ARNs to enforce least privilege.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
iam_policy_no_wildcard_marketplace_subsc.risk: Granting `aws-marketplace:Subscribe` on all resources allows subscribing to any Marketplace product, including expensive Bedrock foundation models, leading to uncontrolled costs, shadow AI usage, and compliance violations from unapproved deployments.

wui.description: Replace `Resource: "*"` with specific, approved AWS Marketplace product ARNs. Apply the principle of least privilege to `aws-marketplace:Subscribe` permissions to prevent unauthorized subscriptions to costly Bedrock models and other Marketplace products.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, open IAM > Policies
2. Find the custom policy that allows aws-marketplace:Subscribe on Resource: *
3. Click Edit and switch to the JSON editor
4. Replace "Resource": "*" with specific, approved AWS Marketplace product ARNs
5. Save changes and re-run the check to confirm it passes

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
Resources:
  ScopedMarketplacePolicy:
    Type: AWS::IAM::ManagedPolicy
    Properties:
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Action:
              - aws-marketplace:Subscribe  # FIX: scope to specific product ARNs
            Resource:
              - arn:aws:aws-marketplace::123456789012:product/approved-product-id
```

iam_policy_no_wildcard_marketplace_subsc.notes: This check only evaluates customer-managed IAM policies. AWS managed policies are maintained by AWS and cannot be modified. See iam_inline_policy_no_wildcard_marketplace_subscribe for the inline policy variant.

compliances.name: AWS Well Architected Framework Security Pillar

app_ensure_http_is_redirected_to_https.title: App Service web app redirects HTTP to HTTPS
app_ensure_http_is_redirected_to_https.description: **Azure App Service web apps** redirect `HTTP` traffic to `HTTPS` when the `HTTPS Only` setting is enabled. This evaluation identifies apps that do not force secure transport by checking whether plaintext requests are automatically redirected to encrypted endpoints.
app_ensure_http_is_redirected_to_https.risk: Leaving **HTTP accessible** enables **man-in-the-middle** interception, credential and cookie theft, and response tampering. This undermines **confidentiality** and **integrity**, and can lead to session hijacking or downgrade attacks that bypass TLS.

wui.description:
Enforce **HTTPS-only** for all apps.
- Use trusted certificates and require `TLS 1.2` or later
- Enable **HSTS** to prevent downgrade/mixed-content
- Redirect legacy `http` links to `https`
- Minimize HTTP exposure via WAF/CDN or private access
Apply **defense in depth** to protect data in transit.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal and go to App Services
2. Select your web app
3. Go to TLS/SSL settings and set HTTPS Only to On
4. Click Save

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Enforce HTTPS-only on an App Service
resource "azurerm_windows_web_app" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<example_location>"
  service_plan_id     = "<example_resource_id>"

  https_only = true # Critical: redirects HTTP to HTTPS
}
```

app_ensure_http_is_redirected_to_https.notes: When it is enabled, every incoming HTTP request is redirected to the HTTPS port. This means an extra level of security will be added to the HTTP requests made to the app.

app_ensure_java_version_is_latest.title: App Service web app uses the latest supported Java version or 17 by default
app_ensure_java_version_is_latest.description:
**Azure App Service web apps** that run **Java** are assessed to ensure their configured runtime uses the **latest supported major version** (LTS) for the environment, across Linux and Windows.

*Only apps with Java enabled are considered.*
app_ensure_java_version_is_latest.risk: Using an **outdated Java runtime** enables known exploits like **remote code execution**, unsafe **deserialization**, and **cryptographic flaws**, risking data theft and tampering (**confidentiality, integrity**) and outages or takeover (**availability**). Unsupported versions also delay critical security patches.

wui.description:
Adopt the **latest supported LTS Java** (`java <latest LTS>`) and standardize on that major line.
- Enable automatic minor/patch updates
- Validate upgrades in a staging environment before production
- Retire deprecated runtimes and track vendor EOL

Apply **change management** and **defense in depth** to reduce exposure.

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to App Services and open your web app
2. Select Settings > Configuration > General settings
3. For Linux apps: under Stack settings, choose Java and set Java version to 17 (or choose Tomcat/JBoss with Java version 17)
4. For Windows apps: under Stack settings, set Java version to 17
5. Click Save and restart if prompted

app_ensure_java_version_is_latest.notes: If your app is written using version-dependent features or libraries, they may not be available on the latest version. If you wish to upgrade, research the impact thoroughly. Upgrading may have unforeseen consequences that could result in downtime.

cloudsql_instance_sqlserver_external_scr.title: Cloud SQL SQL Server instance has 'external scripts enabled' flag set to 'off'
cloudsql_instance_sqlserver_external_scr.description: **Cloud SQL for SQL Server** instances have the `external scripts enabled` database flag set to `off`
cloudsql_instance_sqlserver_external_scr.risk: Allowing **external scripts** lets SQL invoke language extensions (e.g., R/Python), enabling arbitrary code execution. This can cause data exfiltration (**confidentiality**), tampered query results (**integrity**), and resource exhaustion or service degradation (**availability**), and may facilitate lateral movement from the database layer.

cli.description: gcloud sql instances patch <INSTANCE_NAME> --database-flags="external scripts enabled"=off

wui.description: Keep `external scripts enabled` set to `off`. Apply **least privilege** and **defense in depth** by disabling code-execution features in the database. If analytics are required, use isolated instances, restrict outbound network access, and enforce change control and auditing to prevent misuse.

other.description:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to SQL > Instances and select the SQL Server instance
2. Click Edit
3. In the Flags section, add or locate "external scripts enabled"
4. Set its value to Off
5. Click Save to apply (the instance may restart)

iam_rotate_access_key_90_days.title: IAM user does not have active access keys older than 90 days
iam_rotate_access_key_90_days.description: **IAM user access keys** are assessed via the credential report. For each active key, the `last_rotated` timestamp is compared to `90 days`; keys exceeding this age are identified. Users without keys or with only recent rotations are noted.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark
iam_rotate_access_key_90_days.risk: Long-lived access keys widen the attack window. If a key is leaked in code, logs, or tooling, lack of rotation keeps it valid for abuse, enabling unauthorized API calls, data exfiltration, and tampering. This degrades **confidentiality** and **integrity** and can impact **availability** and cost through destructive or excessive operations.

wui.description:
Apply **least privilege** and limit static credentials:
- Rotate active access keys at or before `90 days`
- Prefer **IAM roles** with short-lived tokens
- Maintain only one active key during rotation; delete the old one
- Monitor `last_used` and remove dormant keys
- Automate alerts and periodic reviews of key age

other.description:
1. Open the IAM console and go to Users
2. Select the affected user
3. Open the Security credentials tab
4. Under Access keys, find any key older than 90 days
5. Click Actions > Deactivate (or Delete) for that key
6. Repeat for any other active keys older than 90 days

compliances.name: AWS Well Architected Framework Security Pillar

app_ensure_php_version_is_latest.title: App Service web app uses the latest supported PHP version or 8.2 by default
app_ensure_php_version_is_latest.description: **Azure App Service web apps** running **PHP** are evaluated to ensure the runtime is configured to the **latest supported** release. The finding compares the app's PHP stack (from `linuxFxVersion` or `php_version`) with the newest available version.
app_ensure_php_version_is_latest.risk: Using **outdated PHP** enables exploitation of known flaws, including **remote code execution**, causing secret disclosure (confidentiality), unauthorized changes (integrity), and crashes or downtime (availability). Deprecated versions lack patches, widening exposure and instability.

wui.description: Standardize on the **latest supported PHP** and avoid EoL releases. Update promptly after security advisories, validate in staging, and automate version governance across apps. Prefer supported Linux runtimes, limit optional extensions, and apply **defense in depth** and **least privilege** to reduce blast radius.

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to App Services and select your app
2. Navigate to Settings > Configuration > General settings
3. Under Stack settings, select PHP and set Version to 8.2
4. Click Save and confirm the restart

app_ensure_php_version_is_latest.notes: If your app is written using version-dependent features or libraries, they may not be available on the latest version. If you wish to upgrade, research the impact thoroughly. Upgrading may have unforeseen consequences that could result in downtime

app_ensure_python_version_is_latest.title: App Service web app uses the latest supported Python version or 3.12 by default
app_ensure_python_version_is_latest.description: **Azure App Service web apps** using **Python** are assessed to confirm the runtime is the **latest supported version** (e.g., `3.12`). The evaluation reads the app's stack configuration to detect Python usage and compares the configured runtime against the defined latest baseline.
app_ensure_python_version_is_latest.risk:
Outdated **Python runtimes** weaken security and reliability:
- Compromise confidentiality via known interpreter/SSL flaws
- Undermine integrity through RCE and package exploitation
- Reduce availability when deprecated versions lose patches and break under load

wui.description:
Adopt the **latest supported Python minor** for App Service and maintain a consistent upgrade policy. Track vendor EOL, test in staging, and roll out via CI/CD.

Apply **defense in depth**: minimize privileges and enforce strong TLS to reduce exposure during updates.

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to App Services and select your app
2. Go to Settings > Configuration > General settings
3. Under Stack settings, set Python version to 3.12
4. Click Save and confirm the restart

app_ensure_python_version_is_latest.notes: If your app is written using version-dependent features or libraries, they may not be available on the latest version. If you wish to upgrade, research the impact thoroughly. Upgrading may have unforeseen consequences that could result in downtime.

app_ensure_using_http20.title: App Service web app has HTTP/2.0 enabled
app_ensure_using_http20.description: **Azure App Service web apps** are evaluated for **HTTP/2 support** via the `http20_enabled` configuration, indicating whether the site serves traffic using the HTTP/2 protocol
app_ensure_using_http20.risk: Without **HTTP/2**, apps remain on **HTTP/1.1**, increasing connection overhead and head-of-line blocking, which can reduce **availability** under load. Inefficient use of TLS sessions raises **DoS susceptibility** and degrades user experience, impacting service reliability

wui.description:
Enable **HTTP/2** (`http20_enabled=true`) to use a modern, efficient transport.

- Enforce `HTTPS Only` and a strong minimum `TLS` version for defense-in-depth
- Validate app/library compatibility before rollout
- Monitor performance and errors post-change; deploy gradually

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal and go to App Services
2. Select your web app
3. Navigate to Settings > Configuration > General settings
4. Set HTTP version to 2.0
5. Click Save

app_ftp_deployment_disabled.title: App Service web app has FTP disabled or FTPS-only enforced
app_ftp_deployment_disabled.description: **Azure App Service web apps** are evaluated for **FTP exposure** via the `ftpsState` setting. Values `FtpsOnly` or `Disabled` indicate FTP is not allowed; `AllAllowed` means both FTP and FTPS are accepted.
app_ftp_deployment_disabled.risk:
Allowing **FTP (unencrypted)** exposes credentials on public endpoints, enabling **credential theft** and **session hijacking**.

Compromise grants write access to code and content, enabling **malicious deployments**, backdoors, and data leakage, degrading **integrity** and **confidentiality**-with greater blast radius if shared, user-scope publishing credentials are used.

wui.description:
Disable FTP or enforce **FTPS** (`ftpsState: FtpsOnly` or `Disabled`).

Prefer **CI/CD** over manual FTP and apply **least privilege** with app-scoped credentials. Rotate publishing secrets, enforce modern TLS, and restrict access via private networking. *If FTP is unavoidable*, require FTPS and monitor publishing logs.

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to App Services and select your app
2. Go to Settings > Configuration > General settings
3. Set FTP state to FTPS only (or Disabled)
4. Click Save

app_ftp_deployment_disabled.notes: Any deployment workflows that rely on FTP or FTPs rather than the WebDeploy or HTTPs endpoints may be affected.

app_function_application_insights_enable.title: Function App has Application Insights configured
app_function_application_insights_enable.description: **Azure Function apps** are configured to send telemetry to **Application Insights** when application settings include `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` or `APPINSIGHTS_INSTRUMENTATIONKEY`.
app_function_application_insights_enable.risk: Without this telemetry, **visibility** into exceptions, dependencies, and performance is lost, reducing **availability** and delaying response. Gaps in traces mask anomalous traffic and failures, enabling prolonged outages and undermining **integrity** of processing (e.g., undetected retries or timeouts).

wui.description: Enable **Application Insights** for each Function App using a `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` and standardize telemetry. Apply **defense in depth**: use distributed tracing, alert on errors/latency, and enforce least-privilege access and retention on logs to prevent blind spots and speed recovery.

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Function App > Configuration > Application settings
2. Click + New application setting
3. Name: APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING
4. Value: paste the connection string from your Application Insights resource (Overview > Connection string)
5. Click OK, then Save
6. If prompted, click Continue to apply the changes

app_function_ftps_deployment_disabled.title: Function app has FTP and FTPS deployments disabled
app_function_ftps_deployment_disabled.description: **Azure Function apps** are evaluated for the `ftps_state` setting that controls **FTP/FTPS deployment endpoints**. Values `AllAllowed` or `FtpsOnly` indicate deployment over FTP/FTPS is enabled, while `Disabled` indicates both endpoints are turned off.
app_function_ftps_deployment_disabled.risk: Enabled **FTP/FTPS deployment** undermines confidentiality and integrity. FTP exposes credentials in cleartext; FTPS still presents a public basic-auth endpoint susceptible to brute force and credential reuse. Compromise enables **unauthorized code pushes**, leading to RCE, data leakage, and service disruption.

wui.description: Disable **FTP and FTPS deployment** on Function apps (`ftps_state: Disabled`). Adopt **defense in depth**: deploy via **CI/CD** with packaged artifacts (zip or containers), enforce **least privilege** publishing access, and limit exposure of build and deployment endpoints. *If unavoidable, use FTPS-only with TLS 1.2 and rotate credentials promptly.*

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to your Function App
2. Select Configuration > General settings
3. Under Platform settings, set FTP state to Disabled
4. Click Save

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Disable FTP and FTPS on a Function App
resource "azurerm_linux_function_app" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                       = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name        = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                   = "<example_location>"
  service_plan_id            = "<example_resource_id>"
  storage_account_name       = "<example_resource_name>"
  storage_account_access_key = "<example_secret_value>"
  functions_extension_version = "~4"

  site_config {
    ftps_state = "Disabled" # CRITICAL: Disables both FTP and FTPS deployments
  }
}
```

app_function_ftps_deployment_disabled.notes: This check ensures that Azure Functions are deployed securely, reducing the attack surface and protecting sensitive information.

app_function_identity_is_configured.title: Function app has a system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity enabled
app_function_identity_is_configured.description:
**Azure Function Apps** are evaluated for an enabled **managed identity** (`SystemAssigned` or `UserAssigned`) configured on the app.

The finding indicates whether an identity is present to support token-based access to other Azure resources.
app_function_identity_is_configured.risk:
Without **managed identities**, apps rely on stored secrets/keys, risking:
- Confidentiality loss from leaked credentials
- Integrity tampering via unauthorized writes
- Availability outages from secret expiry/rotation

Compromised keys enable unauthorized access and lateral movement.

wui.description: Enable a **managed identity** on each Function App (`SystemAssigned` per app, `UserAssigned` for shared/long-lived needs). Replace secrets with token-based access and grant only required RBAC roles (**least privilege**). Remove keys from settings, apply **separation of duties**, and monitor access as part of **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to your Function App
2. Under Settings, select Identity
3. On the System assigned tab, set Status to On
4. Click Save

app_function_latest_runtime_version.title: Function app uses the latest supported runtime version (~4)
app_function_latest_runtime_version.description: **Azure Function apps** are assessed for the **runtime version** set via `FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION`. The finding identifies apps not configured to use the current supported major version `~4`.
app_function_latest_runtime_version.risk:
Outdated Functions runtimes erode CIA:
- **Confidentiality**: known flaws enable unauthorized data access.
- **Integrity**: RCE or binding bugs allow code tampering.
- **Availability**: missing fixes cause crashes and scale faults.

End-of-support versions (e.g., 2.x/3.x) lack security patches, increasing exploitability.

cli.description: az functionapp config appsettings set --name <function_app_name> --resource-group <resource_group_name> --settings FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION=~4

wui.description:
Standardize on supported runtime `~4` and align language/extension versions.
- Enforce upgrades in CI/CD and use staging to validate before rollout.
- Apply **least privilege** for app identities and secrets.
- Prefer automated patching and periodic reviews to avoid drift; avoid downgrades or indefinite minor pinning.

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Function App <example_resource_name>
2. Select Configuration > Application settings
3. Add or edit the setting:
   - Name: FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION
   - Value: ~4
4. Click Save and confirm the restart
5. Verify the setting shows FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION = ~4

app_function_latest_runtime_version.notes: Stay informed about the latest security updates and patch releases for Azure Functions to maintain a secure and up-to-date environment.

app_function_not_publicly_accessible.title: Function app is not publicly accessible
app_function_not_publicly_accessible.description: **Azure Function apps** are assessed for whether they are reachable from the public Internet. The evaluation considers the app's `publicNetworkAccess` state and the presence of access restrictions or private endpoints to limit inbound traffic.
app_function_not_publicly_accessible.risk: Public exposure allows unauthorized invocation, risking data disclosure and tampering (**confidentiality** and **integrity**). Attackers can brute-force tokens or abuse misconfigurations for remote execution. Unrestricted calls also enable abuse and DoS, driving cost and harming **availability**.

wui.description:
Apply network isolation and least privilege:
- Set `publicNetworkAccess=Disabled`
- Use access restrictions for trusted IPs/VNets or **Private Endpoints**
- Require strong auth (e.g., **Microsoft Entra ID**) over shared keys
- Front with **API Management/WAF**
- Keep secrets in **Key Vault** and monitor access logs

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to your Function App
2. Select Networking
3. Under Public access, set Public network access to Disabled
4. Click Save

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Disable public network access for the Function App
resource "azurerm_linux_function_app" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                       = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                   = azurerm_resource_group.main.location
  resource_group_name        = azurerm_resource_group.main.name
  service_plan_id            = azurerm_service_plan.main.id
  storage_account_name       = azurerm_storage_account.main.name
  storage_account_access_key = azurerm_storage_account.main.primary_access_key

  public_network_access_enabled = false # Critical: disables public endpoint access
}
```

app_function_vnet_integration_enabled.title: Function app has Virtual Network integration enabled
app_function_vnet_integration_enabled.description:
**Azure Function apps** configured with **Virtual Network integration** uses a chosen subnet so outbound traffic is routed via the VNet and can reach private or service-endpoint-secured resources.

The finding reflects whether a function app is associated with a subnet resource ID.
app_function_vnet_integration_enabled.risk:
Without VNet integration, function apps send egress directly to the public Internet and cannot reach private endpoints.

This weakens confidentiality and integrity by bypassing NSG/UDR controls, enables data exfiltration from compromised code, and may force exposing backends publicly, increasing attack surface.

wui.description:
Enable **Virtual Network integration** and attach function apps to a dedicated subnet to enforce **least privilege network access**.

Route egress through the VNet (e.g., `Route All`), apply **NSGs/UDRs**, and use **private endpoints** or service endpoints for dependencies. Restrict outbound traffic by default as part of **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to your Function App
2. Select Networking > VNet Integration
3. Click Add VNet
4. Choose the target Virtual network and Subnet
5. Click OK/Save to apply

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Enable VNet integration for an existing Function App
resource "azurerm_app_service_virtual_network_swift_connection" "<example_resource_name>" {
  app_service_id = "/subscriptions/<example_resource_id>/resourceGroups/<example_resource_name>/providers/Microsoft.Web/sites/<example_resource_name>" # CRITICAL: target Function App resource ID
  subnet_id      = "/subscriptions/<example_resource_id>/resourceGroups/<example_resource_name>/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/<example_resource_name>/subnets/<example_resource_name>" # CRITICAL: subnet to integrate with
}
```

app_http_logs_enabled.title: App Service web app has HTTP logs enabled in diagnostic settings
app_http_logs_enabled.description: **Azure App Service web apps** diagnostic settings include **HTTP request logging** when the `AppServiceHTTPLogs` category (or the `allLogs` group) is enabled to capture web access events.
app_http_logs_enabled.risk: Without **HTTP access logs**, visibility into requests is lost, hindering **detection** of brute force, probing, and injection attempts. This weakens **forensics** and reduces **confidentiality** and **integrity** by masking data access paths and blocking reliable incident timelines.

wui.description: Enable **diagnostic settings** with `AppServiceHTTPLogs` (or `allLogs`) and route logs to a centralized store. Enforce **least privilege**, retention, and tamper-resistant storage. Integrate with a **SIEM** for analytics and alerting, and periodically verify logging coverage across all apps and regions.

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to your App Service > Monitoring > Diagnostic settings
2. Click + Add diagnostic setting
3. Under Logs, check AppServiceHTTPLogs (or select the allLogs category group)
4. Choose a destination (Log Analytics workspace, Storage account, or Event Hub)
5. Click Save

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Enable HTTP Logs for App Service via Azure Monitor diagnostic setting
resource "azurerm_monitor_diagnostic_setting" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                       = "<example_resource_name>"
  target_resource_id         = "/subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>/resourceGroups/<RESOURCE_GROUP>/providers/Microsoft.Web/sites/<example_resource_name>"
  log_analytics_workspace_id = "<example_resource_id>" # Destination Log Analytics workspace

  log {                      # Critical: enables the HTTP Logs category
    category = "AppServiceHTTPLogs"
    enabled  = true
  }
}
```

app_http_logs_enabled.notes: Log consumption and processing will incur additional cost.

cloudstorage_audit_logs_enabled.title: Data Access audit logs are enabled for Cloud Storage
cloudstorage_audit_logs_enabled.description: Data Access audit logs (DATA_READ and DATA_WRITE) are enabled for Cloud Storage at the project level. Unlike Admin Activity logs (enabled by default), Data Access logs must be explicitly configured to track read and write operations on Cloud Storage objects.
cloudstorage_audit_logs_enabled.risk: Without Data Access audit logs, you cannot track who accessed or modified objects in your Cloud Storage buckets, making it difficult to detect unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or compliance violations.

wui.description: Enable Data Access audit logs (DATA_READ and DATA_WRITE) for Cloud Storage at the project level to track all read and write operations on storage objects for security monitoring and compliance.

other.description:
1) Console → IAM & Admin → Audit Logs
2) Find 'Google Cloud Storage' in the list of services
3) Check the boxes for 'Data Read' and 'Data Write'
4) Click 'Save' to apply the configuration

Note: This is a project-level setting that applies to all Cloud Storage buckets in the project.

AWS-0152.title: Ensure a log metric filter and alarm exist for AWS Management Console authentication failures
AWS-0152.description:
You can do real-time monitoring of API calls by directing CloudTrail logs to CloudWatch Logs and establishing corresponding metric filters and alarms.
CIS recommends that you create a metric filter and alarm for failed console authentication attempts. Monitoring failed console logins might decrease lead time to detect an attempt to brute-force a credential, which might provide an indicator, such as source IP, that you can use in other event correlations.

wui.description: Create an alarm to alert on console login failures

other.description:
You can do real-time monitoring of API calls by directing CloudTrail logs to CloudWatch Logs and establishing corresponding metric filters and alarms.
CIS recommends that you create a metric filter and alarm for failed console authentication attempts. Monitoring failed console logins might decrease lead time to detect an attempt to brute-force a credential, which might provide an indicator, such as source IP, that you can use in other event correlations.

iam_user_hardware_mfa_enabled.title: IAM user has hardware MFA enabled
iam_user_hardware_mfa_enabled.description: **IAM users** are evaluated for **hardware MFA** enrollment, identifying physical tokens or security keys and distinguishing them from *virtual* or *SMS* MFA, as well as users without any MFA.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark
iam_user_hardware_mfa_enabled.risk:
Without **hardware MFA**, authentication is weaker:
- **SIM-swap** can bypass SMS
- **Phishing** can steal TOTP from virtual apps
- No MFA allows password-only takeover
This enables unauthorized console/API access, causing data exfiltration (C), privilege abuse (I), and service disruption (A).

wui.description: Require **hardware-backed MFA** for all IAM users. Prefer **FIDO2 security keys** for phishing resistance over TOTP or SMS. Disallow SMS/virtual MFA for privileged roles. Enforce MFA for all access paths, apply **least privilege**, and provision multiple MFA devices per user for continuity.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the AWS Console and open IAM
2. Go to Users > select <user> > Security credentials
3. Under Multi-factor authentication (MFA), if a Virtual MFA device or SMS MFA is listed, choose Deactivate/Remove and confirm
4. Click Assign MFA device
5. Select Hardware TOTP token or Security key (FIDO2) and choose Next
6. For Hardware TOTP: enter the device serial, then enter MFA code 1 and MFA code 2 from the token; for Security key: insert/tap the key and follow the prompts
7. Choose Add/Save to complete

compliances.name: AWS Audit Manager Control Tower Guardrails
AWS Well Architected Framework Security Pillar

AWS-0142.title: The "root" account has unrestricted access to all resources in the AWS account. It is highly recommended that this account have MFA enabled.
AWS-0142.description:
MFA adds an extra layer of protection on top of a user name and password. With MFA enabled, when a user signs in to an AWS website, they're prompted for their user name and password and for an authentication code from their AWS MFA device.

When you use virtual MFA for the root user, CIS recommends that the device used is not a personal device. Instead, use a dedicated mobile device (tablet or phone) that you manage to keep charged and secured independent of any individual personal devices. This lessens the risks of losing access to the MFA due to device loss, device trade-in, or if the individual owning the device is no longer employed at the company.

wui.description: Enable MFA on the root user account.

other.description:
MFA adds an extra layer of protection on top of a user name and password. With MFA enabled, when a user signs in to an AWS website, they're prompted for their user name and password and for an authentication code from their AWS MFA device.

When you use virtual MFA for the root user, CIS recommends that the device used is not a personal device. Instead, use a dedicated mobile device (tablet or phone) that you manage to keep charged and secured independent of any individual personal devices. This lessens the risks of losing access to the MFA due to device loss, device trade-in, or if the individual owning the device is no longer employed at the company.

iam_user_with_temporary_credentials.title: IAM user does not use long-lived credentials to access services other than IAM or STS
iam_user_with_temporary_credentials.description: IAM users are assessed for activity using **long-lived access keys**. Use of static credentials to access services other than IAM or STS indicates reliance on permanent keys instead of **temporary role-based credentials**.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Runtime Behavior Analysis
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
iam_user_with_temporary_credentials.risk: Persistent access keys enable attacker **persistence** and replay. Stolen keys allow off-network API calls for data exfiltration, privilege changes, and destructive actions, impacting **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and **availability**. Without expiry, the blast radius grows and containment is harder.

wui.description: Adopt **temporary credentials** via IAM roles and federation for humans and workloads. Remove or restrict long-term keys; *if unavoidable*, apply **least privilege**, require **MFA**, rotate aggressively, and monitor usage. Prefer short session durations and session conditions to limit blast radius.

other.description:
1. In AWS Console, go to IAM > Users and select <example_resource_name>
2. Open the Security credentials tab
3. Under Access keys, deactivate and delete all active access keys
4. Save changes
5. Re-test: the user no longer has long-lived credentials to access non-IAM/STS services

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# Attach a policy to block long-term creds from accessing non-IAM/STS services
Resources:
  DenyLongTermNonIamSts:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Policy
    Properties:
      PolicyName: DenyNonIamStsWithLongTermCreds
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Deny
            NotAction:
              - iam:*
              - sts:*
            Resource: "*"
            Condition:
              Null:
                aws:TokenIssueTime: "true"  # Critical: denies when no session token (i.e., long-lived creds)
      Users:
        - <example_resource_name>  # Critical: attach to the affected IAM user
```

identity_iam_admins_cannot_update_tenanc.title: All IAM policies granting manage/use on groups or users in the tenancy restrict access to the Administrators group
identity_iam_admins_cannot_update_tenanc.description:
**OCI IAM policies** granting **manage/use** on **groups or users** in the tenancy are evaluated for a condition that excludes the **Administrators** group, such as `target.group.name != 'Administrators'`.

Policies missing this restriction are identified.
identity_iam_admins_cannot_update_tenanc.risk: Ability to modify the **Administrators** group enables **privilege escalation** to full tenancy control. This threatens confidentiality (broad data access), integrity (policy/user changes), and availability (resource deletion). Attackers could add persistence accounts, disable safeguards, and evade oversight.

cli.description: oci iam policy update --policy-id <example_resource_id> --statements "[\"Allow group <example_resource_name> to manage groups, users in tenancy where target.group.name != 'Administrators'\"]"

wui.description: Apply **least privilege**: avoid tenancy-wide manage/use on groups or users. When delegation is required, include a condition excluding the **Administrators** group (e.g., `target.group.name != 'Administrators'`). Enforce **segregation of duties**, require approvals for group changes, and monitor/audit identity policy activity.

other.description:
1. In OCI Console, go to Identity & Security > Policies
2. Open any policy that allows a group to manage or use groups/users in the tenancy
3. Click Edit policy and update each affected statement to append exactly:
   where target.group.name != 'Administrators'
4. Save changes
5. Repeat for all such policies

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "oci_identity_policy" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name           = "<example_resource_name>"
  compartment_id = "<example_resource_id>"
  description    = "<example_resource_name>"
  statements = [
    # Critical: Protect the Administrators group from modification by this policy
    # Adds a where clause so the policy can't target the Administrators group
    "Allow group <example_resource_name> to manage groups, users in tenancy where target.group.name != 'Administrators'"
  ]
}
```

AWS-0132.title: S3 encryption should use Customer Managed Keys
AWS-0132.description:
Encryption using AWS keys provides protection for your S3 buckets. To gain greater control over encryption, such as key rotation, access policies, and auditability, use customer managed keys (CMKs) with SSE-KMS.
Note that SSE-KMS is not supported for S3 server access logging destination buckets; in such cases, use SSE-S3 instead.

wui.description: Use SSE-KMS with a customer managed key (CMK)

other.description:
Encryption using AWS keys provides protection for your S3 buckets. To gain greater control over encryption, such as key rotation, access policies, and auditability, use customer managed keys (CMKs) with SSE-KMS.
Note that SSE-KMS is not supported for S3 server access logging destination buckets; in such cases, use SSE-S3 instead.

nativeiac.description:
Resources:
  GoodExample:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - BucketKeyEnabled: true
            ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              KMSMasterKeyID: kms-arn
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms

repository_default_branch_requires_signe.title: Repository default branch requires signed commits
repository_default_branch_requires_signe.description: **GitHub repository default branch** enforces **signed and verified commits** (`Require signed commits`), allowing only commits with valid cryptographic signatures to be pushed or merged.
repository_default_branch_requires_signe.risk:
Without required signing, commit authorship can be spoofed and unverified changes added, impacting integrity.
- Backdoor injection
- History tampering and forged identities
- Release pipeline abuse and supply-chain compromise

wui.description:
Enforce `Require signed commits` on default and release branches.
- Standardize GPG/SSH/S/MIME for humans and bots
- Protect and rotate signing keys; least privilege on bypass
- Pair with required reviews and status checks for defense-in-depth

other.description:
1. In GitHub, go to the repository > Settings
2. Click Branches
3. Edit the rule for the default branch (or Add rule targeting the default branch name)
4. Check Require signed commits
5. Click Save changes

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "github_branch_protection_v3" "<example_resource_name>" {
  repository = "<example_repository_name>"
  pattern    = "<default_branch_name>"

  required_signatures = true # Critical: Enforces signed commits on the default branch
}
```

AWS-0010.title: Cloudfront distribution should have Access Logging configured
AWS-0010.description: You should configure CloudFront Access Logging to create log files that contain detailed information about every user request that CloudFront receives

wui.description: Enable logging for CloudFront distributions

other.description: You should configure CloudFront Access Logging to create log files that contain detailed information about every user request that CloudFront receives

nativeiac.description:
Resources:
  GoodExample:
    Type: AWS::CloudFront::Distribution
    Properties:
      DistributionConfig:
        DefaultCacheBehavior:
          TargetOriginId: target
          ViewerProtocolPolicy: https-only
        Enabled: true
        Logging:
          Bucket: logging-bucket
        Origins:
          - DomainName: https://some.domain
            Id: somedomain1

cloudstorage_bucket_lifecycle_management.title: Cloud Storage bucket has lifecycle management enabled with at least one valid rule
cloudstorage_bucket_lifecycle_management.description: **Cloud Storage buckets** use **Object Lifecycle Management** with at least one valid rule (supported `action` and non-empty `condition`) to automatically transition storage class or delete objects.
cloudstorage_bucket_lifecycle_management.risk: Without lifecycle rules, data and object versions persist indefinitely, expanding the attack surface and hindering mandated erasure. Stale data amplifies exfiltration impact (**confidentiality**) and complicates **integrity** controls, while also driving avoidable cost and retention noncompliance.

wui.description: Define lifecycle policies by data classification to enforce **least data retention**. Use `Delete` for TTL/age and `SetStorageClass` for archival, with version-aware conditions like `isLive=false` or `numNewerVersions`. Test on a limited dataset, review regularly, and align with **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to Storage > Buckets and open <BUCKET_NAME>
2. Click the Lifecycle tab
3. Click Add a rule
4. Action: Delete
5. Condition: Age = 1 day
6. Click Create/Save

identity_user_customer_secret_keys_rotat.title: User customer secret key is rotated within 90 days or less
identity_user_customer_secret_keys_rotat.description: **OCI IAM customer secret keys** are assessed by creation timestamp to determine whether their age exceeds `90` days.
identity_user_customer_secret_keys_rotat.risk:
Long-lived **customer secret keys** keep compromised or brute-forced credentials valid.
Attackers can use them to list, read, write, or delete Object Storage data, enabling exfiltration, tampering, and disruption-impacting confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

wui.description: Rotate **customer secret keys** every `<= 90` days. Apply **least privilege**, remove unused keys, and prefer short-lived identities (instance/resource principals) over static secrets. Automate rotation and alerts, avoid embedding keys in code, and continuously monitor key usage.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Oracle Cloud Console
2. Go to Identity & Security > Domains > <example_resource_name> > Users > select <example_resource_name>
3. Open the Customer secret keys tab and click Generate secret key; save the Access Key and Secret
4. Delete any key older than 90 days: select the old key and click Delete

app_minimum_tls_version_12.title: App Service web app has minimum TLS version set to 1.2 or 1.3
app_minimum_tls_version_12.description: **Azure App Service web apps** are assessed for the configured minimum TLS version for HTTPS. The expected baseline is `1.2` or `1.3`; settings that permit lower versions indicate acceptance of legacy TLS during client negotiation.
app_minimum_tls_version_12.risk: Allowing `TLS 1.0/1.1` enables protocol downgrades and weak cipher negotiation, exposing HTTPS traffic to **MITM** interception, credential theft, and tampering. This undermines the **confidentiality** and **integrity** of sessions and data in transit, and can enable account takeover via stolen tokens.

wui.description: Enforce a minimum of `TLS 1.2` (prefer `1.3`) and disable `1.0/1.1`. Require **HTTPS-only**, enable HSTS, and align with modern cipher suites. Test client compatibility and phase out legacy agents. Document narrow exceptions with compensating controls to uphold **defense in depth** and prevent downgrades.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Azure Portal and go to App Services
2. Select your app
3. Go to Settings > Configuration > General settings
4. Set Minimum TLS Version to 1.2 (or 1.3 if available)
5. Click Save

app_minimum_tls_version_12.notes: By default, TLS Version feature will be set to 1.2 when a new app is created using the command-line tool or Azure Portal console.

app_register_with_identity.title: App Service web app has a managed identity configured
app_register_with_identity.description: **Azure App Service web apps** are configured with a **managed identity** (`identity`: `SystemAssigned` or `UserAssigned`) for token-based access to Azure resources without embedded credentials
app_register_with_identity.risk: **Missing managed identity** drives reliance on stored secrets. Leaked credentials enable **unauthorized access** to SQL, Storage, or Key Vault, leading to **data exfiltration**, tampering, and lateral movement. Secret expiry or revocation can break connectivity, degrading **availability**.

wui.description: Enable a **managed identity** and use it for all service-to-service access. Apply **least privilege** on target resources and eliminate secrets from code and app settings.
