core_minimize_hostIPC_containers.description: **Kubernetes pods** are evaluated for use of the host's IPC namespace via the `hostIPC` setting. Workloads declaring `hostIPC: true` share node IPC resources (shared memory, semaphores, message queues) instead of isolated container IPC.
core_minimize_hostIPC_containers.risk: Sharing the host IPC namespace erodes isolation, exposing host shared memory and semaphores. A compromised pod could snoop or tamper with IPC objects, leading to data disclosure, integrity violations, privilege escalation, and lateral movement across workloads.

wui.description: Disallow `hostIPC` with **Pod Security Admission** enforcing **Pod Security Standards** (Baseline/Restricted) or equivalent policy engines. Apply **least privilege** and defense in depth: keep IPC namespaces isolated, grant tightly scoped exceptions only, and prefer app-level messaging or Services over host IPC.

other.description:
1. Open your cluster UI (Kubernetes Dashboard or cloud provider console) and locate the failing workload (Pod/Deployment/StatefulSet)
2. Click Edit YAML/Manifest
3. Set the field to disable host IPC:
   - For a Pod: spec.hostIPC: false (or remove hostIPC if present)
   - For controllers: spec.template.spec.hostIPC: false (or remove hostIPC if present)
4. Save the change to trigger a rollout
5. If it is a standalone Pod (not managed by a controller), delete and recreate the Pod so the new spec takes effect

core_minimize_hostIPC_containers.notes: Exceptions for hostIPC containers should be clearly defined and monitored.

core_minimize_hostNetwork_containers.title: Pod does not use hostNetwork
core_minimize_hostNetwork_containers.description: **Kubernetes Pods** configured with `hostNetwork: true` are identified, meaning they share the node's network namespace and use the host's IP stack, interfaces, and ports.
core_minimize_hostNetwork_containers.risk: Using the **host network namespace** exposes node-local interfaces and traffic to the pod. A compromise can enable packet capture and request spoofing (**C/I**), access to node services (e.g., kubelet), and port binding conflicts, causing outages (**A**) and enabling **lateral movement** across the cluster.

wui.description: Disallow `hostNetwork` by default. Enforce **least privilege** with admission policies that block it, allowing narrowly scoped exceptions only for trusted system workloads. Prefer standard pod networking with **NetworkPolicies**, and isolate node services for **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. Open Kubernetes Dashboard
2. For controller-managed workloads (Deployment/DaemonSet/StatefulSet):
   - Go to Workloads > select the workload > Edit
   - In the Pod template, set spec.template.spec.hostNetwork to false or remove the field
   - Save to roll out new Pods
3. For standalone Pods:
   - Go to Workloads > Pods > select the Pod > Delete
   - Click Create > upload the Pod YAML without hostNetwork (or with hostNetwork: false) and create the Pod

core_minimize_hostNetwork_containers.notes: Exceptions for hostNetwork containers should be clearly defined and monitored.

core_minimize_hostPID_containers.title: Pod does not use the host PID namespace
core_minimize_hostPID_containers.description: **Kubernetes Pods** configured with `hostPID: true` are identified, indicating the container shares the node's **host PID namespace**.
core_minimize_hostPID_containers.risk: Sharing the **host PID namespace** erodes isolation: containers can list host processes and read `/proc` metadata, enabling **credential exposure**, **privilege escalation**, and **lateral movement**. Limited process interaction can also threaten **integrity** and **availability**.

wui.description: Disallow `hostPID` for application Pods via **admission policies** aligned to **Pod Security Standards (Baseline/Restricted)**. Allow only for tightly controlled system workloads. Apply **least privilege**, isolate such Pods on dedicated nodes, and favor debug/observability methods that avoid host namespace sharing.

other.description:
1. Identify the workload that owns the failing Pod (Deployment/DaemonSet/StatefulSet/Job) or confirm it is a standalone Pod
2. Edit the manifest of the owning workload (or the Pod) and set/remove the field so it is not true:
   - In Pod spec: set `hostPID: false` or delete the `hostPID` line
   - For controllers: set `spec.template.spec.hostPID: false` or delete the line
3. Apply the change (kubectl apply) and allow the workload to restart Pods so they no longer use hostPID

core_minimize_hostPID_containers.notes: Exceptions for hostPID containers should be clearly defined and monitored.

core_minimize_net_raw_capability_admissi.title: Pod containers do not have the NET_RAW capability
core_minimize_net_raw_capability_admissi.description:
**Kubernetes pods** where any container's security context adds the `NET_RAW` Linux capability are identified.

The inspection evaluates container `securityContext.capabilities.add` entries to detect explicit requests for `NET_RAW`.
core_minimize_net_raw_capability_admissi.risk: Granting **NET_RAW** enables raw sockets for packet crafting and sniffing, undermining **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Attackers can run ARP/DNS spoofing, pivot or scan inside the cluster, bypass service isolation, exfiltrate data, and impact **availability** through network abuse.

wui.description: Apply **least privilege**: avoid adding `NET_RAW` and drop unnecessary Linux capabilities by default. Use cluster-wide **admission policies** to block requests for `NET_RAW`. When strictly required, isolate the workload, restrict egress with network controls, and audit capability use as part of **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. Identify the affected workload (Deployment/StatefulSet/Pod) and open its spec for edit (e.g., kubectl edit deployment <example_resource_name>)
2. In each container under: spec.template.spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities.add, remove the entry NET_RAW (or remove the entire add field if it only contains NET_RAW)
3. Save the changes to trigger a rollout (for Pod manifests, kubectl apply -f <file.yaml>)
4. Recreate any standalone Pods if needed so the updated spec takes effect

core_minimize_net_raw_capability_admissi.notes: Exceptions for NET_RAW capability should be clearly defined and monitored.

core_minimize_privileged_containers.title: Pod does not contain a privileged container
core_minimize_privileged_containers.description: **Kubernetes Pods** are evaluated for containers configured with `securityContext.privileged: true`, indicating execution in **privileged mode**.
core_minimize_privileged_containers.risk:
**Privileged containers** can control the host and bypass isolation, enabling:
- Secret theft (confidentiality)
- Workload/node tampering (integrity)
- Service disruption (availability)
Compromise of one pod can drive lateral movement across the cluster.

wui.description:
Block `privileged: true` using **Pod Security Admission** at `restricted`. Apply **least privilege**:
- Run unprivileged; set `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`
- Drop capabilities; avoid host access
- Restrict who can deploy privileged pods with **RBAC**
- Use short-lived, audited exceptions only when strictly required

other.description:
1. Open your Kubernetes UI (e.g., cloud provider console or Dashboard)
2. Navigate to the failing workload (Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet) or Pod and choose Edit YAML/Manifest
3. Set securityContext.privileged: false for each affected container:
   - For controllers: spec.template.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged: false
   - For standalone Pods: spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged: false
4. Save changes (controllers will roll out new Pods). If it is a standalone Pod, delete and recreate it to apply the change

core_minimize_privileged_containers.notes: Exceptions for privileged containers should be clearly defined and monitored.

core_no_secrets_envs.title: Pod does not contain secret environment variables
core_no_secrets_envs.description: **Kubernetes Pods** containers define environment variables sourced from **Secrets** via `secretKeyRef` instead of mounting them as files.
core_no_secrets_envs.risk:
Secrets in env vars weaken **confidentiality**:
- Leak via logs, dumps, `/proc/*/environ`, debug UIs, and pod metadata
- Propagate to child processes; rotation is hard
Attackers can steal credentials for unauthorized access and **lateral movement**, risking data integrity and service availability.

wui.description:
Use **Secrets as files** (read-only volumes) and load at runtime.
- Apply **least privilege** RBAC to Secret access
- Scope Secrets to required containers; avoid logging env
- Prefer short-lived creds and regular rotation; set `immutable: true` when suitable
- Layer **defense in depth** with network and runtime controls

other.description:
1. Open Kubernetes Dashboard and go to Workloads > Deployments (or StatefulSets/Pods)
2. Select <example_resource_name> and click Edit > Edit YAML
3. For each container, remove any env entries that use valueFrom.secretKeyRef
4. If the app still needs the secret, add a volume that references your Secret and mount it into the container (e.g., mountPath /etc/secret)
5. Save the changes

core_no_secrets_envs.notes: Mounting secrets as files allows for dynamic updates of secrets without needing to restart the pod.

cosmosdb_account_firewall_use_selected_n.title: Cosmos DB account firewall allows access only from selected networks
cosmosdb_account_firewall_use_selected_n.description:
**Azure Cosmos DB accounts** limit connectivity to **selected networks** using virtual network rules and/or IP allowlists rather than permitting access from all networks.

The evaluation determines whether the account's network firewall enforces this restriction.
cosmosdb_account_firewall_use_selected_n.risk:
Access from all networks enlarges the attack surface. If keys or tokens are exposed or privileges are misconfigured, attackers anywhere can read or modify data, harming **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

Weak segmentation also enables SSRF/pivot paths from Azure services and can impact **availability** through abuse.

wui.description:
Set network access to `Selected networks` with **least privilege**:
- Prefer **private endpoints** or VNet service endpoints with subnet ACLs
- Keep IP allowlists minimal; avoid `0.0.0.0`
- *When feasible*, set `publicNetworkAccess=Disabled` with Private Link
- Apply **defense in depth** and monitor access and firewall changes

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, open your Cosmos DB account
2. Go to Settings > Networking
3. Select Selected networks
4. Click Add existing virtual network, choose the VNet and Subnet, then click Enable and Add
5. Click Save

cosmosdb_account_firewall_use_selected_n.notes: Failure to whitelist the correct networks will result in a connection loss.

cosmosdb_account_use_aad_and_rbac.title: Cosmos DB account has local authentication disabled and uses Azure AD authentication with Azure RBAC
cosmosdb_account_use_aad_and_rbac.description: **Azure Cosmos DB accounts** configured to use **Microsoft Entra ID** with **Azure RBAC** by disabling key-based credentials (`disableLocalAuth=true`). Clients authenticate with identities rather than account keys.
cosmosdb_account_use_aad_and_rbac.risk: With local/key-based auth enabled, **long-lived account keys** can be leaked or shared, enabling unauthorized reads/writes and tampering. Access bypasses **MFA** and granular **RBAC**, hindering rotation/revocation and increasing persistence and lateral movement risks.

wui.description: Disable local authentication by setting `disableLocalAuth=true` and require **Entra ID + Azure RBAC** for control and data access. Use **managed identities**, apply **least privilege** roles, retire shared keys, and enforce **zero trust** with conditional access and short-lived credentials.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal and open your Cosmos DB account
2. In the left menu, select Keys
3. Turn on Disable key-based authentication (Disable local authentication)
4. Click Save

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: Disable local (key-based) auth on a Cosmos DB account
resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<example_resource_name>"
  offer_type          = "Standard"
  kind                = "GlobalDocumentDB"

  geo_location {
    location          = "<example_resource_name>"
    failover_priority = 0
  }

  local_authentication_disabled = true # Critical: Disables key-based auth to enforce Entra ID + RBAC
}
```

cosmosdb_account_use_private_endpoints.title: Cosmos DB account uses private endpoint connections
cosmosdb_account_use_private_endpoints.description: **Azure Cosmos DB accounts** are assessed for **private endpoint connections** that keep data-plane traffic on private IPs within authorized virtual networks.
cosmosdb_account_use_private_endpoints.risk:
Without **private endpoints**, access may use public endpoints or broad IP rules, enabling:
- interception and credential replay
- unauthorized queries and data exfiltration
- lateral movement via exposed paths

This degrades **confidentiality** and can impact **availability** under abusive traffic.

wui.description:
Adopt **Azure Private Link** for Cosmos DB:
- Create private endpoints for required subresources
- Link a private DNS zone so clients resolve to private IPs
- Set `PublicNetworkAccess=Disabled`; keep tight firewall rules
- Allow only needed VNets/subnets; apply NSGs
- Enforce least privilege and monitor access patterns

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, open your Cosmos DB account
2. Go to Networking > Private access
3. Click + Private endpoint
4. Resource type: Microsoft.AzureCosmosDB/databaseAccounts; Resource: select your account; Target subresource: Sql
5. Select your Virtual network and Subnet
6. Click Review + create, then Create
7. Verify the private endpoint connection appears under Networking > Private access

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Create a Private Endpoint to a Cosmos DB account (adds a private endpoint connection)
resource "azurerm_private_endpoint" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<location>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  subnet_id           = "<example_subnet_id>"

  private_service_connection {
    name                           = "<example_resource_name>"
    private_connection_resource_id = "<example_cosmosdb_account_id>" # CRITICAL: Cosmos DB account ID
    subresource_names              = ["Sql"]                           # CRITICAL: targets Cosmos DB subresource to create the connection
  }
}
```

cosmosdb_account_use_private_endpoints.notes: Only whitelisted services will have access to communicate with the Cosmos DB.

cs_kubernetes_log_service_enabled.title: Kubernetes cluster has Log Service enabled
cs_kubernetes_log_service_enabled.description: **Alibaba Cloud Log Service** supports collection, search, storage, and analysis for container and audit logs in **Kubernetes Engine clusters**. When enabled, it automatically collects `kube-apiserver` audit logs, ingress logs, and stdout/stderr from containers. These logs are stored persistently and are essential for operational visibility, security monitoring, and compliance auditing.
cs_kubernetes_log_service_enabled.risk: Without **Log Service**, there is no centralized collection of container logs or cluster events, impairing **incident investigation**, **compliance auditing**, and **security monitoring**. Attackers could operate undetected with no audit trail of API server calls or pod events, impacting cluster **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

wui.description: Enable **Log Service** during cluster creation by setting `Enable Log Service` to **Enabled**. For existing clusters, verify that `AuditProjectName` is configured in the cluster metadata.

other.description:
1. Log on to the **ACK Console**.
2. Select the target cluster and click its name to open the cluster detail page.
3. Select **Cluster Auditing** on the left column and check if the audit page is shown.
4. To enable: When creating a new cluster, set `Enable Log Service` to **Enabled**.

cs_kubernetes_network_policy_enabled.title: Kubernetes cluster has Network policy enabled
cs_kubernetes_network_policy_enabled.description: **Alibaba Cloud Kubernetes Engine** clusters should enable **Network Policy** via the **Terway** plugin. A `NetworkPolicy` defines how pods communicate using label-based rules. By default, pods accept traffic from any source; NetworkPolicy restricts traffic to explicitly allowed connections, enforcing least privilege at the network level.
cs_kubernetes_network_policy_enabled.risk: Without **Network Policies**, all pods communicate freely, creating an unrestricted flat network. An attacker who compromises a single pod can move **laterally**, accessing sensitive services, databases, and secrets. The absence of network segmentation undermines **defense in depth** and increases the blast radius of any compromise, impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity** of workloads.

wui.description: Select the **Terway** network plugin during cluster creation to enable Network Policy support. Existing clusters using **Flannel** cannot be migrated to Terway and must be recreated.

other.description:
1. When creating a new cluster in the **ACK Console**, select **Terway** in the `Network Plugin` option to enable Network Policy support.
2. Note that existing clusters using **Flannel** cannot be migrated to **Terway**.

cs_kubernetes_private_cluster_enabled.title: Kubernetes cluster is created with private cluster enabled
cs_kubernetes_private_cluster_enabled.description: **Alibaba Cloud Kubernetes Engine** clusters should be configured as **private clusters** so the API server endpoint is not publicly accessible. In a private cluster, nodes lack public IPs and all node-to-master communication occurs through **VPC peering**. This reduces the attack surface by eliminating direct internet exposure of the control plane and worker nodes.
cs_kubernetes_private_cluster_enabled.risk: A public **API server endpoint** allows attackers to probe for vulnerabilities, perform **brute force attacks**, or exploit misconfigurations. Automated scanners and botnets can target it, increasing risk of unauthorized access. This impacts **confidentiality** and **integrity** by potentially allowing attackers to execute commands, deploy malicious workloads, or exfiltrate data.

wui.description: Disable **Public Access** during cluster creation to ensure the API server is not exposed to the public internet. For existing clusters, remove the public endpoint if one was configured.

other.description:
1. Log on to the **ACK Console**.
2. Select the target cluster name and go to the cluster detail page.
3. Check if there is no `API Server Public Network Endpoint` under Cluster Information.
4. When creating a new cluster, make sure **Public Access** is not enabled.

cs_kubernetes_rbac_enabled.title: Kubernetes cluster has RBAC authorization enabled
cs_kubernetes_rbac_enabled.description: **Alibaba Cloud Kubernetes Engine** clusters should have **RBAC** enabled for fine-grained authorization. RBAC lets administrators define roles with specific permissions at cluster and namespace level, ensuring users and service accounts access only needed resources. Legacy **ABAC** grants broad, static permissions and should be disabled in favor of RBAC.
cs_kubernetes_rbac_enabled.risk: Without **RBAC**, clusters may rely on legacy **ABAC** which grants **overly broad permissions** that cannot be scoped to specific namespaces or resources. This increases the risk of **unauthorized access** and **privilege escalation**, where a compromised account could access sensitive resources across the cluster, impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

wui.description: Ensure **RBAC** is enabled on all Kubernetes Engine clusters and that legacy **ABAC** authorization is disabled. Configure RBAC roles and bindings through the ACK Console Authorizations page to enforce least-privilege access.

other.description:
1. Log on to the **ACK Console**.
2. Navigate to **Clusters** -> **Authorizations** page.
3. Select the target RAM sub-account and configure the RBAC roles on specific clusters or namespaces.
4. Ensure **RBAC** is enabled and legacy ABAC authorization is disabled.

database_autonomous_database_access_rest.title: Autonomous Shared Database (ADB) is deployed within a VCN or restricts public access with whitelisted IPs excluding 0.0.0.0/0
database_autonomous_database_access_rest.description: **OCI Autonomous Database (shared)** network exposure is evaluated: instances are treated as restricted when using a **VCN private endpoint** or when **ACLs** allow only specified IPs/VCNs. It identifies configurations with no ACL and no VCN, or ACLs permitting `0.0.0.0/0`.
database_autonomous_database_access_rest.risk:
With **open access**, attackers can probe endpoints, brute-force credentials, or abuse leaked wallets to connect.

Impact:
- Confidentiality: unauthorized queries and data exfiltration
- Integrity: malicious changes
- Availability: heavy queries or scans causing service disruption

wui.description:
Prefer **VCN private endpoints** to eliminate internet exposure. If public access is required, enforce **least privilege** by limiting ACLs to specific CIDRs or VCNs; never use `0.0.0.0/0`.

Add **defense in depth** with NSGs and private connectivity (VPN/peering), monitor access, and rotate client wallets regularly.

other.description:
1. In OCI Console, go to Autonomous Database and select the instance
2. Click More Actions > Update
3. Under Network Access, enable Access control list (ACL)
4. Add an allowed IP/CIDR (exclude 0.0.0.0/0) and remove any 0.0.0.0/0 entry
5. Click Save

databricks_workspace_cmk_encryption_enab.title: Databricks workspace uses a customer-managed key (CMK) for encryption at rest
databricks_workspace_cmk_encryption_enab.description: **Azure Databricks workspaces** are evaluated for use of **customer-managed keys** (`CMK`) on at-rest encryption, based on the workspace's managed disk encryption configuration.
databricks_workspace_cmk_encryption_enab.risk:
Without **CMK**, keys are provider-controlled, degrading **confidentiality** and incident response.
- Slower revoke/rotate during breaches
- Weaker **separation of duties** and audit trails
- Larger blast radius if storage or control plane is compromised

cli.description: az databricks workspace update --name <workspace_name> --resource-group <resource_group_name> --key-source Microsoft.Keyvault --key-name <key_name> --key-vault https://<key_vault_name>.vault.azure.net/ --key-version <key_version>

wui.description:
Enable `CMK` for workspace encryption via **Key Vault** or **Managed HSM** and enforce:
- Least privilege for key usage
- Regular rotation and retire old versions
- Audit logging and alerts on key ops
- Separation of duties for key vs data roles
- Deny-by-default policies limiting scope

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to your Databricks workspace
2. Select Settings > Encryption (or Customer-managed keys)
3. If prompted, click Prepare encryption and wait for completion
4. Set Key source to Microsoft Key Vault
5. Select the Key Vault key and specific key version for managed disks
6. Save to apply customer-managed key encryption

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_databricks_workspace" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<region>"
  sku                 = "premium"

  customer_managed_key_enabled      = true  # CRITICAL: enable CMK
  managed_disk_cmk_key_vault_key_id = "<example_resource_id>" # CRITICAL: key ID (Key Vault key) for managed disks
}
```

databricks_workspace_cmk_encryption_enab.notes: Customer-managed key (CMK) encryption is only available for Databricks workspaces on the Premium tier.

databricks_workspace_vnet_injection_enab.title: Databricks workspace is deployed in a customer-managed VNet (VNet Injection enabled)
databricks_workspace_vnet_injection_enab.description: **Azure Databricks workspaces** using **VNet injection** are placed in a customer-managed VNet rather than a Databricks-managed network. This evaluates whether a workspace is linked to a customer VNet.
databricks_workspace_vnet_injection_enab.risk:
Using a Databricks-managed VNet limits control over routing, egress, and access boundaries, degrading **confidentiality** and **integrity**.
- Unrestricted outbound paths enable **data exfiltration**
- Harder to enforce **private endpoints** and NSG policies
- Increased chance of **lateral movement** into compute nodes

wui.description:
Deploy workspaces in a customer-managed VNet and apply **defense in depth**:
- Enforce egress control with firewalls/NAT and UDRs
- Prefer **private endpoints** to public access
- Apply **least privilege** NSG rules and segregate subnets
- Use DNS controls and monitoring to detect anomalies

other.description:
1. In the Azure Portal, go to Create a resource > Azure Databricks
2. On Basics, enter workspace name, region, and resource group
3. Open the Networking tab and select Your VNet (VNet injection)
4. Choose your Virtual network and select the Host (public) and Container (private) subnets
5. Click Review + create, then Create
6. Migrate workloads to this workspace and delete the non-VNet workspace if no longer needed

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Azure Databricks workspace with VNet injection
resource "azurerm_databricks_workspace" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<region>"
  sku                 = "premium"

  custom_parameters {
    virtual_network_id  = "/subscriptions/<example_resource_id>/resourceGroups/<example_resource_name>/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/<example_resource_name>" # CRITICAL: Enables VNet injection by using your VNet
    public_subnet_name  = "<example_resource_name>-public"   # Required: host (public) subnet
    private_subnet_name = "<example_resource_name>-private"  # Required: container (private) subnet
  }
}
```

dataproc_encrypted_with_cmks_disabled.title: Dataproc cluster is encrypted with a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK)
dataproc_encrypted_with_cmks_disabled.description: Dataproc clusters use **Customer-Managed Encryption Keys** (`CMEK`) for VM **persistent disk** encryption. The finding determines whether a customer KMS key is configured for disk data instead of the default Google-managed keys.
dataproc_encrypted_with_cmks_disabled.risk: Without **CMEK** on Dataproc disks, keys remain provider-controlled, limiting **rotation**, **revocation**, and **location control**. This reduces containment if disks or snapshots are exposed and may block **data sovereignty** requirements, impacting **confidentiality** and incident response.

wui.description:
Enable **CMEK** for Dataproc disk, job-argument, and staging-bucket encryption.
- Grant KMS access with **least privilege** to required service accounts
- Enforce **regular rotation** and support **revocation/disable** procedures
- Keep keys co-located with data and monitor KMS usage
- Consider **Cloud EKM** for external key control

other.description:
1. In Google Cloud Console, go to Dataproc > Clusters
2. Click Create cluster
3. In Cluster configuration, open Security (or Encryption)
4. For Disk encryption key, select Customer-managed key and choose your Cloud KMS key
5. Click Create
6. Migrate workloads to the new cluster and delete the old non-CMEK cluster

datasync_task_logging_enabled.title: DataSync task has CloudWatch Logs log group configured for logging
datasync_task_logging_enabled.description:
**AWS DataSync tasks** are evaluated for a configured **CloudWatch Logs** destination (`CloudWatchLogGroupArn`).

Tasks that specify a log group are recognized as logging-enabled; those without one are identified as not publishing execution events.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
datasync_task_logging_enabled.risk: **Absent DataSync task logs** create blind spots, preventing timely detection of **failed or partial transfers**, unexpected deletions, or anomalies. This undermines data **integrity** verification, obscures potential **exfiltration** indicators, and slows forensics and recovery, reducing **availability** during incidents.

wui.description: Configure each task to publish logs to a dedicated CloudWatch Logs group. Select an appropriate log level (e.g., `BASIC` or `TRANSFER`), enforce **least privilege** for log access, set **retention** and immutability, and integrate alerts. Centralize and monitor logs to support **defense in depth** and incident response.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to DataSync > Tasks
2. Select the task and click Edit
3. In the Logging section, set CloudWatch Log group to an existing log group
4. Click Save

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable CloudWatch Logs for a DataSync task
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::DataSync::Task
    Properties:
      SourceLocationArn: <example_source_location_arn>
      DestinationLocationArn: <example_destination_location_arn>
      CloudWatchLogGroupArn: <example_log_group_arn>  # Critical: attaches a CloudWatch Logs group to enable task logging
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Enable CloudWatch Logs for a DataSync task
resource "aws_datasync_task" "<example_resource_name>" {
  source_location_arn      = "<example_source_location_arn>"
  destination_location_arn = "<example_destination_location_arn>"
  cloudwatch_log_group_arn = "<example_log_group_arn>"  # Critical: attaches a CloudWatch Logs group to enable task logging
}
```

defender_additional_email_configured_wit.title: Security contact has additional email addresses configured
defender_additional_email_configured_wit.description: **Microsoft Defender for Cloud** security contact settings include **additional email recipients** defined in the `emails` field to receive alert notifications.
defender_additional_email_configured_wit.risk: Relying only on subscription owners for alerts creates a **single point of failure**. Missed or delayed notifications extend attacker dwell time, enabling data exfiltration (**confidentiality**), unauthorized changes (**integrity**), and service disruption (**availability**). Absence or turnover can silently suppress alerts.

wui.description: Use a monitored, team-managed distribution list as the **security contact** in `emails`. Include SOC/on-call for 24/7 coverage and enable role-based notifications for redundancy. Tune severities to reduce noise while capturing high-risk events, and integrate alerts with ticketing/SIEM for **defense in depth** and rapid response.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal
2. Go to Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings
3. Select the target subscription
4. Click Email notifications
5. In Email addresses, enter at least one email (comma-separated for multiple)
6. Click Save

dms_instance_multi_az_enabled.title: DMS replication instance has Multi-AZ enabled
dms_instance_multi_az_enabled.description: **AWS DMS replication instances** are evaluated for **Multi-AZ** configuration. Instances with `multi_az` enabled are treated as having a cross-AZ standby; those without it are identified as single-AZ.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
dms_instance_multi_az_enabled.risk: Without **Multi-AZ**, a single-AZ failure or maintenance event can halt migrations, causing extended downtime (**availability**) and replication gaps or rollbacks (**integrity**). Tasks may stall, increase cutover risk, and require manual recovery when the replication instance is unavailable.

wui.description:
Enable **Multi-AZ** (set `multi_az` to `true`) on DMS replication instances that handle production or time-sensitive migrations to ensure redundancy and automatic failover.

Apply HA principles: distribute across AZs, test failover, monitor health, and plan maintenance to minimize impact.

other.description:
1. Open the AWS DMS console
2. Go to Replication instances and select your instance
3. Click Modify
4. Check Multi-AZ
5. Check Apply immediately
6. Click Modify to save

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable Multi-AZ on a DMS replication instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::DMS::ReplicationInstance
    Properties:
      ReplicationInstanceClass: dms.t3.micro
      MultiAZ: true  # Critical: enables Multi-AZ to pass the check
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Enable Multi-AZ on a DMS replication instance
resource "aws_dms_replication_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  replication_instance_id   = "<example_resource_name>"
  replication_instance_class = "dms.t3.micro"
  multi_az                  = true  # Critical: enables Multi-AZ to pass the check
}
```

defender_antispam_outbound_policy_config.title: Defender outbound spam policy is configured to notify recipients when senders are blocked or exceed sending limits
defender_antispam_outbound_policy_config.description: **Microsoft Defender for Office 365 outbound spam policies** must send **administrator alerts** and Bcc **suspicious outbound messages** when a sender exceeds limits or is blocked. The assessment checks for `notify limit exceeded` and `notify sender blocked` with recipient addresses in the default policy and any applicable custom policies.
defender_antispam_outbound_policy_config.risk: Absent alerts and copies, **compromised mailboxes** can exfiltrate data and send phishing undetected. This harms **email deliverability** through blocklisting and throttling (**availability**), undermines domain **integrity**, and impedes **forensics** by removing evidence needed to triage abusive outbound traffic.

wui.description: Enable outbound spam notifications and Bcc suspicious messages to a monitored mailbox, applying them consistently to default and scoped policies. Set prudent sending limits and block actions, disable unnecessary external forwarding, and monitor alerts-aligning with **least privilege** and **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Microsoft 365 Defender: https://security.microsoft.com
2. Go to Email & collaboration > Policies & rules > Threat policies > Anti-spam
3. Open Anti-spam outbound policy (Default) and select Edit protection settings
4. Under Notifications:
   - Check "Send a copy of suspicious outbound messages or messages that exceed these limits to these users and groups" and add <EMAIL>
   - Check "Notify these users and groups if a sender is blocked due to sending outbound spam" and add <EMAIL>
5. Click Save

defender_antispam_outbound_policy_config.notes: Ensure settings are applied to the highest priority policy if custom policies exist. Default values do not notify or copy outbound spam messages by default.

defender_antispam_outbound_policy_forwar.title: Defender Outbound Spam policy disables mail forwarding
defender_antispam_outbound_policy_forwar.description: **Microsoft Defender for Office 365 outbound spam policies** are evaluated to confirm that automatic mail forwarding is disabled in the default policy and in any custom policies applied to users, groups, or domains.
defender_antispam_outbound_policy_forwar.risk: Allowing **automatic forwarding** enables covert **data exfiltration**, eroding **confidentiality**. Attackers or insiders can auto-route mail to external inboxes, persist access, evade monitoring, and harvest sensitive content (tickets, approvals, MFA codes), enabling **lateral movement** and fraud while reducing auditability.

wui.description: Disable **automatic forwarding** globally in outbound spam policies to enforce **least privilege** on data flows. *If exceptions are required*, restrict to named senders or domains, document approvals, and review regularly. Add **DLP**, alerts on new forwarding rules, and mailbox auditing for **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. Sign in to https://security.microsoft.com
2. Go to Email & collaboration > Policies & rules > Threat policies > Anti-spam
3. Open Anti-spam outbound policy (Default) or the target custom policy
4. Click Edit protection settings and set Automatic forwarding rules to Off - Forwarding is disabled, then Save
5. For custom policies, ensure the policy Status is On (enabled); repeat for any additional policies

defender_antispam_outbound_policy_forwar.notes: Ensure settings are applied to the highest priority policy if custom policies exist.

defender_antispam_policy_inbound_no_allo.title: Inbound anti-spam policy does not contain allowed domains
defender_antispam_policy_inbound_no_allo.description:
**Microsoft Defender for Office 365 inbound anti-spam policies** are evaluated for domains listed in `AllowedSenderDomains`.

The finding identifies any policy where this list is populated rather than empty.
defender_antispam_policy_inbound_no_allo.risk: Populating `AllowedSenderDomains` makes messages from those domains skip **spam filtering** and **email authentication** (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), often delivered with SCL `-1`. Attackers can spoof such domains to phish credentials, enable BEC, and alter mailboxes, undermining **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

wui.description:
- Keep `AllowedSenderDomains` empty.
- Use narrowly scoped allow logic that requires authentication alignment and additional conditions (sender, IP, headers).
- Make any exceptions temporary and reviewed.

Apply **least privilege** and **defense in depth** to email trust decisions.

other.description:
1. Open Microsoft 365 Defender: https://security.microsoft.com/antispam
2. Open each inbound anti-spam policy (Default and any custom).
3. Click Edit allowed and blocked senders and domains.
4. Select Allow domains.
5. Remove all domains, then click Done and Save.
6. Repeat for any remaining inbound anti-spam policies.

defender_assessments_vm_endpoint_protect.title: All virtual machines in the subscription have endpoint protection installed
defender_assessments_vm_endpoint_protect.description: **Azure virtual machines** are assessed for the presence of an **endpoint protection (antimalware)** solution and its reported health across the subscription
defender_assessments_vm_endpoint_protect.risk:
Absent or unhealthy **endpoint protection** lets malware execute on VMs, risking:
- Data exfiltration (confidentiality)
- Tampering and credential theft (integrity)
- Ransomware, cryptomining, and outages (availability)

It also enables persistence and lateral movement to other cloud resources.

wui.description: Enforce an **endpoint protection/EDR** baseline on every VM. Enable real-time protection, automatic updates, and alerting; use tamper protection and keep exclusions minimal. Apply **least privilege**, keep OS and agents patched, and continuously monitor coverage and health via Defender for Cloud.

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Microsoft Defender for Cloud
2. Open Recommendations and search for "Install endpoint protection solution on virtual machines"
3. Select the recommendation, click Fix
4. Select all affected VMs and click Remediate (or Apply)
5. Wait for remediation to complete and the recommendation status to turn Healthy

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Install Microsoft Antimalware (endpoint protection) on a VM
resource "azurerm_virtual_machine_extension" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                 = "IaaSAntimalware"
  virtual_machine_id   = "<example_resource_id>"
  publisher            = "Microsoft.Azure.Security"  # Critical: Antimalware extension publisher
  type                 = "IaaSAntimalware"           # Critical: installs endpoint protection
  type_handler_version = "1.5"
}
```

defender_assessments_vm_endpoint_protect.notes: Endpoint protection will incur an additional cost to you.

defender_attack_path_notifications_prope.title: Security contact has attack path email notifications enabled at or above the configured minimum risk level
defender_attack_path_notifications_prope.description: **Microsoft Defender for Cloud** attack path email notifications are configured per subscription with a defined **minimal risk level**, and the setting is present and meets the required threshold.
defender_attack_path_notifications_prope.risk: Without alerts on **exploitable attack paths**, security teams lose visibility, enabling **lateral movement**, **privilege escalation**, and **data exfiltration** before containment, degrading confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

wui.description: Enable and maintain **attack path notifications** with a minimal risk level at or above your tolerance (e.g., `High`). Send to monitored, role-based recipients. Apply **defense in depth** by integrating alerts with central monitoring and automation for prompt triage.

other.description:

2. Select the target subscription
3. Open Email notifications
4. Enable "Notify about attack paths with the following risk level (or higher)"

defender_auto_provisioning_log_analytics.title: Defender auto-provisioning of Log Analytics agent for Azure VMs is enabled

Attackers can persist or move laterally unnoticed, undermining **confidentiality** and **integrity**, while delayed detection hampers effective response.

cli.description: az security auto-provisioning-setting update --name default --auto-provision On

wui.description:
Set **Defender for Cloud auto-provisioning** to `On` so all VMs receive the monitoring agent consistently.

Apply **defense in depth** by enforcing coverage for new and existing machines, standardizing workspaces, and auditing enrollment. Use **least privilege** for data access and integrate with endpoint protection and vulnerability assessment.

other.description:

2. Select Environment settings, then choose your subscription
3. Open Auto provisioning
4. Set Auto-provisioning of Log Analytics agent to On
5. Click Save

defender_auto_provisioning_vulnerabilty_.title: All virtual machines in the subscription have a vulnerability assessment solution installed
defender_auto_provisioning_vulnerabilty_.description: **Microsoft Defender for Cloud** evaluates whether **Azure VMs** and **Arc-enabled machines** have a **vulnerability assessment solution** deployed and reporting healthy coverage across the subscription.
defender_auto_provisioning_vulnerabilty_.risk:
Without continuous **vulnerability assessment**, unpatched flaws persist, enabling:
- **Remote code execution** and privilege escalation
- **Ransomware** disrupting availability
- **Data exfiltration** via lateral movement

Confidentiality, integrity, and availability are reduced across affected machines.

wui.description:
Enable subscription-wide **auto-provisioning** of a **vulnerability assessment** for all Azure and Arc machines and enforce it with **policy** for existing and new hosts.

Apply **least privilege** to deployment identities, integrate with **patch management**, and monitor findings for timely remediation.

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Microsoft Defender for Cloud
2. Open Environment settings and select your <subscription>
3. Go to Settings & monitoring (Auto-provisioning)
4. Find Vulnerability assessment for machines, set to On, and select Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management
5. Click Save

defender_auto_provisioning_vulnerabilty_.notes: Additional licensing is required and configuration of Azure Arc introduces complexity beyond this recommendation.

defender_container_images_resolved_vulne.title: All Azure running container images in the subscription have no unresolved vulnerabilities
defender_container_images_resolved_vulne.description: **Running container images** are evaluated for unresolved **vulnerability findings** (`CVEs`) reported by Microsoft Defender for Cloud. The check reviews images currently in use across Kubernetes workloads and identifies where vulnerabilities remain unremediated.
defender_container_images_resolved_vulne.risk:
Unremediated `CVEs` in active images enable:
- **RCE**, container escape, and node takeover affecting **integrity/availability**
- **Data exfiltration** and secret theft compromising **confidentiality**
Adversaries can use public exploits to pivot across clusters and pipelines, tamper images, and disrupt services.

wui.description:
Adopt **risk-based patching** and **least privilege**:
- Rebuild from updated bases; pin versions, avoid `latest`
- Sign images; enforce **admission control** to block high-severity CVEs
- Drop root, restrict capabilities, isolate networks
- Continuously scan in CI/CD and at runtime; retire vulnerable images

other.description:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Recommendations
2. Open "Azure running container images should have vulnerabilities resolved"
3. Under Affected resources, select a running workload and view its vulnerable image findings
4. Rebuild the image with patched packages or a newer base image and push it to your registry
5. Go to your AKS cluster > Workloads > Deployments, edit the deployment, and update the container image to the patched tag; Save
6. Wait for pods to roll out and Defender to rescan; the recommendation should turn Healthy after the next scan

defender_container_images_scan_enabled.title: Subscription has container image vulnerability scanning enabled
defender_container_images_scan_enabled.description: **Azure subscriptions** have **container image vulnerability assessment** enabled for **Azure Container Registry** via Microsoft Defender for Cloud (`ContainerRegistriesVulnerabilityAssessments`). Images in registries are evaluated for known package vulnerabilities in their packages and dependencies.
defender_container_images_scan_enabled.risk: Without registry scanning, **known CVEs** in images can reach runtime, enabling **RCE**, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This undermines data confidentiality and integrity and can reduce availability through cryptomining or service disruption.

wui.description:
Enable **Defender for Cloud** image assessment for registries and adopt **shift-left scanning**.
- Block deployment of images with high-severity findings
- Rebuild from patched base images regularly
- Enforce **least privilege** on registry access
- Use image signing and admission controls

other.description:
1. In Azure Portal, open Microsoft Defender for Cloud
2. Go to Environment settings and select your subscription
3. Open Settings (or Defender plans)
4. Find Containers and set Plan to On/Standard
5. Enable Container registries vulnerability assessments
6. Click Save

defender_container_images_scan_enabled.notes: When using an Azure container registry, you might occasionally encounter problems. For example, you might not be able to pull a container image because of an issue with Docker in your local environment. Or, a network issue might prevent you from connecting to the registry.

defender_ensure_defender_for_app_service.title: Defender for App Services is set to On (Standard pricing tier)

- Integrity compromise through web shells or code tampering
- Availability impact from takeover and resource abuse

defender_ensure_defender_for_arm_is_on.title: Defender for Azure Resource Manager is set to On (Standard pricing tier)

defender_ensure_defender_for_azure_sql_d.title: Defender for Azure SQL databases is set to On (Standard pricing tier)

defender_ensure_defender_for_containers_.title: Defender for Containers is set to On (Standard pricing tier)

cli.description: az security pricing create --name Containers --tier Standard

other.description:

defender_ensure_defender_for_cosmosdb_is.title: Defender for Cosmos DB is set to On (Standard pricing tier)

wui.description: Enable **Defender for Databases** at the `Standard` tier for all supported database types across subscriptions. other.description:

defender_ensure_defender_for_dns_is_on.title: Defender for DNS is set to On (Standard pricing tier)

other.description:

defender_ensure_defender_for_keyvault_is.title: Defender for Key Vaults is set to On (Standard pricing tier)

defender_ensure_iot_hub_defender_is_on.title: Defender for IoT Hub is set to On

defender_ensure_iot_hub_defender_is_on.notes: Enabling Microsoft Defender for IoT will incur additional charges dependent on the level of usage.

defender_ensure_mcas_is_enabled.title: Defender for Cloud Apps is enabled
