1. Create **RAM user groups** and assign policies to those groups.
2. Add users to the appropriate groups.
3. Detach any policies directly attached to users using the RAM Console or CLI.

ram_rotate_access_key_90_days.title: Access keys are rotated every 90 days or less
ram_rotate_access_key_90_days.description: **Alibaba Cloud RAM** access keys consist of an access key ID and a secret, which are used to sign programmatic requests. RAM users need their own access keys to make programmatic calls from SDKs, CLIs, or direct API calls. It is recommended that all access keys be **regularly rotated** every 90 days or less to reduce the window of opportunity for compromised keys to be used.
ram_rotate_access_key_90_days.risk: Access keys might be compromised by being left in code, configuration files, or cloud storage and then stolen by attackers. Without regular **access key rotation**, a compromised key can remain valid indefinitely, allowing persistent unauthorized access. This threatens the **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and **availability** of all resources accessible via those credentials.

cli.description: aliyun ram CreateAccessKey --UserName <ram_user> && aliyun ram UpdateAccessKey --UserAccessKeyId <old_access_key_ID> --Status Inactive --UserName <ram_user> && aliyun ram DeleteAccessKey --UserAccessKeyId <old_access_key_ID> --UserName <ram_user>

wui.description: Rotate all RAM user access keys every 90 days or less to limit the impact of compromised credentials.

other.description:
1. Create a new **AccessKey pair** for rotation.
2. Update all applications and systems to use the new AccessKey pair.
3. **Disable** the original AccessKey pair.
4. Confirm that your applications and systems are working.
5. **Delete** the original AccessKey pair.

ram_user_console_access_unused.title: RAM user not logged on for 90 days or longer has console logon disabled
ram_user_console_access_unused.description: **Alibaba Cloud RAM** users can log on to the console by using their username and password. If a user has not logged on for **90 days or longer**, it is recommended to disable the console access of the user. Disabling unused console access reduces the attack surface by removing unnecessary logon capabilities from potentially abandoned or dormant accounts.
ram_user_console_access_unused.risk: Inactive accounts with console access are common targets for **account takeover**. An abandoned account or one with a **compromised password** unused for over 90 days may go unmonitored, allowing undetected unauthorized access. This risks the **confidentiality** and **integrity** of cloud resources accessible through the account.

wui.description: Disable console access for RAM users that have not logged on for 90 days or longer to reduce the attack surface.

other.description:
1. Log on to the **RAM Console**.
2. Choose **Identities** > **Users**.
3. In the User Logon Name/Display Name column, click the username of the target RAM user.
4. In the Console Logon Management section, click **Modify Logon Settings**.
5. In the Console Password Logon section, select **Disabled**.
6. Click **OK**.

rbac_cluster_admin_usage.title: Cluster role binding does not grant the cluster-admin role
rbac_cluster_admin_usage.description: RBAC ClusterRoleBindings that bind to the `cluster-admin` ClusterRole are identified, showing where subjects receive super-user permissions across all namespaces.
rbac_cluster_admin_usage.risk:
**Excessive `cluster-admin` grants** give full API control, risking:
- Secret exfiltration (confidentiality)
- RBAC tampering (integrity)
- Destructive actions causing outages (availability)

A compromised subject can escalate, persist via new bindings, and laterally impact all namespaces.

wui.description: Apply **least privilege**: replace `cluster-admin` with narrowly scoped Roles/ClusterRoles and bind per namespace. Reserve super-user access for break-glass, time-bound with approval and audit. Enforce **separation of duties**, review RBAC regularly, and monitor role/binding changes for **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. List ClusterRoleBindings that use cluster-admin:
   ```
   kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .metadata.name'
   ```
2. For each name returned, delete the binding:
   ```
   kubectl delete clusterrolebinding <example_resource_name>
   ```
3. If access is still required, recreate with least privilege (example uses view):
   ```
   kubectl create clusterrolebinding <example_resource_name> --clusterrole=view --user=<example_resource_id>
   ```

rbac_cluster_admin_usage.notes: Modifying ClusterRoleBindings should be done with caution to avoid unintended access issues. Always ensure that critical system components have the necessary permissions to operate effectively.

rbac_minimize_csr_approval_access.title: User or group lacks update and patch access to the certificatesigningrequests/approval sub-resource
rbac_minimize_csr_approval_access.description:
**RBAC assignments** that grant `update` or `patch` on the `certificatesigningrequests/approval` subresource to **users or groups** via cluster-wide roles and bindings.

This highlights principals allowed to approve CSRs based on permissions defined in referenced ClusterRoles.
rbac_minimize_csr_approval_access.risk: Excess CSR approval rights enable **privilege escalation**. A malicious user can approve CSRs to mint client certificates for arbitrary identities, gaining unauthorized API access, impersonating system components, and enabling **data exfiltration** and tampering, harming **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

wui.description:
Apply **least privilege**: allow CSR approval only to a small, trusted approver role.
- Enforce **separation of duties** between CSR creation and approval
- Prefer automated approver controllers over manual grants
- Regularly review RBAC and remove broad ClusterRoleBindings
- Use **defense in depth** with auditing and short-lived credentials

other.description:
1. Open the Kubernetes Dashboard
2. Go to Access control (RBAC) > Cluster Role Bindings
3. Find the binding that assigns a User or Group to a role permitting certificatesigningrequests/approval
4. Click the binding, then Delete to remove it
5. If you must keep the binding: go to Access control (RBAC) > Cluster Roles, open the referenced role, click Edit (YAML), remove the rule that has resource "certificatesigningrequests/approval" with verbs ["update", "patch"], and save

rbac_minimize_csr_approval_access.notes: Carefully evaluate which users or service accounts require the ability to update the approval sub-resource of CSR objects.

rbac_minimize_node_proxy_subresource_acc.title: User or group has no get, list, or watch permissions on the nodes/proxy sub-resource
rbac_minimize_node_proxy_subresource_acc.description: **RBAC permissions** to the `nodes/proxy` subresource are analyzed. Any user or group granted `get`, `list`, or `watch` via cluster-wide bindings is reported.
rbac_minimize_node_proxy_subresource_acc.risk: Access to `nodes/proxy` exposes the **Kubelet API** through the apiserver proxy, which can bypass **audit** and **admission** controls. An adversary could execute commands in pods, read sensitive data, and pivot across nodes, impacting confidentiality and integrity; broad access also risks node-wide service disruption.

wui.description: Apply **least privilege**: avoid granting any verbs on `nodes/proxy` to users or groups. If access is unavoidable, limit it to trusted admins, scope narrowly, make it time-bound, and enforce **separation of duties**. Prefer namespace roles over cluster-wide bindings and review RBAC regularly as part of **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. Identify the ClusterRoleBinding that grants the user/group access: in your RBAC list, locate the binding referencing a ClusterRole that includes resources: nodes/proxy with verbs get, list, or watch
2. Edit the ClusterRole: run `kubectl edit clusterrole <example_resource_name>`
3. In `rules`, remove any entry where `resources` includes `nodes/proxy` and `verbs` includes `get`, `list`, or `watch`; save and exit
4. If you cannot modify the role (shared role), delete the specific ClusterRoleBinding that attaches it to the user/group: `kubectl delete clusterrolebinding <example_resource_name>`

rbac_minimize_node_proxy_subresource_acc.notes: Carefully evaluate which users or service accounts require the ability to access the proxy sub-resource of node objects.

rbac_minimize_pod_creation_access.title: Role or ClusterRole does not grant create permission on pods
rbac_minimize_pod_creation_access.description:
**Kubernetes RBAC** Roles and ClusterRoles that grant the `create` verb on `pods` are identified.

Rules are examined to find permissions allowing pod creation at namespace or cluster scope.
rbac_minimize_pod_creation_access.risk: Overly broad pod-creation rights allow adversaries to run **malicious pods**, mount service account tokens, or request privileged configs, enabling lateral movement. This endangers **confidentiality** (secrets), **integrity** (unauthorized changes), and **availability** (resource abuse, disruption).

wui.description: Apply **least privilege**: limit `pods` `create` to narrowly scoped service accounts and namespaces. Use **separation of duties** and avoid wildcards. Enforce controls with **Pod Security Admission** and policy engines (OPA/Kyverno) to block risky specs. Review RBAC regularly and remove unused grants.

other.description:
1. Identify the failing RBAC object (Role or ClusterRole) that allows pods create
2. For a ClusterRole: run `kubectl edit clusterrole <CLUSTERROLE_NAME>`
3. For a namespaced Role: run `kubectl edit role <ROLE_NAME> -n <NAMESPACE>`
4. In `rules`, find entries with `resources: ["pods"]` and remove `create` from `verbs` (keep only read verbs like get/list/watch)
5. Save and exit; verify with `kubectl get` that the change applied

rbac_minimize_pod_creation_access.notes: Care should be taken to ensure that restrictions do not disrupt normal operations of the cluster.

rbac_minimize_pv_creation_access.title: User or group does not have permission to create PersistentVolumes
rbac_minimize_pv_creation_access.description:
**Kubernetes RBAC** mapping of **users or groups** with the `create` verb on `persistentvolumes` through ClusterRoleBindings.

Shows which principals can provision PersistentVolumes cluster-wide.
rbac_minimize_pv_creation_access.risk:
With `create` on `persistentvolumes`, a principal can define **hostPath PVs** and mount them via claims, exposing node files and bypassing pod safeguards.

Results include secret disclosure and filesystem tampering (**confidentiality**/**integrity**), and potential node compromise affecting **availability**.

wui.description:
Enforce **least privilege**: permit `create` on `persistentvolumes` only for trusted storage controllers and select administrators.

Adopt **dynamic provisioning**, maintain **separation of duties**, and use **defense in depth** (Pod Security and admission policies) to prevent unsafe volumes like `hostPath`.

other.description:
1. Open the Kubernetes Dashboard (or your cluster RBAC UI)
2. Navigate to ClusterRoles and select the role referenced by the failing ClusterRoleBinding
3. Edit the role and locate the rule for resources: persistentvolumes
4. Remove the verb "create" from that rule's verbs list
5. Save the change to apply updated permissions

rbac_minimize_pv_creation_access.notes: Carefully evaluate which users or service accounts require the ability to create PersistentVolumes and restrict access accordingly.

rbac_minimize_secret_access.title: Role or ClusterRole does not grant get, list, or watch access to Kubernetes Secrets
rbac_minimize_secret_access.description: RBAC Roles and ClusterRoles granting read permissions to **Kubernetes Secrets** are identified. The evaluation looks for rules that allow `get`, `list`, or `watch` on `secrets`, either namespace-scoped or cluster-wide.
rbac_minimize_secret_access.risk: Excessive Secret read access compromises confidentiality of tokens, keys, and credentials. Attackers can harvest service account tokens to impersonate workloads, pivot across namespaces, and modify resources, threatening integrity and availability via lateral movement.

wui.description: Apply **least privilege**: avoid granting `get`, `list`, or `watch` on `secrets` except to narrowly scoped subjects. Constrain by namespace and `resourceNames` where feasible, use dedicated service accounts, avoid wildcards, and enforce **separation of duties** with policy and reviews.

other.description:
1. Identify the offending Role or ClusterRole name
2. Edit it: run either `kubectl edit clusterrole <example_resource_name>` or `kubectl edit role <example_resource_name> <namespace>`
3. In `rules`, remove any entry where `resources` contains `secrets` with verbs `get`, `list`, or `watch` (or delete those verbs/resources from the rule)
4. Save and exit; the change applies immediately

rbac_minimize_secret_access.notes: Care should be taken to avoid disrupting system components that require access to secrets for proper functioning.

rbac_minimize_service_account_token_crea.title: User or group does not have permission to create service account tokens
rbac_minimize_service_account_token_crea.description:
Cluster-wide RBAC identifies users or groups granted `create` on `serviceaccounts/token` via **ClusterRoles/ClusterRoleBindings**.

Highlights principals allowed to mint **service account tokens** through the TokenRequest subresource.
rbac_minimize_service_account_token_crea.risk:
Ability to mint **service account tokens** lets users assume those accounts' API rights, bypassing intended boundaries.

This enables privilege escalation, persistent access, and lateral movement, threatening confidentiality and integrity of cluster resources.

wui.description:
Enforce **least privilege**: avoid granting `create` on `serviceaccounts/token` to human users or broad groups. Restrict to trusted controllers and scope narrowly with namespaced **Role**/**RoleBinding**.

Apply **separation of duties**, periodic RBAC reviews, and **defense in depth** to limit token issuance.

other.description:
1. Identify the ClusterRoleBinding that grants a User/Group the role with create on serviceaccounts/token
2. Edit the referenced ClusterRole and remove any rule that allows create on resource "serviceaccounts/token":
   - kubectl edit clusterrole <example_resource_name>
   - In .rules[], delete entries with resources: ["serviceaccounts/token"] and verb: ["create"]
3. If the permission is only needed for other subjects, alternatively remove the specific User/Group from the ClusterRoleBinding:
   - kubectl edit clusterrolebinding <example_resource_name>
   - Delete the matching subject under .subjects and save

rbac_minimize_service_account_token_crea.notes: Consider using role-based access control to precisely define and manage permissions related to service account token creation.

rbac_minimize_webhook_config_access.title: User or group does not have create, update, or delete permissions on webhook configurations
rbac_minimize_webhook_config_access.description:
User or group RBAC assignments that grant privileges to `create`, `update`, or `delete` `validatingwebhookconfigurations` and `mutatingwebhookconfigurations` are identified.

Focus is on permissions that allow modifying **admission webhook** configuration objects.
rbac_minimize_webhook_config_access.risk:
Excess rights over **admission webhooks** allow reading or mutating all admitted API objects, undermining **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

An attacker could inject privileged mutations, bypass policy, or block admissions, leading to **privilege escalation** and cluster-wide **denial of service**.

wui.description:
- Enforce **least privilege**; limit webhook config `create`, `update`, `delete` to a small, trusted admin group.
- Avoid wildcard resources/verbs and use **separation of duties** with change approval.
- Monitor changes via **audit logging** to provide **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. Identify the ClusterRoleBinding that assigns a User or Group to a ClusterRole with create, update, or delete on validatingwebhookconfigurations or mutatingwebhookconfigurations (e.g., kubectl get clusterrolebindings).
2. Delete that ClusterRoleBinding, or edit the bound ClusterRole to remove any rules granting those verbs on these resources.
3. Save/apply the change; no restart is required.

rbac_minimize_webhook_config_access.notes: Consider using role-based access control to precisely define and manage permissions related to webhook configurations.

rds_cluster_copy_tags_to_snapshots.title: RDS DB cluster has copy tags to snapshots enabled
rds_cluster_copy_tags_to_snapshots.description:
**RDS DB clusters** are evaluated for the `CopyTagsToSnapshot` setting that propagates cluster tags to their DB snapshots.

*Aurora tagging is configured at the cluster level; instance-level copying isn't supported.*
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_copy_tags_to_snapshots.risk: **Missing tag propagation** leaves snapshots without consistent metadata, weakening **ABAC**, ownership tracking, and retention controls. This can allow overly broad access to backups, hinder incident scoping, and inflate costs-impacting **confidentiality** and operational governance.

wui.description:
Enable `CopyTagsToSnapshot` on all applicable **RDS/Aurora clusters**.
- Standardize required tags (owner, environment, data class)
- Use **least privilege** and **ABAC** based on tags
- Automate tagging and periodic audits so snapshots inherit metadata and lifecycle policies

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the DB cluster and choose Modify
3. Check Copy tags to snapshots
4. Click Continue, then Apply changes

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable copying tags to snapshots on an RDS DB cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      CopyTagsToSnapshot: true  # CRITICAL: ensures cluster tags are copied to snapshots
```

rds_cluster_critical_event_subscription.title: RDS cluster event subscription is enabled for maintenance and failure categories
rds_cluster_critical_event_subscription.description: **RDS event subscriptions** for the `db-cluster` source type are enabled and cover critical cluster event categories: **`maintenance`** and **`failure`** (or all cluster events).
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_critical_event_subscription.risk: Without notifications for **cluster maintenance** and **failure**, teams may miss engine updates, failovers, or node crashes, impacting **availability** and increasing MTTR. Prolonged degraded states can cause replication lag and potential **data integrity** issues, hindering timely containment.

cli.description: aws rds create-event-subscription --subscription-name <example_resource_name> --sns-topic-arn <example_resource_arn> --source-type db-cluster --event-categories maintenance failure --enabled

wui.description:
Enable **event subscriptions** for RDS clusters that include `maintenance` and `failure`, delivered via **SNS** to monitored channels.
- Enforce **least privilege** on topics
- Separate topics per environment
- Integrate with on-call/IR playbooks and test alerts
- Add multiple recipients and escalation for **defense in depth**

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Event subscriptions > Create event subscription
2. Name: enter <example_resource_name>
3. Send notifications to: Choose existing Amazon SNS ARN and select <example_resource_arn>
4. Source type: select Clusters
5. Event categories: select only Maintenance and Failure (unselect others)
6. Ensure Enabled is on
7. Click Create

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::EventSubscription
    Properties:
      SnsTopicArn: <example_resource_arn>       # Critical: SNS topic to receive notifications
      SourceType: db-cluster                    # Critical: Scope to DB clusters
      EventCategories:                          # Critical: Subscribe to required categories only
        - maintenance
        - failure
      Enabled: true                             # Critical: Must be enabled to pass
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
resource "aws_db_event_subscription" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name            = "<example_resource_name>"
  sns_topic       = "<example_resource_arn>"           # Critical: SNS topic ARN
  source_type     = "db-cluster"                        # Critical: Scope to clusters
  event_categories = ["maintenance", "failure"]        # Critical: Required categories
  enabled         = true                                  # Critical: Must be enabled
}
```

rds_cluster_default_admin.title: RDS cluster master username is not admin or postgres
rds_cluster_default_admin.description: RDS DB clusters are evaluated for use of a **custom administrator username**, flagging clusters that use defaults such as `admin` or `postgres`.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_default_admin.risk: Using a well-known admin username simplifies **credential stuffing** and **brute-force** attempts. Attackers can focus on password guessing, increasing chances of compromise. A successful login enables data theft (**confidentiality**), unauthorized changes (**integrity**), and destructive operations or outages (**availability**).

wui.description: Create databases with a **unique, non-default admin username** that doesn't reveal environment or org. Apply **least privilege** by using separate, non-admin accounts for applications. Prefer **IAM database authentication** and manage secrets centrally with rotation. Restrict admin access and monitor login attempts.

other.description:
1. In the AWS console, go to RDS > Databases > Create database
2. Choose Amazon Aurora and the same engine family as your current cluster
3. Under Settings, set Master username to a custom value that is not "admin" or "postgres" (CRITICAL)
4. Create the new cluster, migrate your workload to it, update application connections, then delete the old cluster

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# Create an RDS DB cluster with a custom admin username
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: aurora-mysql
      MasterUsername: <custom_admin_username>  # CRITICAL: use a non-default username (not "admin" or "postgres")
      MasterUserPassword: <example_password>
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Create an RDS DB cluster with a custom admin username
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier = "<example_resource_id>"
  engine             = "aurora-mysql"
  master_username    = "<custom_admin_username>" # CRITICAL: non-default username (not admin/postgres)
  master_password    = "<example_password>"
}
```

rds_cluster_deletion_protection.title: RDS cluster has deletion protection enabled
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_deletion_protection.risk: Without **deletion protection**, a cluster can be removed by error or misuse, causing sudden **availability** loss and potential **data loss** if backups are outdated. Compromised identities or faulty automation can trigger destructive deletes, degrading **recoverability** and data **integrity**.

wui.description: Enable **deletion protection** (`deletion_protection=true`) on production and other critical clusters. Enforce via IaC and organizational guardrails; apply **least privilege** to delete/modify actions; require **change control** and approvals. Maintain reliable **backups** to restore when protection must be lifted.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the DB cluster (type: DB cluster)
3. Click Modify
4. Enable Deletion protection
5. Choose Apply immediately and click Modify cluster

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable deletion protection on an RDS DB Cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: aurora-mysql
      DeletionProtection: true  # Critical: prevents cluster deletion and passes the check
```

rds_cluster_iam_authentication_enabled.title: RDS cluster has IAM authentication enabled
rds_cluster_iam_authentication_enabled.description: **RDS DB clusters** on supported engines (MySQL/MariaDB/PostgreSQL/Aurora) have **IAM database authentication** enabled for database logins, indicating token-based access managed by IAM instead of static passwords.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_iam_authentication_enabled.risk: Without **IAM DB authentication**, databases depend on long-lived passwords. Stolen or reused creds can enable unauthorized connections, data exfiltration, and tampering, harming **confidentiality** and **integrity**. Lacking short-lived tokens and centralized revocation expands blast radius and weakens **access control**.

wui.description: Enable **IAM database authentication** on supported clusters and enforce **least privilege**. Grant only necessary `rds-db:connect` permissions to specific principals, prefer role-based access for workloads to obtain short-lived tokens, require **TLS**, and deprecate static DB passwords. Pair with auditing and segmentation for **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the DB Cluster (not the instances)
3. Click Modify
4. In Database authentication, enable IAM database authentication
5. Choose Apply immediately and click Modify cluster

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable IAM authentication on an existing RDS/Aurora DB Cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      EnableIAMDatabaseAuthentication: true  # Critical: turns on IAM DB auth for the cluster
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Enable IAM authentication on an existing RDS/Aurora cluster
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier                   = "<example_resource_id>"
  iam_database_authentication_enabled = true  # Critical: enables IAM DB auth so the check passes
}
```

rds_cluster_integration_cloudwatch_logs.title: RDS cluster has CloudWatch Logs export enabled
rds_cluster_integration_cloudwatch_logs.description: **RDS clusters** running Aurora MySQL, Aurora PostgreSQL, MySQL, or PostgreSQL are assessed for **CloudWatch Logs publishing**, confirming that database logs are exported to a CloudWatch Logs group.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Runtime Behavior Analysis
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_integration_cloudwatch_logs.risk:
Without publishing to CloudWatch, database events lack centralized visibility and retention.
Brute-force, SQL injection, or privilege misuse may go undetected, hindering forensics and response, risking data confidentiality and integrity and delaying recovery.

wui.description:
Publish RDS/Aurora logs to **CloudWatch Logs** and centralize analysis.
Select appropriate types (e.g., `error`, `general`, `slowquery`, `audit`), define retention, and create alarms. Limit log access with **least privilege** and integrate with SIEM for defense-in-depth monitoring.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select your DB cluster and choose Modify
3. Under Log exports, check at least one supported log type for your engine (e.g., error/general/slowquery/audit for MySQL, postgresql for PostgreSQL)
4. Choose Continue, then Apply immediately, and click Modify cluster

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable CloudWatch Logs export for an RDS/Aurora DB cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: <engine>
      MasterUsername: <example_username>
      MasterUserPassword: <example_password>
      EnableCloudwatchLogsExports:
        - <engine_supported_log_type>  # CRITICAL: Enables at least one supported log type (e.g., 'error' for MySQL or 'postgresql' for PostgreSQL) to pass the check
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: Enable CloudWatch Logs export for an RDS/Aurora DB cluster
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  engine            = "<engine>"
  master_username   = "<example_username>"
  master_password   = "<example_password>"

  enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports = [
    "<engine_supported_log_type>" # CRITICAL: Enables at least one supported log type (e.g., "error" for MySQL or "postgresql" for PostgreSQL) to pass the check
  ]
}
```

rds_cluster_minor_version_upgrade_enable.title: RDS cluster has automatic minor version upgrades enabled
rds_cluster_minor_version_upgrade_enable.description:
**RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters** are configured for **automatic minor engine upgrades** via `auto_minor_version_upgrade`.

The evaluation checks these clusters to see if this setting is enabled so preferred minor releases are applied during the maintenance window.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_minor_version_upgrade_enable.risk: Without automatic minor upgrades, clusters can miss **security patches**, enabling exploitation of known flaws (confidentiality). Unfixed defects may corrupt data (**integrity**) or trigger crashes and failovers (**availability**). Emergency patching raises downtime and operational risk.

wui.description: Enable `auto_minor_version_upgrade` on **RDS Multi-AZ clusters** and align updates with approved maintenance windows. Validate changes in non-production, and document any exceptions with a strict manual patch cadence. This strengthens **defense in depth** and improves **availability**.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases
2. Select your Multi-AZ DB cluster
3. Click Modify
4. Set Auto minor version upgrade to Enabled
5. Click Continue, then Modify cluster

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation snippet to enable automatic minor version upgrades on an RDS DB cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      AutoMinorVersionUpgrade: true  # Critical: enables automatic minor engine version upgrades to pass the check
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform snippet to enable automatic minor version upgrades on an RDS DB cluster
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier         = "<example_resource_id>"
  auto_minor_version_upgrade = true  # Critical: enables automatic minor engine version upgrades to pass the check
}
```

rds_cluster_multi_az.title: RDS cluster has Multi-AZ enabled
rds_cluster_multi_az.description: **RDS DB clusters** are assessed for deployment across **multiple Availability Zones** (*Multi-AZ*), verifying that redundant instances exist to support **automatic failover** instead of a single-AZ configuration.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_multi_az.risk: A **single-AZ cluster** is a single point of failure. AZ outages, instance/storage faults, or maintenance can cause extended **downtime**, failed transactions, and worse **RTO/RPO**. Without cross-AZ replicas, recovery may require restores, increasing outage duration and risking service disruption and data consistency impacts.

wui.description: Enable **Multi-AZ** for production DB clusters to ensure cross-AZ redundancy and **automatic failover**. Choose a model that meets your SLA (one standby or two readable standbys; Aurora spans 3 AZs). Place subnets in distinct AZs, implement connection retries, and regularly test failover to validate **RTO/RPO** and readiness.

other.description:
1. In the AWS console, go to RDS > Databases > Create database
2. Engine: select MySQL or PostgreSQL
3. Under Availability and durability, select Multi-AZ DB cluster
4. Enter DB cluster identifier and master credentials
5. Choose a DB instance class and create the database
6. Migrate data to this new Multi-AZ DB cluster and switch your applications to its endpoint

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: create an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster (non-Aurora)
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: mysql  # CRITICAL: using mysql/postgres with the properties below creates a Multi-AZ DB cluster
      DBClusterInstanceClass: db.r6g.large  # CRITICAL: required to make it a Multi-AZ DB cluster (creates 1 writer + 2 readers across AZs)
      AllocatedStorage: 100  # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
      Iops: 1000             # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
      StorageType: io1       # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
      MasterUsername: <USERNAME>
      MasterUserPassword: <PASSWORD>
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: create an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster (non-Aurora)
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  cluster_identifier         = "<example_resource_id>"
  engine                     = "mysql"           # CRITICAL: mysql/postgres with the lines below creates a Multi-AZ DB cluster
  db_cluster_instance_class  = "db.r6g.large"    # CRITICAL: makes this a Multi-AZ DB cluster (1 writer + 2 readers across AZs)
  storage_type               = "io1"             # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
  allocated_storage          = 100                # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
  iops                       = 1000               # CRITICAL: required for Multi-AZ DB clusters
  master_username            = "<USERNAME>"
  master_password            = "<PASSWORD>"
}
```

s3_account_level_public_access_blocks.title: S3 account-level Block Public Access ignores public ACLs and restricts public buckets
s3_account_level_public_access_blocks.description: **Amazon S3** account-level **Block Public Access** is assessed for `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` to confirm centralized blocking of ACL-based public access and limiting buckets with public policies to in-account principals.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark
s3_account_level_public_access_blocks.risk:
Absent these settings, **public ACLs** and broad bucket policies may grant internet or cross-account access. This risks:
- Confidentiality: bulk data exfiltration
- Integrity: object overwrite/tampering
- Availability: malicious deletions or malware hosting, triggering takedowns

wui.description: Turn on account-level **Block Public Access** (prefer enabling all four: `block_public_acls`, `ignore_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to enforce least privilege. For legitimate access, use private buckets with **CloudFront**, VPC endpoints, or presigned URLs. Regularly review policies with IAM Access Analyzer.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to S3
2. Click Block public access (account settings)
3. Click Edit
4. Turn on: Ignore public ACLs and Restrict public buckets
5. Click Save changes

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Enable required S3 Account-level Block Public Access settings
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::S3::AccountPublicAccessBlock
    Properties:
      AccountId: !Ref AWS::AccountId
      IgnorePublicAcls: true         # Critical: Ignores any public ACLs at the account level
      RestrictPublicBuckets: true    # Critical: Restricts buckets with public policies to only same-account principals
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: Enable required S3 Account-level Block Public Access settings
resource "aws_s3_account_public_access_block" "<example_resource_name>" {
  ignore_public_acls     = true  # Critical: Ignores any public ACLs account-wide
  restrict_public_buckets = true # Critical: Restricts buckets with public policies to same-account principals
}
```

compliances.name: AWS Audit Manager Control Tower Guardrails
AWS Well Architected Framework Security Pillar

rds_cluster_protected_by_backup_plan.title: RDS cluster is protected by an AWS Backup plan
rds_cluster_protected_by_backup_plan.description: **RDS DB clusters** are covered by an **AWS Backup backup plan** when resource assignments include the cluster, either explicitly, by tags, or via an appropriate resource scope.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_protected_by_backup_plan.risk: Lack of centralized backups enables irreversible **data loss** and **corruption**, reducing **availability** and **integrity**. Accidental deletion, ransomware, or bad changes may become unrecoverable. Weak retention or no immutability undermines rollback and can breach recovery objectives.

wui.description: Include RDS clusters in an **AWS Backup backup plan**. Apply **defense in depth**: define schedules and retention, enable immutable vault controls and cross-Region copies, use tags for consistent coverage, enforce **least privilege** for backup roles, and regularly test restores to validate RPO/RTO.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Backup console, go to Settings > Service opt-in and enable RDS if it is not enabled.
2. Go to Backup plans and select an existing plan (create a minimal plan if none exists).
3. Click Assign resources.
4. Set a name and choose IAM role: AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole.
5. Under Resources, choose By resource ID and select the target RDS DB cluster (or use the ARN), then click Assign resources.
6. The cluster now appears as protected by the backup plan.

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: assign RDS clusters to an AWS Backup plan
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupSelection
    Properties:
      BackupPlanId: "<example_backup_plan_id>"
      BackupSelection:
        SelectionName: "rds-clusters"
        IamRoleArn: "arn:aws:iam::<example_account_id>:role/service-role/AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole"
        Resources:
          - "arn:aws:rds:*:*:cluster:*"  # Critical: includes all RDS clusters in the plan to mark them protected
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Assign RDS clusters to an existing AWS Backup plan
resource "aws_backup_selection" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name         = "rds-clusters"
  plan_id      = "<example_backup_plan_id>"
  iam_role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::<example_account_id>:role/service-role/AWSBackupDefaultServiceRole"

  resources = [
    "arn:aws:rds:*:*:cluster:*" # Critical: includes all RDS clusters in the plan to pass the check
  ]
}
```

rds_cluster_storage_encrypted.title: RDS cluster storage is encrypted
rds_cluster_storage_encrypted.description: **RDS DB clusters** are assessed for **encryption at rest** via AWS KMS. It determines whether cluster storage-and related artifacts like automated backups and snapshots-are encrypted with a KMS key.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
rds_cluster_storage_encrypted.risk: Unencrypted clusters expose data on disk, logs, and snapshots to unauthorized reading if storage or backups are obtained. This compromises **confidentiality**, enables offline exfiltration from leaked snapshots, and can widen blast radius during incidents and migrations.

wui.description: Create clusters with `StorageEncrypted=true` using **AWS KMS**, preferably **customer-managed keys**. Apply **least privilege** to key usage, enable rotation and monitoring, and separate key administration from DB operations. Ensure snapshots and cross-account copies remain encrypted for **defense in depth**.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases > Create database
2. Select your engine (Aurora or Multi-AZ DB cluster)
3. In the configuration, enable Storage encryption (Enable encryption)
4. Leave the KMS key as default (aws/rds or aws/aurora) unless you require a custom key
5. Create the cluster, migrate traffic, then delete the unencrypted cluster

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Create an encrypted RDS/Aurora DB cluster
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: <ENGINE>
      MasterUsername: <MASTER_USERNAME>
      MasterUserPassword: <MASTER_PASSWORD>
      StorageEncrypted: true  # Critical: enables encryption at rest for the cluster
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: Create an encrypted RDS/Aurora DB cluster
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "<example_resource_name>" {
  engine          = "<ENGINE>"
  master_username = "<MASTER_USERNAME>"
  master_password = "<MASTER_PASSWORD>"
  storage_encrypted = true  # Critical: enables encryption at rest for the cluster
}
```

rds_instance_backup_enabled.title: RDS instance has backup retention period greater than 0 days
rds_instance_backup_enabled.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for **automated backups** by confirming the backup retention period is greater than `0` days, indicating point-in-time recovery is configured.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
rds_instance_backup_enabled.risk:
Without automated backups, you lose **point-in-time recovery**, impacting **availability** and **integrity**.

Accidental deletes, destructive queries, or compromised accounts can cause unrecoverable data loss and prolonged outages, preventing reliable rollback during incidents.

wui.description:
Enable **automated backups** with retention > `0` aligned to RPO/RTO. Regularly test restores to validate **PITR**.

Apply **least privilege** to backup access, encrypt snapshots, and replicate critical backups to separate locations for **defense in depth** and resilient recovery.

other.description:
1. Open the AWS Management Console and go to RDS > Databases
2. Select the target DB instance and click Modify
3. In Backup section, set Backup retention period to 1 day (or more)
4. Check Apply immediately
5. Click Continue (if shown) and then Modify DB instance

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable automated backups on an RDS instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceClass: db.t3.micro
      Engine: mysql
      AllocatedStorage: 20
      MasterUsername: admin
      MasterUserPassword: <example_password>
      BackupRetentionPeriod: 1  # CRITICAL: Enables automated backups (>0 days)
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: enable automated backups on an RDS instance
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  allocated_storage      = 20
  engine                 = "mysql"
  instance_class         = "db.t3.micro"
  username               = "admin"
  password               = "<example_password>"
  backup_retention_period = 1  # CRITICAL: Enables automated backups (>0 days)
}
```

compliances.name: AWS Well Architected Framework Reliability Pillar

rds_instance_copy_tags_to_snapshots.title: RDS DB instance has copy tags to snapshots enabled
rds_instance_copy_tags_to_snapshots.description:
**RDS DB instances** are assessed for propagating instance tags to their **DB snapshots** using `CopyTagsToSnapshot`.

*Aurora engines manage this at the cluster level and aren't evaluated per instance.*
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
rds_instance_copy_tags_to_snapshots.risk: Snapshots without inherited tags lose ownership, environment, and sensitivity context, degrading visibility and governance. Missing metadata weakens **ABAC**, cost allocation, and lifecycle policies, enabling unintended backup access, orphaned snapshots, and retention drift that impact confidentiality and availability.

wui.description: Enable `CopyTagsToSnapshot` on non-Aurora RDS instances so snapshots inherit required metadata. Establish a consistent **tag taxonomy** and automate enforcement to support **least privilege** via ABAC, cost tracking, and retention controls. For Aurora, configure tag copy at the cluster level.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases and select the non-Aurora DB instance
2. Click Modify
3. Under Additional configuration, enable Copy tags to snapshots
4. Check Apply immediately and click Modify DB instance

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable copying tags to snapshots on an RDS DB instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      CopyTagsToSnapshot: true  # Critical: ensures DB instance tags are copied to snapshots
```

rds_instance_critical_event_subscription.title: RDS instance event subscription is enabled for maintenance, configuration change, and failure categories
rds_instance_critical_event_subscription.description:
**RDS event subscriptions** for DB instances are assessed for coverage of the critical categories `maintenance`, `configuration change`, and `failure`.

The evaluation looks for enabled `db-instance` subscriptions and confirms these categories are included or that all events are selected.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
rds_instance_critical_event_subscription.risk: Without these notifications, critical DB events go unseen, undermining **availability** and **integrity**. Missed outages, unexpected restarts, or silent parameter changes can delay response, prolong downtime, corrupt data flows, and leave misconfigurations unaddressed.

wui.description:
Establish and sustain **RDS event subscriptions** for `db-instance` that include `maintenance`, `configuration change`, and `failure`.
- Deliver to monitored channels (ticketing/chat/paging)
- Enforce **least privilege** on topics
- Test alert delivery and runbooks
- Periodically review coverage across Regions

other.description:
1. Open the AWS Console and go to RDS
2. In the left menu, select Event subscriptions > Create event subscription
3. Send notifications to: select an existing SNS topic (<sns-topic-arn>)
4. Source type: choose Instances
5. Event categories: select Maintenance, Configuration change, and Failure
6. Create the subscription

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: RDS DB instance event subscription
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::EventSubscription
    Properties:
      SnsTopicArn: <sns-topic-arn>           # critical: SNS topic to receive notifications
      SourceType: db-instance                # critical: subscribe to DB instance events
      EventCategories:                       # critical: required categories for PASS
        - maintenance
        - configuration change
        - failure
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: RDS DB instance event subscription
resource "aws_db_event_subscription" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name            = "<example_resource_name>"
  sns_topic       = "<sns-topic-arn>"
  source_type     = "db-instance"                           # critical: DB instance events
  event_categories = ["maintenance", "configuration change", "failure"]  # critical: required categories
}
```

rds_instance_default_admin.title: RDS instance does not use the default master username (admin or postgres)
rds_instance_default_admin.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for use of a **custom administrator username**. The finding identifies instances or clusters where the admin user matches common defaults like `admin` or `postgres` (checked at the instance or cluster level).
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices
rds_instance_default_admin.risk: Using a predictable admin name enables **password spraying**, **credential stuffing**, and username **enumeration**. A successful login can expose data (**confidentiality**), allow tampering (**integrity**), and disrupt service (**availability**). Defaults also attract automated scans targeting known usernames.

wui.description:
Adopt a **unique, non-default admin username** for each database and avoid enabling default accounts.
- Enforce **least privilege** with separate admin and app users
- Use strong, rotated secrets in a manager and prefer **IAM DB authentication**
- Restrict network exposure and audit authentication activity

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases and click Create database
2. Choose your engine and select Standard create
3. In Settings, set Master username to a value that is not "admin" or "postgres"
4. Complete creation and note the new endpoint
5. Migrate data from the old instance to the new one (e.g., dump/restore or replication)
6. Update applications to use the new endpoint, then delete the old instance
7. If the instance is part of an Aurora cluster, create a new cluster with a non-default master username and migrate to it

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: Create an RDS instance with a non-default master username
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      Engine: mysql
      DBInstanceClass: db.t3.micro
      AllocatedStorage: 20
      MasterUsername: <non_default_username>  # Critical: use a custom admin username (not "admin" or "postgres")
      MasterUserPassword: <example_password>
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Terraform: Create an RDS instance with a non-default master username
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  engine            = "mysql"
  instance_class    = "db.t3.micro"
  allocated_storage = 20
  username          = "<non_default_username>" # Critical: custom admin username (not "admin" or "postgres")
  password          = "<example_password>"
}
```

rds_instance_enhanced_monitoring_enabled.title: RDS instance has enhanced monitoring enabled
rds_instance_enhanced_monitoring_enabled.description: **RDS DB instances** are evaluated for **Enhanced Monitoring** being enabled, which publishes real-time **OS-level metrics** (CPU, memory, disk, network) to CloudWatch Logs for each instance.
type: Software and Configuration Checks/AWS Security Best Practices/Runtime Behavior Analysis
Software and Configuration Checks/Industry and Regulatory Standards/AWS Foundational Security Best Practices
rds_instance_enhanced_monitoring_enabled.risk:
Without **Enhanced Monitoring**, you lack **real-time OS telemetry**, delaying detection of resource saturation and abnormal activity.

This raises MTTR and risks **availability** impacts (timeouts, failovers), reduces **integrity** assurance during incidents, and weakens forensic visibility.

wui.description: Enable **Enhanced Monitoring** on RDS, using a `>0s` collection interval aligned to workload and cost. Assign a **least-privilege** role for log delivery, and apply **defense in depth** by centralizing logs, setting **alerts** on key OS metrics, and defining **retention** to support incident response and trend analysis.

other.description:
1. In the AWS Console, go to RDS > Databases and select the DB instance
2. Click Modify
3. In Monitoring, check Enable Enhanced Monitoring and set Granularity to any non-zero value (e.g., 60 seconds)
4. Set Monitoring role to Default (creates rds-monitoring-role) or select an existing role
5. Click Continue, then Modify DB instance to apply

nativeiac.description:
```yaml
# CloudFormation: enable Enhanced Monitoring on an existing RDS instance
Resources:
  <example_resource_name>:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
    Properties:
      DBInstanceIdentifier: <example_resource_id>
      MonitoringRoleArn: <monitoring_role_arn>   # CRITICAL: IAM role RDS uses to publish OS metrics to CloudWatch Logs
      MonitoringInterval: 60                     # CRITICAL: >0 enables Enhanced Monitoring (seconds)
```

terraform.description:
```hcl
# Enable Enhanced Monitoring on an existing RDS instance
resource "aws_db_instance" "<example_resource_name>" {
  # ...existing required configuration...
  monitoring_role_arn = "<monitoring_role_arn>"  # CRITICAL: Role for publishing OS metrics
  monitoring_interval = 60                        # CRITICAL: >0 enables Enhanced Monitoring (seconds)
}
```
