auth0_tenant_attack_protection_enabled.risk: Auth0 login endpoints are internet-facing and enumerable, so without throttling an attacker can run **credential stuffing at full speed** against your entire user base using passwords from unrelated breaches. Breached password detection is what catches the accounts that will fall first, and its absence means those compromises are only discovered after the account is used.

wui.description: Enable brute force protection, suspicious IP throttling and breached password detection with blocking shields, allowlist your own automation, and stream the resulting events to your SIEM.

other.description:
1. In the Auth0 Dashboard, go to **Security > Attack Protection**
2. Enable **Bot Detection**, **Suspicious IP Throttling**, **Brute-force Protection** and **Breached Password Detection**
3. For each, configure the shields — blocking and administrator notification rather than notification alone
4. Add your monitoring and load-testing egress ranges to the allowlist so legitimate automation is not throttled
5. Route the resulting security events into your SIEM through a log stream

auth0_tenant_mfa_factor_enabled.title: Auth0 tenants have at least one multi-factor authentication factor enabled
auth0_tenant_mfa_factor_enabled.description: This check verifies that the tenant has at least one **Guardian MFA factor** enabled, and reports tenants where SMS is the only available factor.
auth0_tenant_mfa_factor_enabled.risk: Auth0 fronts authentication for every application connected to it, so a tenant with no MFA factor means **none of those applications can require a second factor** regardless of their own configuration. Where SMS is the sole factor, SIM swap and SS7 interception defeat it, which is why phishing-resistant factors matter most at the identity provider layer.

wui.description: Enable a phishing-resistant WebAuthn factor as primary with OTP or push as fallback, avoid SMS-only configurations, and set an explicit MFA policy.

other.description:
1. In the Auth0 Dashboard, go to **Security > Multi-factor Auth**
2. Enable **WebAuthn with Security Keys** or **WebAuthn with Device Biometrics** as the primary factor
3. Enable a push or OTP factor as a fallback
4. Avoid making SMS the only available factor
5. Define the MFA policy — always, or adaptive based on risk — under **Define policies**
6. Verify enrolment coverage across your user base before requiring it

auth0_tenant_log_streaming_configured.title: Auth0 tenants stream logs to an external system
auth0_tenant_log_streaming_configured.description: Auth0 retains tenant logs for a limited period that varies by plan. This check verifies that at least one **active log stream** delivers events to an external system such as a SIEM.
auth0_tenant_log_streaming_configured.risk: Auth0 log retention is measured in **days on most plans**, so by the time an account compromise is detected the authentication events that would explain it have often already aged out. Streamed logs are also the only source that shows failed login patterns, MFA enrolment changes and token exchanges — the primary indicators of an identity attack in progress.

wui.description: Stream tenant logs to a SIEM, confirm the stream stays active, alert on failed logins, MFA changes and Management API calls, and monitor stream health so a paused stream is noticed.

other.description:
1. In the Auth0 Dashboard, go to **Monitoring > Streams**
2. Create a stream to your SIEM (HTTP endpoint, Datadog, Splunk or an event bus)
3. Verify the stream status is **Active** and that events are arriving
4. Alert on `f` (failed login), `gd_*` (MFA), `sapi`/`fapi` (Management API) and `limit_*` (rate limiting) event codes
5. Retain streamed events for at least your incident investigation window
6. Monitor stream health — a paused or failing stream is a silent gap

auth0_application_confidential_client_au.title: Auth0 confidential applications authenticate at the token endpoint
auth0_application_confidential_client_au.description: This check verifies that regular web and machine-to-machine applications set a **token endpoint authentication method** other than `none`, and reports single-page applications that hold a client secret they cannot protect.
auth0_application_confidential_client_au.risk: A confidential client with `token_endpoint_auth_method` set to `none` will exchange an authorization code **without proving its identity**, so any party holding a stolen code can complete the exchange. Conversely, a browser-based application configured as confidential ships a client secret that is trivially extractable from its bundle, giving that secret away to every visitor.

wui.description: Match the application type to how the app runs, require token endpoint authentication for confidential clients, use PKCE without a secret for SPAs, and rotate secrets that were shipped to browsers.

other.description:
1. Open the application in the Auth0 Dashboard
2. Confirm the **Application Type** matches how the application actually runs
3. For regular web and M2M applications, set **Token Endpoint Authentication Method** to `Post` or `Basic`, or use Private Key JWT for stronger assurance
4. For single-page applications, set the type to `SPA` so no secret is issued, and use Authorization Code with PKCE
5. Rotate any client secret that has been embedded in browser or mobile code — treat it as public

bitbucket_repository_main_branch_restric.title: Bitbucket repositories restrict direct pushes to the main branch
bitbucket_repository_main_branch_restric.description: Bitbucket **branch restrictions** control who may push to, merge into or delete a branch. This check verifies that each repository carries a `push` restriction covering its main branch, so changes must arrive through a pull request rather than a direct write.
bitbucket_repository_main_branch_restric.risk: An unrestricted main branch allows any user with write access to commit straight to the branch that drives **deployment pipelines**, with no pull request and no reviewer. It also permits branch deletion and history rewrites that destroy the evidence of what was actually built and shipped.

wui.description: Add push, history-rewrite and delete restrictions to the main branch of every repository so all changes arrive through reviewed pull requests.

other.description:
1. Open the repository in Bitbucket
2. Go to **Repository settings > Branch restrictions**
3. Click **Add a branch restriction**
4. Select the main branch (or the `Production` branch type)
5. Enable **Prevent a write** with no users or groups exempted
6. Enable **Prevent rewriting branch history** and **Prevent deletion**
7. Click **Save**

bitbucket_repository_pull_request_approv.title: Bitbucket repositories require pull request approvals before merge
bitbucket_repository_pull_request_approv.description: The `require_approvals_to_merge` branch restriction sets the minimum number of approvals a pull request must collect before it can be merged. This check verifies that each repository requires at least one approval on its main branch.
bitbucket_repository_pull_request_approv.risk: Without a required approval, a single account both authors and merges the change, so the pull request workflow records a review that never occurred. An attacker holding one developer credential can introduce a **malicious build step or dependency** and merge it immediately, defeating the primary control over what enters the release pipeline.

wui.description: Require at least one approval to merge into the main branch, and add the `reset_pullrequest_approvals_on_change` restriction so approvals do not carry over to a rewritten diff.

other.description:
1. Open the repository in Bitbucket
2. Go to **Repository settings > Branch restrictions**
3. Edit the restriction covering the main branch
4. Enable **Check for at least N approvals** and set N to `1` or higher (`2` for production repositories)
5. Enable **Check for unresolved pull request tasks**
6. Click **Save**

terraform.description:
resource "bitbucket_branch_restriction" "approvals" {
  owner      = var.workspace
  repository = bitbucket_repository.example.name
  kind       = "require_approvals_to_merge"
  pattern    = "main"
  value      = 2
}

bitbucket_repository_pipeline_variables_.title: Bitbucket Pipelines variables holding credentials are secured
bitbucket_repository_pipeline_variables_.description: A **secured** Bitbucket Pipelines variable is encrypted at rest, hidden in the UI and masked in build logs. This check reports repository pipeline variables whose names indicate a credential but that are not marked secured.
bitbucket_repository_pipeline_variables_.risk: An unsecured variable is readable in the repository settings by every user with write access and is printed verbatim into **build logs** by any step that dumps its environment. Build logs are retained and widely readable, so an unsecured deployment credential is effectively published to the whole workspace.

wui.description: Mark every credential-bearing pipeline variable as secured, scope production secrets to deployment environments, and rotate any secret that was stored unsecured.

other.description:
1. Open the repository in Bitbucket
2. Go to **Repository settings > Pipelines > Repository variables**
3. Delete each credential variable that is not secured
4. Re-add it with **Secured** ticked
5. Rotate the credential, since the previous value may already appear in retained build logs
6. Prefer **deployment**-scoped variables so production secrets are only available to production deployment steps

terraform.description:
resource "bitbucket_pipeline_variable" "deploy" {
  workspace  = var.workspace
  repository = bitbucket_repository.example.name
  key        = "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"
  value      = var.aws_secret
  secured    = true
}

bitbucket_repository_not_public.title: Bitbucket repositories are private
bitbucket_repository_not_public.description: A public Bitbucket repository is readable by anonymous users, including its source, wiki, downloads and pull request history. This check reports repositories whose `is_private` flag is false.
bitbucket_repository_not_public.risk: Public repositories are continuously indexed by **automated credential scanners**, so a key committed to one is typically harvested within minutes of the push. Beyond source, the exposed pull request and issue history reveals internal service names, infrastructure detail and contributor identities that support **targeted phishing**.

wui.description: Keep repositories private unless publication is intentional, and set the fork policy to disallow public forks so a private repository cannot be re-exposed through a fork.

other.description:
1. Open the repository in Bitbucket
2. Go to **Repository settings > Repository details**
3. Tick **Private repository**
4. Set **Forking** to `No forks` or `Allow only private forks`
5. Click **Save repository details**
6. Treat every credential in the repository history as compromised and rotate it

bitbucket_repository_deploy_keys_rotated.title: Bitbucket repository deploy keys are in active use and rotated
bitbucket_repository_deploy_keys_rotated.description: Repository **deploy keys** are long-lived SSH credentials that grant automated access to a repository. This check reports deploy keys that have never been used or that have been idle beyond the configured threshold, indicating an unmanaged standing credential.
bitbucket_repository_deploy_keys_rotated.risk: A deploy key does not expire, is not tied to a person, and survives the offboarding of whoever created it. An unused key is therefore a **standing credential with no owner** — if the private half was copied to a developer laptop or a decommissioned CI host, it stays valid indefinitely and its use is difficult to attribute during an investigation.

wui.description: Remove unused deploy keys, rotate the remainder on a fixed schedule, and migrate automation to scoped workspace access tokens which can be revoked and audited centrally.

other.description:
1. Open the repository in Bitbucket
2. Go to **Repository settings > Access keys**
3. Remove any key with no recorded last-used date or a stale one
4. For keys still needed, generate a fresh key pair and replace the registered public key
5. Prefer a workspace access token with repository scope over an SSH deploy key, since tokens can be scoped and revoked centrally

bitbucket_workspace_two_factor_enforced.title: Bitbucket workspaces enforce two-step verification
bitbucket_workspace_two_factor_enforced.description: Bitbucket workspaces can require every member to enable **two-step verification** before accessing workspace content. This check verifies that the enforcement setting is on.
bitbucket_workspace_two_factor_enforced.risk: Bitbucket credentials unlock source code and the pipelines that deploy it, making them a high-value target for **credential stuffing** against reused passwords. Without enforced two-step verification a single leaked password grants an attacker repository write access, and from there the ability to alter build definitions that run with production credentials.

wui.description: Enforce two-step verification for the workspace, or govern it centrally with an Atlassian authentication policy so the requirement applies across Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket together.

other.description:
1. Open the workspace in Bitbucket
2. Go to **Settings > Access controls**
3. Enable **Enforce two-step verification**
4. Notify members before enabling: those without 2SV configured lose access until they enrol
5. Where the workspace is governed by an Atlassian organization, enforce it centrally through **Atlassian Administration > Security > Authentication policies** instead

bitbucket_workspace_ip_allowlist_enabled.title: Bitbucket workspaces restrict access with an IP allowlist
bitbucket_workspace_ip_allowlist_enabled.description: Bitbucket premium workspaces can limit access to a set of approved IP addresses and CIDR ranges. This check verifies that an IP allowlist is in force for the workspace.
bitbucket_workspace_ip_allowlist_enabled.risk: App passwords and access tokens are **bearer credentials** that work from any network, and their theft produces no failed-login signal to alert on. An IP allowlist forces a stolen token to be replayed from inside an approved range, which both blocks opportunistic use and narrows the set of hosts an investigation must consider.

wui.description: Restrict workspace access to the CIDR ranges of your corporate egress, VPN and CI runners, and include pipeline egress ranges before enabling so automation is not cut off.

other.description:
1. Open the workspace in Bitbucket
2. Go to **Settings > IP allowlist**
3. Add the CIDR ranges for your corporate egress, VPN and CI runners
4. Verify your own address is covered before enabling, or you will lock yourself out
5. Enable the allowlist and confirm pipelines still run

bitbucket_workspace_no_inactive_admins.title: Bitbucket workspaces have no inactive administrator accounts
bitbucket_workspace_no_inactive_admins.description: Workspace members holding the `owner` permission can change access controls, delete repositories and manage every pipeline. This check reports owner accounts whose Atlassian account status is not active, which indicates a deactivated or unverified identity still holding administrative rights.
bitbucket_workspace_no_inactive_admins.risk: An inactive account retaining owner permission is an **orphaned administrative path**: nobody monitors it, its password may never be rotated, and reactivating it — through account recovery or an IdP mistake — silently restores full workspace control. Offboarding processes that only disable the identity provider entry frequently leave this Bitbucket-side grant in place.

wui.description: Remove workspace admin permission from inactive accounts, keep the owner set as small as practical, and review it on a recurring schedule tied to your joiner-mover-leaver process.

other.description:
1. Open the workspace in Bitbucket
2. Go to **Settings > User groups** and the workspace members list
3. Review every member holding **Admin**
4. Remove members whose Atlassian account is inactive or no longer employed
5. Reduce remaining owners to the minimum, and record who is expected to hold the role
6. Add a recurring access review so the list is re-confirmed each quarter

databricks_cluster_init_scripts_from_tru.title: Databricks cluster init scripts come from a governed source
databricks_cluster_init_scripts_from_tru.description: Cluster **init scripts** run as root on every node before Spark starts. This check reports clusters whose init scripts are loaded from DBFS or a plain cloud storage URI rather than from a workspace file or a Unity Catalog volume, where access is governed and changes are attributable.
databricks_cluster_init_scripts_from_tru.risk: DBFS-hosted init scripts are writable by **any workspace user**, so anyone who can attach a notebook can modify a script that then executes as root on every node of every cluster using it. That is a direct path from ordinary analyst access to full compute takeover, including theft of the instance profile credentials the cluster uses to read the data lake.

wui.description: Host init scripts in workspace files or Unity Catalog volumes with write access limited to the platform team, and disable DBFS-hosted init scripts at the workspace level.

other.description:
1. Move each init script to a workspace file (`/Shared/init/...`) or a Unity Catalog volume
2. Restrict write permission on that path to the platform team
3. Update the cluster definition to reference the new location
4. Disable DBFS-hosted init scripts at the workspace level so the pattern cannot return
5. Review the DBFS script's history: if it was writable by all users, treat any credential the cluster could reach as potentially exposed

databricks_cluster_unity_catalog_isolati.title: Databricks clusters enforce a Unity Catalog access mode
databricks_cluster_unity_catalog_isolati.description: A cluster's **data security mode** determines whether Unity Catalog governance applies to workloads running on it. This check reports clusters running in `NONE` or legacy no-isolation modes, where table ACLs and row filters are not enforced.
databricks_cluster_unity_catalog_isolati.risk: A no-isolation cluster executes every user's code in the **same JVM with the same identity**, so one user can read another's credentials in memory and bypass Unity Catalog grants entirely. The governance model appears intact in the catalog while the compute layer ignores it, which makes the gap easy to miss during review.

wui.description: Run clusters in Shared (user isolation) or Single user access mode so Unity Catalog grants are enforced at compute time, and pin the setting with a cluster policy.

other.description:
1. Open the cluster in the Databricks workspace
2. Click **Edit** and set **Access mode** to `Shared` (user isolation) or `Single user`
3. Migrate workloads that require a legacy mode to a supported runtime
4. Use a cluster policy to prevent creation of no-isolation clusters
5. Assign the workspace to a Unity Catalog metastore if it is not already

databricks_cluster_no_public_ip.title: Databricks clusters run without public IP addresses
databricks_cluster_no_public_ip.description: **Secure cluster connectivity** provisions cluster nodes without public IP addresses, so all communication with the control plane is outbound only. This check reports clusters whose cloud attributes still assign a public IP.
databricks_cluster_no_public_ip.risk: Cluster nodes with public IPs are **directly addressable from the internet**, exposing any service that binds to a routable interface — Spark UI ports, debugging endpoints and anything an init script starts. Because nodes carry the instance profile or managed identity used to read the data lake, a reachable node is a direct route to the underlying storage.

wui.description: Enable secure cluster connectivity so nodes have no public IPs, provide outbound access through a NAT gateway, and pin no_public_ip in a cluster policy.

other.description:
1. Enable secure cluster connectivity on the workspace (it is the default for workspaces created recently; older workspaces may need recreation)
2. Provision a NAT gateway so nodes retain outbound internet access for library installs
3. Set `no_public_ip: true` in the cluster's cloud attributes
4. Enforce it through a cluster policy so new clusters inherit it
5. Restrict the workspace VPC/VNet security groups to the documented Databricks control plane ranges

databricks_cluster_local_disk_encryption.title: Databricks clusters encrypt local disks
databricks_cluster_local_disk_encryption.description: Databricks can encrypt the temporary storage attached to cluster nodes, covering shuffle files, cached data and spill. This check verifies that `enable_local_disk_encryption` is set on each cluster.
databricks_cluster_local_disk_encryption.risk: Spark writes intermediate results to local disk whenever a join or aggregation exceeds memory, so **production data lands unencrypted on node storage** even when the source tables are encrypted at rest. Snapshots, forensic images or a recovered instance store therefore expose data that governance controls in the catalog would otherwise protect.

wui.description: Enable local disk encryption on all clusters and enforce it through a cluster policy so shuffle and spill data is protected on node storage.

other.description:
1. Open the cluster in the Databricks workspace
2. Click **Edit > Advanced options**
3. Enable **Local disk encryption**
4. Restart the cluster for the setting to take effect
5. Add the setting to a cluster policy so new clusters inherit it
6. Note the small performance cost on shuffle-heavy workloads and size accordingly

databricks_workspace_ip_access_list_enab.title: Databricks workspaces enforce IP access lists
databricks_workspace_ip_access_list_enab.description: **IP access lists** restrict which source addresses may reach the Databricks workspace UI and REST API. This check verifies that the feature is enabled and that at least one enabled ALLOW list exists.
databricks_workspace_ip_access_list_enab.risk: A Databricks personal access token is a **bearer credential usable from anywhere**, and it grants the ability to launch compute that reads the data lake. Without an IP access list, a token leaked through a notebook, a CI log or a laptop compromise can be used directly from the attacker's own infrastructure with no further obstacle.

cli.description:
databricks workspace-conf set-status --json '{"enableIpAccessLists":"true"}'
databricks ip-access-lists create --json '{"label":"corp-egress","list_type":"ALLOW","ip_addresses":["203.0.113.0/24"]}'

wui.description: Enable IP access lists with an ALLOW list covering corporate, VPN and CI egress ranges, and use Private Link for front-end access where available.

other.description:
1. Collect the egress CIDR ranges for your offices, VPN and CI systems
2. Create an ALLOW list containing those ranges
3. Verify your own address is covered — an incorrect list locks everyone out of the workspace
4. Enable the feature with `enableIpAccessLists`
5. For front-end private access, prefer Private Link and keep the list as defence in depth
6. Test that jobs and external tools still connect after enabling

databricks_workspace_token_lifetime_limi.title: Databricks personal access tokens have a bounded lifetime
databricks_workspace_token_lifetime_limi.description: This check verifies that the workspace caps personal access token lifetime through `maxTokenLifetimeDays`, and reports individual tokens issued with no expiry at all.
databricks_workspace_token_lifetime_limi.risk: A personal access token with no expiry is a **permanent credential carrying its owner's full workspace privileges**, and it keeps working after that person changes role or leaves the company. These tokens accumulate in notebooks, CI configuration and local files, so an old leak stays exploitable indefinitely and its use is attributed to the original user rather than the attacker.

cli.description:
databricks workspace-conf set-status --json '{"maxTokenLifetimeDays":"90"}'
databricks token-management delete <token-id>

wui.description: Cap token lifetime at 90 days or less, revoke non-expiring tokens, and move automation to service principal OAuth so credentials are short-lived and not tied to a person.

other.description:
1. Set `maxTokenLifetimeDays` to 90 or less in the workspace configuration
2. List existing tokens and revoke any with no expiry
3. Move automation to **service principals with OAuth (M2M)**, which issue short-lived tokens rather than static ones
4. Restrict who may create personal access tokens through the token permissions API
5. Rotate any token that has appeared in a notebook, log or repository

databricks_workspace_audit_log_delivery_.title: Databricks accounts deliver audit logs to external storage
databricks_workspace_audit_log_delivery_.description: Databricks **audit log delivery** writes account and workspace audit events to a cloud storage bucket you control. This check verifies that at least one enabled log delivery configuration exists.
databricks_workspace_audit_log_delivery_.risk: Without log delivery, audit events are only queryable through the platform's own retention window, so there is **no independent record** of who launched compute, who queried which table, or who changed permissions. An attacker with workspace admin rights can alter configuration knowing the evidence expires, and incident responders lose the timeline needed to scope the breach.

wui.description: Deliver audit logs to a bucket in your own cloud account with immutability enabled, forward them to your SIEM, and alert on permission, metastore and token events.

other.description:
1. Create a storage bucket in your own cloud account for the logs
2. Register a storage configuration and credential in the Databricks account console
3. Create a log delivery configuration with `log_type = AUDIT_LOGS`
4. Apply object-lock or equivalent immutability on the bucket so logs cannot be altered
5. Forward the delivered logs into your SIEM and alert on metastore, permission and token events
6. Confirm delivery is producing files before relying on it

terraform.description:
resource "databricks_mws_log_delivery" "audit" {
  account_id               = var.databricks_account_id
  credentials_id           = databricks_mws_credentials.log_writer.credentials_id
  storage_configuration_id = databricks_mws_storage_configurations.logs.storage_configuration_id
  log_type                 = "AUDIT_LOGS"
  output_format            = "JSON"
}

databricks_workspace_customer_managed_ke.title: Databricks workspaces use customer-managed encryption keys
databricks_workspace_customer_managed_ke.description: Databricks can encrypt managed services (notebooks, secrets, query history) and workspace storage with a **customer-managed key** held in your own cloud KMS. This check verifies that customer-managed keys are registered for both use cases.
databricks_workspace_customer_managed_ke.risk: With platform-managed keys only, you cannot **independently revoke access to your data** — key material is entirely under the provider's control, so containment during a suspected platform compromise depends on the provider acting. Customer-managed keys also give you the audit trail of key usage that most regulated data handling programmes expect.

wui.description: Register customer-managed keys for both managed services and workspace storage, enable rotation, and monitor key usage in your cloud audit log so you retain independent revocation.

other.description:
1. Create a KMS key (or Azure Key Vault key) in your own cloud account
2. Grant the Databricks service principal the minimum key usage permissions
3. Register the key in the Databricks account console for both `MANAGED_SERVICES` and `STORAGE`
4. Attach it to the workspace — managed services keys can be added to an existing workspace, storage keys may require workspace recreation on some clouds
5. Enable key rotation and monitor key usage in your cloud audit log

databricks_unitycatalog_metastore_assign.title: Databricks workspaces are assigned to a Unity Catalog metastore
databricks_unitycatalog_metastore_assign.description: **Unity Catalog** provides centralised access control, lineage and audit for data across workspaces. This check verifies that the workspace has a metastore assignment, without which governance falls back to legacy per-workspace table ACLs.
databricks_unitycatalog_metastore_assign.risk: Outside Unity Catalog, data access is governed by **legacy table ACLs that only some cluster modes enforce**, and there is no lineage or centralised grant audit. Permissions drift independently in each workspace, so an access review in one place gives no assurance about the same data reached from another.

wui.description: Assign each workspace to a Unity Catalog metastore, migrate legacy Hive tables, and move clusters to a governed access mode so grants are enforced consistently.

other.description:
1. Create a Unity Catalog metastore in the account console for the workspace's region
2. Assign the workspace to it and set a default catalog
3. Migrate existing Hive metastore tables using the upgrade wizard or `SYNC`
4. Move clusters to a Unity Catalog access mode so grants are enforced
5. Review and re-apply grants in Unity Catalog — legacy ACLs are not carried over automatically

databricks_unitycatalog_external_locatio.title: Unity Catalog external locations are not granted to all account users
databricks_unitycatalog_external_locatio.description: This check reports Unity Catalog **external locations** that grant privileges to the built-in `account users` group, or that grant `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE` or `WRITE FILES` broadly.
databricks_unitycatalog_external_locatio.risk: An external location maps to a **cloud storage prefix**, so a grant on it bypasses table-level controls entirely — the holder can read the underlying files directly regardless of column masks or row filters applied to the tables above them. Granting to `account users` extends that raw storage access to everyone in the account, including service principals created for unrelated purposes.

wui.description: Remove broad grants from external locations, give raw storage access only to named engineering groups, and prefer table-level grants so masking and row filters remain effective.

other.description:
1. Review grants with `SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION <name>`
2. Remove privileges held by `account users`
3. Grant `READ_FILES` and `WRITE_FILES` only to the specific groups that need raw storage access
4. Prefer granting on catalogs, schemas and tables so column masks and row filters apply
5. Mark locations that should never be written to as `read_only`
6. Scope each external location to the narrowest storage prefix that works

security_actions_default_workflow_permis.title: GitHub Actions workflows default to read-only token permissions
security_actions_default_workflow_permis.description: The organization's **default workflow permissions** set what the automatically-provisioned `GITHUB_TOKEN` can do when a workflow does not declare its own `permissions` block. This check requires the default to be `read`, and that workflows cannot approve pull requests.
security_actions_default_workflow_permis.risk: A write-scoped default token lets **any workflow push commits, publish packages and modify releases**, so a compromised action from the marketplace — or a malicious pull request in a repository that runs workflows on `pull_request_target` — inherits repository write access automatically. Allowing workflows to approve pull requests additionally lets automation satisfy the review requirement that branch protection depends on.

wui.description: Set the default GITHUB_TOKEN permission to read, disallow workflow-created pull request approvals, declare narrow per-workflow permissions where write is needed, and pin third-party actions to commit SHAs.

other.description:
1. Go to the organization's **Settings > Actions > General**
2. Under **Workflow permissions**, select **Read repository contents and packages permissions**
3. Clear **Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests**
4. Declare an explicit `permissions:` block in each workflow that genuinely needs write access, scoped to the specific permission
5. Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA rather than a tag, so the code cannot change under you
6. Restrict which actions may run at all under **Allowed actions**

security_secret_scanning_push_protection.title: GitHub organizations enable secret scanning push protection by default
security_secret_scanning_push_protection.description: **Push protection** blocks a push containing a recognised credential before it reaches the repository. This check verifies that secret scanning and push protection are enabled by default for new repositories in the organization.
security_secret_scanning_push_protection.risk: Secret scanning alone reports a credential **after it has already been pushed**, at which point it exists in every clone, fork and CI cache — and on a public repository, automated harvesters typically find it within seconds. Push protection is the only control that prevents the exposure rather than reporting it, which is the difference between a warning and a mandatory credential rotation.

wui.description: Enable secret scanning and push protection for new and existing repositories, add custom patterns for internal credential formats, and rotate every credential already flagged in history.

other.description:
1. Go to the organization's **Settings > Code security and analysis**
2. Enable **Secret scanning** and **Push protection** for new repositories
3. Click **Enable all** to apply them to existing repositories
4. Add custom patterns for internal credential formats that GitHub does not recognise
5. Review the existing secret scanning alerts and rotate everything already exposed — enabling push protection does not clean up history
6. Restrict who may bypass push protection, and require a reason

security_dependabot_alerts_enabled_by_de.title: GitHub organizations enable Dependabot alerts for new repositories
security_dependabot_alerts_enabled_by_de.description: This check verifies that **Dependabot alerts** are enabled by default for new repositories, so dependency vulnerabilities are surfaced without each team opting in individually.
security_dependabot_alerts_enabled_by_de.risk: Vulnerable transitive dependencies are the **most common route into an application's supply chain**, and they are invisible without automated alerting because nobody reads a lockfile. Where alerting is opt-in per repository, coverage decays as new repositories are created, so the repositories least likely to be monitored are the newest and least reviewed ones.

wui.description: Enable Dependabot alerts and security updates for new and existing repositories, route alerts to owning teams, and set a remediation SLA so alerts translate into fixes.

other.description:
1. Go to the organization's **Settings > Code security and analysis**
2. Enable **Dependabot alerts** and **Dependabot security updates** for new repositories
3. Click **Enable all** to cover existing repositories
4. Enable the **dependency graph** so transitive dependencies are resolved
5. Route alerts to the owning team rather than only to repository admins
6. Set an internal SLA for remediating critical dependency alerts, since alerting without a response process changes nothing

security_webhooks_use_tls_and_secret.title: GitHub organization webhooks verify TLS and are signed with a secret
security_webhooks_use_tls_and_secret.description: This check reports active organization webhooks that disable SSL verification, use a plaintext HTTP endpoint, or have no shared secret configured for payload signing.
security_webhooks_use_tls_and_secret.risk: Webhook payloads carry **repository names, commit contents, branch references and sometimes tokens**, so an unverified TLS connection exposes them to interception and lets an attacker impersonate GitHub to the receiver. Without a signing secret the receiver cannot distinguish a genuine GitHub delivery from a forged one, which turns any webhook-triggered deployment into an unauthenticated remote trigger.

wui.description: Point webhooks at HTTPS endpoints with SSL verification on, sign every payload with a high-entropy secret verified in constant time at the receiver, and delete webhooks for endpoints that no longer exist.

other.description:
1. Go to the organization's **Settings > Webhooks**
2. For each webhook, set the payload URL to an HTTPS endpoint with a valid certificate
3. Set **SSL verification** to enabled
4. Generate a high-entropy secret and set it on the webhook
5. Update the receiver to verify the `X-Hub-Signature-256` header using a constant-time comparison, and reject unsigned deliveries
6. Delete webhooks pointing at endpoints that no longer exist — a lapsed domain is a webhook takeover

repository_default_branch_requires_pull_.title: GitHub default branches require a pull request before merging
repository_default_branch_requires_pull_.description: This check verifies that the default branch's protection rule requires changes to arrive through a **pull request**, which is the precondition for every other review control to apply.
repository_default_branch_requires_pull_.risk: A protection rule that permits direct pushes makes the **approval count, status checks and code owner requirements irrelevant**, because a commit that never becomes a pull request never encounters them. The repository appears protected in the settings page while the primary control path can simply be bypassed with `git push`.

cli.description:
gh api -X PUT /repos/<owner>/<repo>/branches/<branch>/protection \
  --input - <<'JSON'
{
  "required_pull_request_reviews": {"required_approving_review_count": 1},
  "required_status_checks": null,
  "enforce_admins": true,
  "restrictions": null
}
JSON

wui.description: Require a pull request before merging into the default branch with at least one approval and no admin bypass, and apply it through an organization-wide ruleset rather than per repository.

other.description:
1. Open the repository's **Settings > Branches**
2. Edit the default branch protection rule, or add one
3. Enable **Require a pull request before merging**
4. Set the required approving review count to 1 or more
5. Enable **Do not allow bypassing the above settings** so administrators are included
6. Apply the rule organization-wide with a **repository ruleset** rather than configuring each repository individually

organization_members_cannot_create_publi.title: GitHub organization members cannot create public repositories
organization_members_cannot_create_publi.description: This check verifies that ordinary organization members are not permitted to create **public** repositories, so publishing code is a deliberate decision made by someone accountable for it.
organization_members_cannot_create_publi.risk: When any member can create a public repository, internal code reaches the internet through **ordinary mistakes rather than deliberate publication** — a repository created public by default, or a prototype that was never meant to leave. Automated scrapers index new public repositories within minutes, so the exposure window is effectively zero and any credential inside must be treated as compromised.

wui.description: Disallow member-created public repositories while leaving private and internal creation open, and require a history scan before any repository is published.

other.description:
1. Go to the organization's **Settings > Member privileges**
2. Under **Repository creation**, clear **Public**
3. Leave **Private** and **Internal** enabled so teams are not blocked from ordinary work
4. Define a review path for publishing a repository publicly, including a scan of the full history for credentials
5. Audit the existing public repositories and confirm each is intentionally public

gitlab_project_default_branch_protected.title: GitLab project default branches are protected
gitlab_project_default_branch_protected.description: **GitLab protected branches** restrict who may push to and merge into a branch, and whether history may be rewritten. This check verifies that each project's **default branch** carries a protection rule, so that code reaching the branch that feeds production pipelines has passed the project's review controls.
gitlab_project_default_branch_protected.risk: An unprotected default branch lets any project member push directly to the branch that triggers **production pipelines**, bypassing merge request review entirely. It also permits **force pushes** that rewrite history, which can quietly remove a malicious commit from the log after it has already been built and deployed.

wui.description: Protect the default branch of every project: disallow direct pushes, restrict merge rights to maintainers, and keep force push disabled so history cannot be rewritten after review.

other.description:
1. Open the project in GitLab
2. Go to **Settings > Repository > Protected branches**
3. Select the default branch
4. Set **Allowed to push and merge** to `No one`
5. Set **Allowed to merge** to `Maintainers` or a narrower role
6. Leave **Allow force push** disabled
7. Click **Protect**

terraform.description:
resource "gitlab_branch_protection" "main" {
  project                = gitlab_project.example.id
  branch                 = "main"
  push_access_level      = "no one"
  merge_access_level     = "maintainer"
  allow_force_push       = false
  code_owner_approval_required = true
}

gitlab_project_merge_request_approvals_r.title: GitLab projects require merge request approvals
gitlab_project_merge_request_approvals_r.description: **Merge request approval rules** require a minimum number of reviewers to approve a change before it can be merged. This check verifies that each project requires at least one approval, establishing the four-eyes control that separates authoring a change from admitting it into the mainline.
gitlab_project_merge_request_approvals_r.risk: Without a required approval, a single compromised or malicious account can author and merge a change on its own, introducing a **backdoor** or an exfiltrating build step into the pipeline with no second party ever seeing the diff. This removes the primary detective control over source code changes.

wui.description: Require at least one approval on every merge request, and two for projects that deploy to production. Back the rule with a CODEOWNERS file so the right reviewers are pulled in automatically.

other.description:
1. Open the project in GitLab
2. Go to **Settings > Merge requests**
3. Under **Merge request approvals**, click **Add approval rule**
4. Set **Approvals required** to `1` or higher (`2` for production-facing projects)
5. Add the approver group or users
6. Click **Save changes**

gitlab_project_prevent_approval_by_autho.title: GitLab projects prevent merge request authors from approving their own changes
gitlab_project_prevent_approval_by_autho.description: GitLab can prevent the **author of a merge request** — and optionally anyone who added commits to it — from satisfying its approval requirement. This check verifies that self-approval is disabled so the required approval represents genuine independent review.
gitlab_project_prevent_approval_by_autho.risk: If authors may approve their own merge requests, a required-approvals rule becomes **decorative**: one account both writes and admits the change, and the audit trail shows a satisfied review that never happened. An attacker holding a single developer credential can push code to production unreviewed while appearing compliant.

wui.description: Disable approval by the merge request author and by users who add commits to it, and reset approvals when new commits are pushed, so an approval always reflects review of the final diff by an independent party.

other.description:
1. Open the project in GitLab
2. Go to **Settings > Merge requests**
3. Under **Approval settings**, enable **Prevent approval by author**
4. Enable **Prevent approvals by users who add commits**
5. Enable **Remove all approvals when commits are added to the source branch**
6. Click **Save changes**

gitlab_project_ci_variables_masked_and_p.title: GitLab CI/CD variables are masked and protected
gitlab_project_ci_variables_masked_and_p.description: **Masked** CI/CD variables are redacted from job logs, and **protected** variables are exposed only to jobs running on protected branches and tags. This check verifies that every project CI/CD variable carries both flags, so pipeline credentials cannot leak through logs or be read by code on an unprotected branch.
gitlab_project_ci_variables_masked_and_p.risk: An unmasked variable is printed verbatim into **job logs** by any command that echoes its environment, and those logs are readable by every project member and often retained indefinitely. An unprotected variable is injected into pipelines on **any branch**, so anyone who can open a merge request can add a job that prints or exfiltrates the deployment credential.

wui.description: Mask and protect every CI/CD variable that carries a secret, and prefer short-lived OIDC-issued credentials over long-lived static tokens. Rotate any secret that was stored unmasked.

other.description:
1. Open the project in GitLab
2. Go to **Settings > CI/CD > Variables**
3. Edit each variable holding a credential
4. Enable **Mask variable** and **Protect variable**
5. Click **Update variable**
6. Rotate any credential that was previously stored unmasked, since it may already be present in retained job logs

terraform.description:
resource "gitlab_project_variable" "deploy_token" {
  project   = gitlab_project.example.id
  key       = "DEPLOY_TOKEN"
  value     = var.deploy_token
  masked    = true
  protected = true
}

gitlab_project_pipeline_job_token_scope_.title: GitLab CI job token scope is restricted to an allowlist
gitlab_project_pipeline_job_token_scope_.description: The **CI job token** (`CI_JOB_TOKEN`) is minted automatically for every pipeline job and carries the permissions of the user who triggered it. **Inbound token scope** limits which other projects may use their job token to reach this project. This check verifies that the restriction is enabled rather than left open to every project the token's user can see.
gitlab_project_pipeline_job_token_scope_.risk: With job token scope unrestricted, a pipeline in **any** project can present its `CI_JOB_TOKEN` to this project's API and read its repository, packages and registry. A single low-value project with a permissive `.gitlab-ci.yml` becomes a pivot into every other repository its members can access — a well-worn **lateral movement** path in CI supply chain attacks.

wui.description: Enable inbound job token scope on every project and allowlist only the pipelines that genuinely need cross-project access. Review the allowlist whenever a project is archived or changes ownership.

other.description:
1. Open the project in GitLab
2. Go to **Settings > CI/CD > Job token permissions**
3. Enable **Limit access _to_ this project**
4. Add only the projects whose pipelines legitimately need access
5. Click **Save changes**

gitlab_project_push_rules_prevent_secret.title: GitLab projects reject commits containing secrets
gitlab_project_push_rules_prevent_secret.description: GitLab **push rules** can reject a push server-side when a commit contains a file matching known credential patterns. This check verifies that the `prevent_secrets` push rule is enabled, blocking committed keys at the point of entry rather than detecting them after they have been distributed.
gitlab_project_push_rules_prevent_secret.risk: Once a credential is committed it exists in the **git history of every clone and fork**, and rewriting history does not recall the copies already pulled by CI runners, mirrors and developer machines. Treating the secret as compromised and rotating it is the only real remedy, so preventing the push is materially cheaper than detecting it afterwards.

wui.description: Enable the secret-prevention push rule on every project, and pair it with pipeline secret detection. Rotate any credential found in history rather than only removing the commit.

other.description:
1. Open the project in GitLab
2. Go to **Settings > Repository > Push rules**
3. Enable **Prevent pushing secret files**
4. Click **Save push rules**
5. Consider enabling secret detection in the pipeline as a second layer for credentials the file-name rules do not catch

gitlab_project_not_publicly_visible.title: GitLab projects are not publicly visible
gitlab_project_not_publicly_visible.description: A **public** GitLab project exposes its repository, issues, pipelines, job logs and package registry to anonymous users on the internet. This check reports projects whose visibility is `public`, so that public exposure is a deliberate decision rather than an inherited default.
gitlab_project_not_publicly_visible.risk: Public projects leak far more than source: **job logs** often contain internal hostnames and unmasked variable values, and the commit history exposes contributor identities and internal service names useful for **reconnaissance**. Public repositories are continuously scraped by automated credential harvesters, so an accidentally public project is typically enumerated within minutes.

wui.description: Set project visibility to private or internal unless publication is intentional. Where a project must stay public, review job logs and artifacts for internal detail and enforce masked variables.

other.description:
1. Open the project in GitLab
2. Go to **Settings > General > Visibility, project features, permissions**
3. Set **Project visibility** to `Private` (or `Internal` for instance-wide access)
4. Click **Save changes**
5. Review job logs and the package registry for anything that was exposed while the project was public, and rotate affected credentials

gitlab_group_two_factor_authentication_r.title: GitLab groups require two-factor authentication
gitlab_group_two_factor_authentication_r.description: GitLab groups can require every member to enrol in **two-factor authentication** before accessing group resources. This check verifies that the requirement is enabled and that any grace period is short, so a stolen password alone is not sufficient to reach source code and pipelines.
gitlab_group_two_factor_authentication_r.risk: Source control is a **primary target for credential stuffing**, because a single valid password grants the ability to modify code that is automatically built and deployed. Without enforced 2FA, one reused developer password compromises the group's repositories, CI variables and package registry, and the attacker's activity is indistinguishable from the legitimate user's.

wui.description: Require two-factor authentication for all group members with a grace period of 24 hours or less. Prefer WebAuthn hardware keys over TOTP where the plan allows, since they resist phishing relay.

other.description:
1. Open the group in GitLab
2. Go to **Settings > General > Permissions and group features**
3. Enable **Require all users in this group to set up two-factor authentication**
4. Set the grace period to `24` hours or less
5. Click **Save changes**

gitlab_group_ip_restriction_enabled.title: GitLab groups restrict access by IP address range
gitlab_group_ip_restriction_enabled.description: GitLab groups can limit access to a list of **allowed IP ranges**, so group resources are reachable only from corporate networks or egress gateways. This check reports groups with no IP allowlist configured.
gitlab_group_ip_restriction_enabled.risk: Without an IP allowlist, a **stolen personal access token** is usable from anywhere in the world, and token theft leaves no authentication trail to alert on. Network-level scoping turns an exfiltrated credential into a much weaker artifact, because it must also be replayed from inside an approved network range.

wui.description: Restrict top-level group access to the CIDR ranges of your corporate egress, VPN and CI runners. Note that this control applies to top-level groups only and does not cover public project content.

other.description:
1. Open the top-level group in GitLab
2. Go to **Settings > General > Permissions and group features**
3. Enter the approved CIDR ranges in **Restrict access by IP address**
4. Include the egress ranges of your CI runners and VPN before saving, or automation will break
5. Click **Save changes**

gitlab_group_audit_events_streaming_enab.title: GitLab groups stream audit events to an external destination
gitlab_group_audit_events_streaming_enab.description: **Audit event streaming** forwards group audit events to an external SIEM or log sink in near real time. This check verifies that at least one streaming destination is configured, so the record of privilege changes and access grants survives outside GitLab itself.
gitlab_group_audit_events_streaming_enab.risk: Audit events held only inside GitLab are subject to **retention limits** and, more importantly, are visible to the same administrators whose actions they record. An attacker who reaches owner privileges can alter group configuration and let the in-product record age out, leaving no independent evidence for **incident reconstruction**.

wui.description: Stream group audit events to a SIEM held outside GitLab's administrative boundary, verify the receiver validates the streaming token, and alert on owner-role grants and protected-branch changes.

other.description:
1. Open the top-level group in GitLab
2. Go to **Secure > Audit events**
3. Select the **Streams** tab
4. Click **Add streaming destination** and enter the HTTPS endpoint of your SIEM
5. Record the verification token and configure the receiver to validate it
6. Click **Add**

gitlab_runner_not_privileged.title: GitLab runners do not execute jobs in privileged containers
gitlab_runner_not_privileged.description: A GitLab runner using the Docker executor in **privileged mode** grants each CI job full capabilities on the host kernel. This check reports runners configured with `privileged = true`, which is commonly enabled to support Docker-in-Docker image builds.
gitlab_runner_not_privileged.risk: A privileged container is not a security boundary: any job can mount the **host filesystem**, reach the Docker socket and read the build caches, registry credentials and job tokens of **every other project** that shares the runner. A single untrusted merge request pipeline therefore escalates to full compromise of the runner host and lateral access across tenants.

cli.description:
# Edit /etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml on the runner host:
#   [runners.docker]
#     privileged = false
sudo gitlab-runner restart

wui.description: Disable privileged mode on shared runners and build images with a rootless builder such as Kaniko or Buildah. If a privileged runner is unavoidable, isolate it to a single trusted project on ephemeral infrastructure.

other.description:
1. Open `/etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml` on the runner host
2. Under `[runners.docker]`, set `privileged = false`
3. Replace Docker-in-Docker image builds with a rootless builder such as Buildah, Kaniko or BuildKit in rootless mode
4. Restart the runner with `gitlab-runner restart`
5. Where privileged builds remain unavoidable, dedicate a single-tenant ephemeral runner to them and never share it with other projects

terraform.description:
# helm_release values for gitlab-runner
runners:
  privileged: false
  config: |
    [[runners]]
      [runners.kubernetes]
        privileged = false

gitlab_runner_shared_runners_restricted.title: GitLab shared runners are locked and do not run untagged jobs
gitlab_runner_shared_runners_restricted.description: A **shared runner** that accepts untagged jobs will pick up work from any project in its scope, and an **unlocked** runner can be assigned to further projects after registration. This check verifies that shared runners are locked to their current projects and require an explicit tag, so pipeline placement is deliberate.
gitlab_runner_shared_runners_restricted.risk: When a runner accepts untagged jobs from any project, an attacker who can open a merge request in the **least protected project** in the group can land a job on the same executor used by production pipelines. Build caches, mounted volumes and leftover credentials on that host then become reachable across trust boundaries that the project permissions imply are separate.

wui.description: Lock shared runners to their intended projects, require explicit tags, and set runners that hold deployment credentials to protected so they only serve protected branches and tags.

other.description:
1. Go to **Admin area > CI/CD > Runners** (or the group's **Runners** page)
2. Select the shared runner
3. Enable **Lock to current projects**
4. Disable **Run untagged jobs**
5. Set **Protected** so the runner only picks up jobs on protected branches and tags
6. Tag production pipelines explicitly in `.gitlab-ci.yml`

terraform.description:
resource "gitlab_user_runner" "build" {
  runner_type = "group_type"
  group_id    = gitlab_group.example.id
  tag_list    = ["build"]
  untagged    = false
  locked      = true
  access_level = "ref_protected"
}

jenkins_controller_authorization_strateg.title: Jenkins controllers do not use a permissive authorization strategy
jenkins_controller_authorization_strateg.description: The Jenkins **authorization strategy** decides what an authenticated user may do. `AuthorizationStrategy$Unsecured` grants everyone full control, and `FullControlOnceLoggedInAuthorizationStrategy` grants every logged-in user administrator rights. This check requires a granular strategy such as matrix or project-based matrix authorization.
jenkins_controller_authorization_strateg.risk: Administrator rights on a Jenkins controller are equivalent to **arbitrary code execution on every agent**, plus read access to every stored credential. With a permissive strategy, any user who can authenticate — including through an open signup realm — can reach the Groovy script console, decrypt stored deployment credentials and push code to production. Internet-exposed Jenkins instances left in this state are routinely mass-exploited.

wui.description: Use matrix or project-based matrix authorization, grant Overall/Administer to a named platform group only, and strip all permissions from the anonymous user. Manage the strategy through Configuration as Code so it cannot drift.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Jenkins as an administrator
2. Go to **Manage Jenkins > Security**
3. Under **Authorization**, select `Matrix-based security` or `Project-based Matrix Authorization Strategy`
4. Grant `Overall/Administer` only to the platform team
5. Grant `Overall/Read` plus per-job permissions to everyone else, and remove all permissions from `Anonymous`
6. Save, then confirm from a non-admin session that the script console is unreachable

terraform.description:
# Jenkins Configuration as Code (jenkins.yaml)
jenkins:
  authorizationStrategy:
    projectMatrix:
      entries:
        - group:
            name: "platform-admins"
            permissions: ["Overall/Administer"]
        - group:
            name: "developers"
            permissions: ["Overall/Read", "Job/Build"]

jenkins_controller_security_realm_config.title: Jenkins controllers use a managed security realm
jenkins_controller_security_realm_config.description: The **security realm** determines how Jenkins authenticates users. `SecurityRealm$None` disables authentication, and the built-in database with signup enabled lets anyone create an account. This check requires a managed realm — LDAP, SAML, OIDC or the built-in database with signup disabled.
jenkins_controller_security_realm_config.risk: With authentication disabled or open signup enabled, **anyone who can reach the controller** becomes a user, and combined with a permissive authorization strategy that means immediate administrative access. Because Jenkins holds the credentials used to deploy, this is one of the shortest paths from network exposure to full production compromise.

wui.description: Authenticate Jenkins against your corporate identity provider so joiner-mover-leaver processes apply, and never leave signup enabled on the built-in user database.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Jenkins as an administrator
2. Go to **Manage Jenkins > Security**
3. Under **Security Realm**, select your identity provider (SAML, OpenID Connect or LDAP)
4. If using the built-in database, clear **Allow users to sign up**
5. Save and verify that an unauthenticated session is redirected to the login page
6. Disable any local accounts that duplicate identities now managed by the IdP

terraform.description:
# Jenkins Configuration as Code (jenkins.yaml)
jenkins:
  securityRealm:
    oic:
      clientId: "${JENKINS_OIDC_CLIENT_ID}"
      wellKnownOpenIDConfigurationUrl: "https://idp.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration"
  # or, for the built-in database:
  # local:
  #   allowsSignup: false

jenkins_controller_csrf_protection_enabl.title: Jenkins controllers enable CSRF protection
jenkins_controller_csrf_protection_enabl.description: Jenkins issues a **crumb** that state-changing requests must present, preventing another site from acting as an authenticated user's browser. This check verifies that a crumb issuer is configured and that it does not exclude the client IP from the crumb, which weakens the token.
jenkins_controller_csrf_protection_enabl.risk: Without CSRF protection, visiting a hostile page while signed in to Jenkins is enough for that page to **trigger builds, modify jobs or create an administrator account** using the victim's session. Because Jenkins builds execute arbitrary code with production credentials, a single click by an administrator can hand over the build system.

wui.description: Keep the default crumb issuer enabled and leave proxy compatibility off so the crumb remains bound to the client IP. Update API clients to fetch and send the crumb header rather than disabling the protection.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Jenkins as an administrator
2. Go to **Manage Jenkins > Security**
3. Under **CSRF Protection**, ensure a crumb issuer is selected
4. Clear **Enable proxy compatibility** unless a reverse proxy genuinely requires it, since it removes the client IP from the crumb
5. Save and confirm that scripted API clients send the `Jenkins-Crumb` header

terraform.description:
# Jenkins Configuration as Code (jenkins.yaml)
jenkins:
  crumbIssuer:
    standard:
      excludeClientIPFromCrumb: false

jenkins_controller_agent_to_controller_a.title: Jenkins controllers enforce agent-to-controller access control
jenkins_controller_agent_to_controller_a.description: **Agent-to-controller access control** restricts which commands and file paths a build agent may invoke on the controller. This check verifies that the protection is enabled rather than disabled by the master kill switch.
jenkins_controller_agent_to_controller_a.risk: Build agents run **untrusted code by design** — every merge request compiles on them. With agent-to-controller access control disabled, a build can read and write arbitrary files on the controller, including the `secrets/` directory holding the master key used to encrypt every stored credential. One malicious pull request then yields the entire credential store.

wui.description: Enable agent-to-controller access control, set the built-in node's executor count to zero so no build runs on the controller, and keep the file access rules as narrow as the builds allow.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Jenkins as an administrator
2. Go to **Manage Jenkins > Security**
3. Under **Agent → Controller Security**, ensure the access control is **enabled**
4. Review the file access rules and command allowlist, removing entries that are no longer needed
5. Save, then run a representative build to confirm nothing legitimate was relying on the bypass
6. Do not run builds on the built-in node: set its executor count to `0`

terraform.description:
# Jenkins Configuration as Code (jenkins.yaml)
jenkins:
  numExecutors: 0
  remotingSecurity:
    enabled: true

jenkins_controller_https_enforced.title: Jenkins controllers are served over HTTPS
jenkins_controller_https_enforced.description: This check verifies that the Jenkins root URL uses `https`, so session cookies, API tokens and build output are encrypted in transit between users and the controller.
jenkins_controller_https_enforced.risk: Over plain HTTP, the Jenkins **session cookie and API token travel in cleartext** and can be captured by anyone positioned on the network path, including on a shared office or VPN segment. Because a captured administrator session grants script console access, this escalates directly to code execution on every build agent.

wui.description: Serve Jenkins over HTTPS with a valid certificate, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, set the Jenkins URL to the https address, and bind the plain HTTP listener to localhost only.

other.description:
1. Terminate TLS at a reverse proxy (nginx, Apache, or a cloud load balancer) in front of Jenkins, or configure the built-in Jetty listener with a keystore
2. Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS at the proxy
3. Go to **Manage Jenkins > System** and set the **Jenkins URL** to the `https://` address
4. Enable HSTS at the proxy
5. Bind the Jenkins HTTP listener to `127.0.0.1` so it is reachable only through the proxy

terraform.description:
# Jenkins Configuration as Code (jenkins.yaml)
unclassified:
  location:
    url: "https://jenkins.example.com/"
    adminAddress: "platform@example.com"

jenkins_plugin_no_known_vulnerabilities.title: Jenkins plugins have no known security advisories
jenkins_plugin_no_known_vulnerabilities.description: The Jenkins update centre publishes **security warnings** for plugin versions with known vulnerabilities. This check reports installed plugins that carry an advisory for the version in use.
jenkins_plugin_no_known_vulnerabilities.risk: Plugins execute inside the controller JVM with **full controller privileges**, so a vulnerable plugin is not a peripheral concern — advisories routinely describe unauthenticated remote code execution or credential disclosure. Jenkins plugin CVEs are widely weaponised within days of publication, and an exposed controller running a flagged plugin is a standard mass-scanning target.

wui.description: Update or remove every plugin carrying a security advisory, restart the controller, and pin plugin versions in a managed manifest so updates go through change control instead of ad-hoc clicks.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Jenkins as an administrator
2. Go to **Manage Jenkins > Plugins > Updates**
3. Update every plugin listed with a security warning to the fixed version
4. Where no fix exists, uninstall the plugin and remove the jobs that depend on it
5. Restart the controller to load the updated plugins
6. Subscribe to the Jenkins security advisory mailing list so future advisories are seen promptly

terraform.description:
# plugins.txt consumed by the jenkins/jenkins image plugin installer
# Pin fixed versions and update them through your normal change process.
git:5.2.2
credentials:1337.v60b_d7b_c7b_c9d
workflow-cps:3908.vd6b_b_5a_a_74b_45

jenkins_plugin_no_deprecated_or_unmainta.title: Jenkins plugins are not deprecated and are up to date
jenkins_plugin_no_deprecated_or_unmainta.description: This check reports installed plugins marked **deprecated** by the update centre, and enabled plugins with a pending update, both of which indicate that the controller is drifting away from a supportable configuration.
jenkins_plugin_no_deprecated_or_unmainta.risk: A deprecated plugin receives **no security fixes**, so any vulnerability found in it stays permanently unpatched inside the controller JVM. Accumulated pending updates also make emergency patching slower: when an advisory lands, a controller many versions behind cannot take the fix without a risky bulk upgrade, extending the exposure window.

wui.description: Replace deprecated plugins with their documented successors, keep the remainder current on a regular cadence, and uninstall plugins no job uses so the update surface stays small.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Jenkins as an administrator
2. Go to **Manage Jenkins > Plugins > Installed plugins**
3. Identify plugins flagged as deprecated and find the documented replacement
4. Migrate the affected jobs, then uninstall the deprecated plugin
5. Apply pending updates on a regular cadence rather than only when an advisory forces it
6. Uninstall plugins that no job actually uses — the smallest plugin set is the easiest to keep current

terraform.description:
# Track the intended plugin set in version control and apply it on rebuild:
#   docker build --build-arg PLUGINS_FILE=plugins.txt .
# Review plugins.txt each release for deprecated entries.

jenkins_job_no_plaintext_secrets_in_conf.title: Jenkins job configurations contain no plaintext secrets
jenkins_job_no_plaintext_secrets_in_conf.description: This check scans each job's `config.xml` for credential-like literals — API keys, tokens, passwords and private key blocks — that are stored directly in the job definition rather than referenced from the Jenkins credentials store.
jenkins_job_no_plaintext_secrets_in_conf.risk: A secret written into `config.xml` is stored **unencrypted on the controller filesystem**, is visible to every user with Job/Configure, and is copied into any backup, `job/*/config.xml` API response and Configuration-as-Code export. Unlike a credentials-store entry it is never masked in build logs, so it also leaks to anyone who can read a build.

wui.description: Move every literal secret from job configuration into the Jenkins credentials store, reference it through withCredentials so it is masked in logs, and rotate anything that was previously stored in plaintext.

other.description:
1. Add the secret to **Manage Jenkins > Credentials** as a Secret text or Username with password credential
2. Reference it from the pipeline with `withCredentials([string(credentialsId: 'my-secret', variable: 'TOKEN')])`
3. Remove the literal from the job configuration
4. Rotate the secret: it has been readable on disk, in backups and in the config API
5. Restrict `Job/Configure` so fewer users can read job definitions
6. Prefer short-lived credentials issued per build over long-lived stored secrets

jenkins_job_build_log_retention_configur.title: Jenkins jobs have a build log retention policy
jenkins_job_build_log_retention_configur.description: This check verifies that each job defines a **build discarder**, setting how many builds and logs are kept. A defined policy makes retention an explicit decision rather than an accident of disk space.
jenkins_job_build_log_retention_configur.risk: With no discarder, build history grows without bound until the controller **runs out of disk** and stops scheduling, and administrators then delete history in bulk under pressure — destroying the record needed to determine what a compromised pipeline actually built. Conversely, indefinite retention keeps build logs containing internal hostnames and occasionally leaked secrets available far longer than any policy intends.

wui.description: Declare a build discarder in the Jenkinsfile so retention is version controlled, keep artifacts for a shorter window than logs, and forward logs to a central store when longer retention is required for investigations.

other.description:
1. Open the job in Jenkins
2. Click **Configure**
3. Enable **Discard old builds**
4. Set **Max # of builds to keep** and **Days to keep builds** to match your retention policy
5. Use **Advanced** to keep artifacts for a shorter window than logs
6. For pipelines, declare it in the Jenkinsfile so the policy is version controlled
7. Ship build logs to a central log store if you need retention beyond the controller

access_database_user_no_admin_roles.title: Atlas database users do not hold cluster-wide administrative roles
access_database_user_no_admin_roles.description: This check reports database users granted `atlasAdmin`, `dbAdminAnyDatabase`, `readWriteAnyDatabase` or `root`, which apply across every database in the cluster rather than to the one an application needs.
access_database_user_no_admin_roles.risk: An application credential holding `readWriteAnyDatabase` can read and modify **every database on the cluster**, so a single SQL-injection-equivalent flaw or a leaked connection string exposes unrelated tenants and services sharing that cluster. `atlasAdmin` goes further, allowing the user to alter the cluster itself — including disabling the auditing that would record what happened.

wui.description: Replace cluster-wide roles with database-scoped ones or custom roles, and reserve atlasAdmin for a small named set of human administrators.

other.description:
1. In the Atlas UI, go to **Database Access**
2. Edit each user holding an `*AnyDatabase` or `atlasAdmin` role
3. Replace it with a role scoped to the specific database the application uses, such as `readWrite@appdb`
4. Create a **custom role** where the built-in roles are still broader than needed
5. Restart the application and confirm it operates correctly on the narrowed role
6. Keep `atlasAdmin` for a small number of named human administrators only

access_database_user_scoped_to_clusters.title: Atlas database users are scoped to specific clusters
access_database_user_scoped_to_clusters.description: Atlas lets a database user be **restricted to named clusters or data lakes** within the project. This check reports users with no scope set, which grants them access to every cluster in the project including ones created later.
access_database_user_scoped_to_clusters.risk: An unscoped user automatically gains access to **clusters created after the credential was issued**, so a project's blast radius grows silently as new environments are added. Where production and non-production clusters share a project, an unscoped development credential is a working production credential.

wui.description: Scope each database user to the clusters it needs, and put production in a separate project from non-production rather than relying on scoping alone.

other.description:
1. In the Atlas UI, go to **Database Access** and edit the user
2. Under **Restrict Access to Specific Clusters/Federated Database Instances**, select only the clusters the credential needs
3. Separate production and non-production workloads into **different projects** rather than relying on scope alone
4. Re-test the application after scoping
5. Review scopes when a new cluster is added to the project

access_database_user_workload_identity_a.title: Atlas application database users authenticate with workload identity
access_database_user_workload_identity_a.description: Atlas supports **AWS IAM, OIDC and X.509** authentication in place of SCRAM passwords. This check reports database users still authenticating with a static SCRAM password.
access_database_user_workload_identity_a.risk: A SCRAM password is embedded in the **connection string**, which propagates into environment files, container images, CI logs and application error traces. It does not expire and rotating it requires a coordinated deployment, so in practice it stays unchanged for years. Workload identity removes the stored secret entirely: the credential is issued per session against an identity the cloud provider attests.

cli.description:
atlas dbusers create --projectId <project-id> \
  --awsIAMType ROLE --username arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/app \
  --role readWrite@appdb

wui.description: Move application users to AWS IAM, OIDC or X.509 authentication so no static password is stored, and delete the SCRAM user once connectivity is verified.

other.description:
1. Identify the workload's cloud identity — an IAM role, a Kubernetes service account, or a workload federation identity
2. Create an Atlas database user of the corresponding type (`AWS_IAM`, `OIDC` or `X509`)
3. Grant it the same scoped roles the password user held
4. Update the application's connection string to use the matching auth mechanism
5. Verify connectivity, then delete the SCRAM user
6. For human access, use federated authentication rather than shared database passwords

access_api_key_least_privilege.title: Atlas organization API keys do not hold owner privileges
access_api_key_least_privilege.description: This check reports organization API keys granted `ORG_OWNER` or `GROUP_OWNER`, which allow creating and deleting clusters, changing network access lists and issuing further credentials.
access_api_key_least_privilege.risk: An owner-scoped API key is a **long-lived credential with full control of the Atlas organization**, and it is typically stored in the automation that provisions clusters — CI variables, Terraform state, or a configuration file. Its compromise allows an attacker to open the network access list to the internet and create a database user, reaching the data without touching any existing credential.

wui.description: Reduce API keys to the narrowest project-scoped role that works, bind each key to an API access list, rotate on a schedule, and store them in a secrets manager.

other.description:
1. In Atlas, go to **Organization Settings > Access Manager > API Keys**
2. For each key, review its roles and reduce them to the minimum the automation needs
3. Prefer project-scoped keys (`GROUP_DATA_ACCESS_READ_ONLY`, `GROUP_CLUSTER_MANAGER`) over organization-wide ones
4. Set an **API access list** on every key so it only works from your automation's egress addresses
5. Rotate keys on a schedule and delete those with no recent use
6. Store keys in a secrets manager, never in a repository or CI variable in plaintext

access_private_endpoint_configured.title: Atlas projects reach clusters over a private endpoint
access_private_endpoint_configured.description: A **private endpoint** connects Atlas clusters to your VPC over the cloud provider's private link, removing the need to expose them to public internet addresses. This check reports projects with no available private endpoint service.
access_private_endpoint_configured.risk: Without a private endpoint, cluster connections traverse the **public internet** and access depends entirely on the IP access list — which breaks the moment an application's egress address changes and is routinely widened under operational pressure. Private endpoints make the cluster unreachable from the internet regardless of what the access list says, which is a materially stronger control.

wui.description: Create a private endpoint for each region your workloads run in, move connection strings to the private SRV address, and then remove public entries from the IP access list.

other.description:
1. In Atlas, go to **Network Access > Private Endpoint**
2. Create a private endpoint service for the cloud provider and region your workloads run in
3. Create the corresponding VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link, GCP Private Service Connect) in your own account
4. Update application connection strings to the private endpoint SRV address
5. Once traffic is confirmed flowing privately, remove the public entries from the IP access list
6. Enable the private endpoint **regional mode** where you have workloads in multiple regions
