access_alert_configurations_defined.title: Atlas projects define enabled alert configurations
access_alert_configurations_defined.description: This check verifies that each project has **enabled alert configurations**, so security-relevant events — user additions, access list changes and authentication failures — generate a notification.
access_alert_configurations_defined.risk: Atlas auditing records events but does not act on them, so without alerts a **network access list widened to 0.0.0.0/0 or a new database user created by an attacker** goes unnoticed until someone happens to review the configuration. Those two actions are precisely how an intruder converts stolen API access into data access, and both are cheap to alert on.

cli.description:
atlas alerts settings create --projectId <project-id> \
  --event USER_ROLES_CHANGED_AUDIT --enabled \
  --notificationType GROUP --notificationEmailEnabled

wui.description: Enable alerts on role changes, network access list additions and project membership changes, route them to a monitored channel rather than an individual, and test that each fires.

other.description:
1. In Atlas, go to **Project Settings > Alerts**
2. Enable alerts for `USER_ROLES_CHANGED_AUDIT`, `NETWORK_PERMISSION_ENTRY_ADDED`, `JOINED_GROUP` and authentication failure conditions
3. Route notifications to a monitored channel — PagerDuty, a SIEM webhook or a team alias, not an individual
4. Add operational alerts for disk usage and replication lag alongside the security ones
5. Test each alert fires as expected rather than assuming it will

user_mfa_factor_enrolled.title: Okta users have an active multi-factor authentication factor enrolled
user_mfa_factor_enrolled.description: This check verifies that every active Okta user has at least one **active MFA factor** enrolled, and flags users whose only factor is SMS or voice.
user_mfa_factor_enrolled.risk: Okta is the **front door to every application it federates**, so a user without a second factor is a single password away from every downstream system at once. Where SMS is the only factor, SIM swap and interception defeat it — and because attackers target the identity provider specifically to reach everything behind it, weak factors here have the widest possible blast radius.

wui.description: Require a phishing-resistant factor (FIDO2/WebAuthn or Okta Verify with push) for every active user, and restrict SMS and voice to a recovery role at most.

other.description:
1. In the Okta Admin Console, go to **Security > Authenticators**
2. Enable FIDO2 (WebAuthn) and Okta Verify with push
3. Under **Enrollment**, set FIDO2 or Okta Verify to `Required`
4. Set SMS and Voice to `Disabled` or `Optional` only as a recovery path
5. Create an enrolment window and monitor progress in the MFA usage report
6. For administrators, require a phishing-resistant factor with no fallback

user_no_dormant_accounts.title: Okta has no active users that are dormant or have never signed in
user_no_dormant_accounts.description: This check reports active Okta users who have never signed in, or whose last sign-in predates the configured dormancy threshold (90 days by default).
user_no_dormant_accounts.risk: A dormant Okta account still **federates into every application assigned to it**, and because nobody uses it legitimately, nobody notices when someone else does. These accounts also tend to have older passwords and outdated factor enrolments, making them the easiest targets in the directory and the least likely compromise to be reported by the account's owner.

wui.description: Suspend then deactivate dormant accounts, and drive lifecycle from your HR system so deprovisioning is automatic rather than dependent on periodic review.

other.description:
1. Run the **Okta user activity** report filtered on last sign-in
2. Confirm with the owning manager whether each account is still needed
3. Suspend rather than deactivate first, so any dependency surfaces safely
4. Deactivate accounts that remain unclaimed after the grace period
5. Connect Okta to your HR system so joiner-mover-leaver events deprovision automatically
6. Check service accounts separately: they may legitimately never sign in interactively

policy_password_strength_enforced.title: Okta password policies enforce length, dictionary and lockout controls
policy_password_strength_enforced.description: This check verifies that each active password policy requires a minimum length of 12 or more, excludes the username, enables the common-password dictionary check, and locks accounts after a bounded number of failed attempts.
policy_password_strength_enforced.risk: Okta's sign-in endpoint is internet-facing by design, so password policy directly determines how effective **password spraying** is against your whole directory at once. The common-password dictionary check matters most: spraying uses a small list of predictable passwords across many accounts precisely because lockout thresholds are per-account, and a dictionary check is what removes those passwords from the pool.

wui.description: Require 12+ characters with the common-password dictionary check and username exclusion, lock out after 5 failed attempts, and enable ThreatInsight to block spraying at the network layer.

other.description:
1. In the Okta Admin Console, go to **Security > Authentication policies > Password**
2. Set the minimum length to 12 or more
3. Enable **Common password check** and **Do not allow parts of the username**
4. Set **Lock out user after** to 5 or fewer failed attempts
5. Enable **Breached password detection** through ThreatInsight where licensed
6. Configure ThreatInsight to block requests from known-malicious IPs, which stops spraying before it reaches the policy

terraform.description:
resource "okta_policy_password" "default" {
  name                     = "Password Policy"
  status                   = "ACTIVE"
  password_min_length      = 12
  password_exclude_username = true
  password_dictionary_lookup = true
  password_max_lockout_attempts = 5
}

policy_mfa_enrollment_required.title: Okta orgs have an active MFA enrollment policy
policy_mfa_enrollment_required.description: This check verifies that the org has at least one **active MFA enrollment policy**, which is what obliges users to register a factor rather than leaving enrolment optional.
policy_mfa_enrollment_required.risk: Without an active enrolment policy, MFA is **available but not required**, so coverage depends entirely on individual users choosing to enrol. In practice that leaves a long tail of unprotected accounts — and attackers specifically enumerate for them, since one unenrolled user provides the same federated access as any other.

wui.description: Activate an MFA enrollment policy requiring a phishing-resistant factor, assign it to all users with a stricter variant for admins, and prompt for enrolment at next sign-in.

other.description:
1. In the Okta Admin Console, go to **Security > Authenticators > Enrollment**
2. Create or edit an enrolment policy and set it to **Active**
3. Set FIDO2 (WebAuthn) or Okta Verify to `Required`
4. Assign the policy to all users, with a stricter policy for administrator groups
5. Add a rule that prompts for enrolment at next sign-in rather than deferring indefinitely
6. Track enrolment completion and follow up with the remaining users

application_sign_on_mode_federated.title: Okta applications use federated sign-on rather than stored passwords
application_sign_on_mode_federated.description: This check reports active applications using `SECURE_PASSWORD_STORE`, `BASIC_AUTH` or `BOOKMARK` sign-on modes, where Okta stores and replays a password rather than issuing a federated assertion.
application_sign_on_mode_federated.risk: Password-replay sign-on modes mean Okta **holds a reusable credential for the downstream application**, so compromising the Okta org yields working passwords for those systems directly rather than only session assertions. Those credentials also bypass the downstream application's own MFA, and they survive an Okta session revocation because the password itself is unchanged.

wui.description: Migrate applications to SAML or OIDC federation, restrict assignment for those that only support password replay, and rotate the passwords Okta stores for them.

other.description:
1. In the Okta Admin Console, list applications and review the **Sign-On Method** of each
2. For applications that support SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect, migrate them to federated sign-on
3. Where an application only supports password replay, restrict its assignment to the smallest possible group
4. Ensure those applications enforce their own MFA independently
5. Remove BOOKMARK apps that point at systems now reachable through federation
6. Rotate the stored passwords for any application that remains on password replay

user_password_rotated.title: Okta user passwords have been changed within the rotation window
user_password_rotated.description: This check reports active users whose password has not changed within the configured window (365 days by default), or for whom no password change is recorded at all.
user_password_rotated.risk: A password unchanged for years is one that has had the **maximum possible exposure to credential breaches elsewhere**, since reuse is common and breach corpora accumulate over time. While forced frequent rotation is no longer recommended practice, an unchanged credential of this age combined with weak or absent MFA is a meaningful indicator of an account worth attention.

wui.description: Drive password resets from breach detection rather than a calendar, ensure flagged accounts have a strong factor enrolled, and move suitable accounts to passwordless FIDO2 authentication.

other.description:
1. Prefer breach-driven rotation over calendar-driven: enable **breached password detection** so a credential is reset when it is known to be exposed
2. Where a maximum password age is required by policy, configure it under **Security > Authentication policies > Password**
3. For the accounts flagged here, confirm a strong MFA factor is enrolled — that matters more than the password age
4. Consider moving the account to passwordless authentication with FIDO2
5. Reset passwords for any account appearing in a breach corpus regardless of age

openai_organization_mfa_required.title: OpenAI organizations require multi-factor authentication
openai_organization_mfa_required.description: This check verifies that the OpenAI organization requires **multi-factor authentication** for console sign-in, so that access to API keys, billing and project configuration is not protected by a password alone.
openai_organization_mfa_required.risk: Console access is what mints and reads **API keys**, so a password-only account is the shortest path to a durable credential for your models and, through those keys, to any data your prompts carry. Because usage is billed, a compromised organization also produces immediate financial loss through model abuse before the intrusion is even noticed.

wui.description: Require MFA for every member of the OpenAI organization, or enforce it upstream in your identity provider if console access is federated through SSO.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the OpenAI platform console as an owner
2. Go to **Settings > Organization > General**
3. Enable the requirement for multi-factor authentication
4. Notify members before enforcing, since those without MFA lose access until they enrol
5. Where the organization is federated, enforce MFA in the identity provider's conditional access policy instead so it applies uniformly

openai_organization_sso_enforced.title: OpenAI organizations enforce SSO with a verified domain
openai_organization_sso_enforced.description: This check verifies that the organization enforces **single sign-on** and has verified its email domain, so membership follows the corporate identity provider rather than individually created accounts.
openai_organization_sso_enforced.risk: Without enforced SSO, members sign in with **personal credentials outside your control**, so leavers keep access until someone remembers to remove them manually, and there is no conditional access or central session revocation. An unverified domain also allows anyone with a company email address to self-register outside the governed organization entirely.

wui.description: Verify your domain and enforce SSO so OpenAI membership is governed by your identity provider, with SCIM provisioning where available so leavers are deprovisioned automatically.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the OpenAI platform console as an owner
2. Go to **Settings > Organization > Security**
3. Verify your email domain by publishing the supplied DNS record
4. Configure the SAML connection to your identity provider
5. Test with a pilot user, then enable **Enforce SSO**
6. Remove any accounts using personal email addresses once federation is proven

openai_organization_audit_log_export_con.title: OpenAI organizations export audit logs to an external system
openai_organization_audit_log_export_con.description: This check verifies that the organization's **audit log** is readable and exported to an external system, so records of key creation, member changes and project configuration survive outside the platform.
openai_organization_audit_log_export_con.risk: API key creation is the single most security-relevant event in an OpenAI organization, and without exported logs there is **no durable record of who minted which key and when**. During an investigation into leaked model access or unexpected spend, that gap makes it impossible to distinguish legitimate provisioning from an attacker establishing persistence.

wui.description: Export the OpenAI audit log into your SIEM on a schedule and alert on API key creation, member invitations and organization setting changes.

other.description:
1. Confirm your plan includes audit log access
2. Build or enable a scheduled export that pulls `/v1/organization/audit_logs` into your SIEM
3. Alert on `api_key.created`, `invite.sent`, `organization.updated` and `project.created` events
4. Alert specifically on admin key creation, which grants organization-wide control
5. Retain the exported logs according to your incident investigation window

openai_organization_data_retention_limit.title: OpenAI organizations limit prompt data retention and opt out of training
openai_organization_data_retention_limit.description: This check verifies that the organization opts out of using API data for **model training** and has a bounded retention window — ideally zero data retention — for prompts and completions.
openai_organization_data_retention_limit.risk: Prompts routinely carry **customer records, source code and internal documents** that were never classified for third-party storage. Where retention is unbounded, that content sits outside your environment beyond the reach of your own deletion and residency commitments, and any breach of the provider's storage becomes a breach of your data.

wui.description: Opt out of training, request zero data retention where eligible, and redact sensitive identifiers before they are sent so the control does not depend solely on the provider's configuration.

other.description:
1. Sign in to the OpenAI platform console as an owner
2. Go to **Settings > Organization > Data controls**
3. Confirm that API data is not used for model training
4. Request **Zero Data Retention** for eligible endpoints if your data handling requirements call for it
5. Record the configured retention window in your processing register
6. Independently reduce what is sent: redact identifiers before they reach the API rather than relying on retention settings alone

openai_apikey_scoped_to_project.title: OpenAI API keys are scoped to a project rather than the organization
openai_apikey_scoped_to_project.description: **Project API keys** are limited to one project's models, rate limits and budget, while **admin keys** carry organization-wide control. This check reports keys issued at organization scope, which should exist only for administrative automation.
openai_apikey_scoped_to_project.risk: An organization-scoped admin key can **create further keys, add members and change billing**, so leaking one is equivalent to losing the console itself rather than losing access to a single workload. Because these keys are often pasted into shared automation, one exposure grants durable, self-renewing control of the entire account.

wui.description: Issue one service-account-owned project key per workload, keep admin keys to the minimum needed for provisioning automation, and bound each project with its own rate limit and budget.

other.description:
1. Create a project for each workload in **Settings > Projects**
2. Issue a project API key owned by a **service account**, not a person
3. Update the workload to use the project key
4. Delete the admin key it replaced
5. Retain admin keys only for provisioning automation, and store them in a secrets manager with access logging
6. Set per-project rate limits and budgets so a compromised project key has a bounded cost

openai_apikey_no_stale_keys.title: OpenAI API keys are rotated and unused keys are removed
openai_apikey_no_stale_keys.description: This check reports API keys that have never been used, or whose last use predates the configured staleness threshold (90 days by default), and keys older than the configured maximum age.
openai_apikey_no_stale_keys.risk: OpenAI API keys **do not expire**, so a key pasted into a notebook, a container image or a chat message stays valid until someone deletes it. Unused keys are the ones nobody will notice being used, and because billing is per-token, a stolen key produces cost and data exposure long before anyone connects the spend to a leak.

wui.description: Delete unused keys, rotate active ones on a fixed schedule with an overlap window, store them in a secrets manager, and enable spend alerts so misuse is detected by cost anomaly.

other.description:
1. List the keys in each project and identify those with no recent use
2. Confirm with the owning team, then delete them
3. Rotate keys still in use on a fixed schedule: create the replacement, deploy it, verify traffic moved, then delete the old key
4. Store keys in a secrets manager rather than in environment files committed to source control
5. Enable spend alerts so anomalous usage on a leaked key surfaces quickly

openai_project_service_accounts_used_for.title: OpenAI projects use service accounts for automated workloads
openai_project_service_accounts_used_for.description: A **service account** is a project-scoped, non-human identity whose keys survive personnel changes. This check reports active projects with no service account, which indicates that automation is running on keys owned by individual users.
openai_project_service_accounts_used_for.risk: When production traffic runs on a personal API key, **removing that person from the organization breaks production**, so offboarding is quietly skipped and their access persists. Attribution also breaks down: every request in the audit log appears to come from an individual who may have had nothing to do with the workload.

wui.description: Create a service account per automated workload and issue its keys from that identity, so offboarding a person never disrupts production and audit records attribute traffic correctly.

other.description:
1. Open the project in **Settings > Projects**
2. Create a service account for each automated workload
3. Issue an API key owned by that service account
4. Deploy the new key, verify traffic has moved, then delete the user-owned key it replaced
5. Archive projects that are no longer in use so their keys stop working

openai_project_rate_limits_configured.title: OpenAI projects define per-project rate limits
openai_project_rate_limits_configured.description: Per-project **rate limits** cap the request and token throughput a project may consume. This check reports active projects with no rate limit override, which leaves them able to consume the whole organization's capacity and budget.
openai_project_rate_limits_configured.risk: Without per-project limits, a leaked key or a runaway retry loop consumes the **entire organization's quota and budget**, taking every other project down with it — a denial of service against your own production traffic. Uncapped spend on a stolen key also converts a credential leak directly into unbounded financial loss.

wui.description: Set per-project request, token and budget limits sized to each workload's real peak, and handle rate limit responses with backoff so a single project cannot exhaust organization capacity.

other.description:
1. Open the project in **Settings > Projects > Limits**
2. Set request and token per-minute limits sized to the workload's actual peak plus headroom
3. Set a monthly budget for the project and enable notification thresholds
4. Handle 429 responses in the client with exponential backoff rather than raising the limit
5. Review limits when traffic patterns change

salesforce_user_mfa_registered.title: Salesforce users have a multi-factor verification method registered
salesforce_user_mfa_registered.description: This check verifies that every active Salesforce user has registered at least one **multi-factor verification method** — an authenticator app, security key or built-in authenticator.
salesforce_user_mfa_registered.risk: Salesforce orgs hold the **complete customer record**: contacts, pipeline, contracts and often payment detail. A password-only login is directly usable from anywhere, and credential phishing against Salesforce users is a standing, well-tooled attack because the export capability built into the platform turns one session into a full data set.

wui.description: Require MFA for all direct UI logins, prefer security keys or built-in authenticators over SMS, and enforce MFA in the upstream IdP for federated users.

other.description:
1. In Setup, go to **Identity > Identity Verification**
2. Enable **Require multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all direct UI logins**
3. For profile-scoped enforcement, assign the **Multi-Factor Authentication for User Interface Logins** permission
4. Give users an enrolment window and monitor registration in the Identity Verification report
5. Prefer security keys or built-in authenticators over SMS, which is vulnerable to SIM swap
6. Where users sign in through an external IdP, enforce MFA in that IdP's conditional access policy

salesforce_user_no_excessive_admin_permi.title: Salesforce users do not hold excessive administrative permissions
salesforce_user_no_excessive_admin_permi.description: This check reports active users whose profile grants **Modify All Data**, **Manage Users** or **Author Apex** — permissions that together allow reading every record, creating accounts and deploying executable code.
salesforce_user_no_excessive_admin_permi.risk: **Modify All Data** overrides every sharing rule, field permission and record ownership control in the org, so a single compromised account with it holds the entire data set regardless of the sharing model. **Author Apex** additionally allows deploying code that runs in system context, giving an attacker a persistent, auditable-looking mechanism to exfiltrate data on a schedule.

wui.description: Move from broad profile grants to narrowly scoped permission sets, restrict Modify All Data and Author Apex to a small named group, and review holders on a recurring schedule.

other.description:
1. In Setup, run the **Permission Set and Profile** reports to list holders of Modify All Data
2. For each, determine whether the access is genuinely required
3. Replace broad profile grants with narrowly scoped **permission sets** assigned only when needed
4. Use **permission set groups with a muting permission set** to remove specific dangerous permissions from otherwise appropriate roles
5. Restrict Author Apex to a small named release team
6. Review the remaining holders on a recurring schedule and require MFA for all of them

salesforce_org_password_policy_strong.title: Salesforce orgs enforce a strong password policy
salesforce_org_password_policy_strong.description: This check verifies that the org's password policy requires a minimum length of at least 12 characters, mixed character complexity, and account lockout after a bounded number of failed attempts.
salesforce_org_password_policy_strong.risk: Salesforce login endpoints are **publicly reachable and continuously targeted** by credential stuffing, so a weak minimum length or an unbounded retry count makes automated guessing practical. Because a successful login grants export capability over the customer record, the cost of a single guessed password is disproportionate to the effort required.

wui.description: Require at least 12 characters with mixed complexity, lock accounts after a small number of failed attempts, and pair the policy with enforced MFA.

other.description:
1. In Setup, go to **Security > Password Policies**
2. Set **Minimum password length** to 12 or more
3. Set **Password complexity requirement** to require letters, numbers and special characters
4. Set **Maximum invalid login attempts** to 5 or fewer with a lockout period
5. Configure **Password question requirement** to disallow the password itself
6. Note that a strong password policy complements but does not replace MFA — configure both

salesforce_org_session_settings_hardened.title: Salesforce orgs harden session settings
salesforce_org_session_settings_hardened.description: This check verifies that the org locks sessions to the originating IP address and applies a session timeout no longer than the configured maximum (two hours by default).
salesforce_org_session_settings_hardened.risk: A Salesforce session ID that is not bound to its originating address can be **replayed from anywhere** once stolen through a malicious browser extension, an XSS flaw in a Visualforce page, or a phishing proxy. Long timeouts widen that replay window considerably, and because sessions survive password changes, revocation during an incident is slower than administrators expect.

wui.description: Lock sessions to their originating IP, cap the session timeout at two hours with forced logout, and require HTTPS — testing IP locking against rotating VPN egress before enforcement.

other.description:
1. In Setup, go to **Security > Session Settings**
2. Set **Timeout value** to 2 hours or less and enable **Force logout on session timeout**
3. Enable **Lock sessions to the IP address from which they originated**
4. Enable **Require secure connections (HTTPS)**
5. Enable **Force relogin after Login-As-User**
6. Test with users behind rotating egress addresses before enforcing IP locking — some VPN configurations break it

salesforce_org_login_ip_ranges_configure.title: Salesforce orgs restrict login to trusted IP ranges
salesforce_org_login_ip_ranges_configure.description: This check verifies that the org defines **trusted login IP ranges**, and reports ranges so wide that they provide no meaningful restriction.
salesforce_org_login_ip_ranges_configure.risk: Without login IP ranges, a phished credential is usable **immediately from the attacker's own infrastructure**, and the identity verification challenge that would otherwise fire for an unrecognised address can be satisfied by the same phishing proxy that captured the password. Network scoping breaks that chain at a layer the phishing kit cannot relay.

wui.description: Define trusted IP ranges for the org and profile-level login IP ranges for privileged profiles, keeping them narrow and confirming integration egress is covered first.

other.description:
1. In Setup, go to **Security > Network Access**
2. Add the egress ranges for your offices, VPN and integration middleware as trusted IP ranges
3. For stricter control, set **Login IP Ranges** on individual profiles, which blocks login outright rather than only skipping verification
4. Verify integration users are covered before enforcing, or scheduled jobs will fail
5. Keep the ranges as narrow as your network allows and review them when egress changes

salesforce_connectedapp_oauth_scopes_lea.title: Salesforce connected apps request least-privilege OAuth scopes
salesforce_connectedapp_oauth_scopes_lea.description: This check reports connected apps requesting the **full**, **refresh_token** with unrestricted access, or **web** scopes without restricting which users may authorise them, and apps whose callback URLs are not exact HTTPS endpoints.
salesforce_connectedapp_oauth_scopes_lea.risk: The `full` scope grants a third-party application **everything the authorising user can do**, including exporting the entire customer record, and the accompanying refresh token makes that access indefinite and survivable across password resets. Connected apps are also a favoured persistence mechanism: an attacker who authorises one retains access long after the compromised session is closed.

wui.description: Replace the full scope with narrow ones, pre-authorise apps to named profiles only, require PKCE, use exact HTTPS callback URLs, and revoke unused apps to invalidate their refresh tokens.

other.description:
1. In Setup, go to **Apps > Connected Apps > Manage Connected Apps**
2. Review the OAuth scopes each app requests and remove `full` where a narrower scope suffices
3. Set **Permitted Users** to `Admin approved users are pre-authorized` and assign only the profiles that need it
4. Enable **Require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)**
5. Set callback URLs to exact HTTPS endpoints — no wildcards, no HTTP
6. Revoke apps that are no longer in use, which also invalidates their refresh tokens

salesforce_org_event_monitoring_enabled.title: Salesforce orgs have Event Monitoring enabled
salesforce_org_event_monitoring_enabled.description: **Event Monitoring** exposes login, API, report export and Apex execution events as downloadable log files. This check verifies that `EventLogFile` is queryable, indicating the capability is licensed and available.
salesforce_org_event_monitoring_enabled.risk: Without Event Monitoring there is **no record of data export**: the setup audit trail captures configuration changes but not who ran which report or pulled which records through the API. That is precisely the evidence needed to scope a data breach, and its absence turns an investigation into guesswork about what an attacker actually took.

wui.description: Enable Real-Time Event Monitoring, pull EventLogFile into your SIEM daily, alert on bulk exports and unusual API access, and add transaction security policies to block the worst cases outright.

other.description:
1. Confirm your edition includes Event Monitoring, or add the Salesforce Shield licence
2. Enable **Real-Time Event Monitoring** in Setup > Event Manager for the events you need, particularly ReportEvent, ApiEvent and LoginEvent
3. Configure a scheduled job or the Event Monitoring Analytics app to pull EventLogFile daily into your SIEM
4. Alert on large report exports, API access from unrecognised addresses and Login-As-User events
5. Add **Transaction Security Policies** to block the highest-risk actions rather than only recording them

salesforce_org_shield_platform_encryptio.title: Salesforce orgs encrypt sensitive fields with Shield Platform Encryption
salesforce_org_shield_platform_encryptio.description: **Shield Platform Encryption** encrypts field data at rest while preserving platform functionality, using a tenant secret you can rotate and destroy. This check reports orgs with no encrypted fields configured.
salesforce_org_shield_platform_encryptio.risk: Salesforce's default at-rest encryption is transparent to the platform, so it offers **no protection against an authenticated attacker or an over-permissioned integration** reading the data. Shield encryption additionally gives you a tenant secret you control, which is what makes crypto-shredding — destroying the key to render data unrecoverable — possible at all.

wui.description: Encrypt fields holding regulated data with Shield Platform Encryption, review the functional trade-offs before rollout, and consider Bring Your Own Key with a documented rotation schedule.

other.description:
1. Confirm the org has the Salesforce Shield or Platform Encryption licence
2. In Setup, go to **Security > Platform Encryption > Key Management** and generate a tenant secret
3. Under **Encryption Policy**, encrypt the fields holding regulated data — national identifiers, payment references, health information
4. Review the documented functional trade-offs first: some filtering, sorting and formula behaviour changes on encrypted fields
5. Consider **Bring Your Own Key** so the tenant secret is derived from key material you hold
6. Establish a tenant secret rotation schedule

slack_workspace_sso_required.title: Slack workspaces require SSO for member sign-in
slack_workspace_sso_required.description: This check verifies that the workspace requires **single sign-on**, so membership and session control follow the corporate identity provider rather than Slack-local passwords.
slack_workspace_sso_required.risk: Slack accumulates an organisation's most sensitive informal record: **credentials pasted into DMs, incident detail, contract discussion and internal architecture**. Without enforced SSO there is no conditional access and no central session revocation, so a leaver or a phished account retains a searchable archive of all of it until someone manually intervenes.

wui.description: Require SAML SSO for all members and enable SCIM provisioning so deprovisioning is automatic rather than dependent on manual offboarding steps.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Slack as a workspace or org owner
2. Go to **Settings & administration > Workspace settings > Authentication**
3. Configure the SAML connection to your identity provider
4. Set SSO to **Required** for all members
5. Enable SCIM provisioning so deactivation in the IdP removes Slack access automatically
6. Decide explicitly whether guests are exempt, and document the exception

slack_workspace_two_factor_required.title: Slack workspaces require two-factor authentication
slack_workspace_two_factor_required.description: This check verifies that the workspace requires **two-factor authentication** for members who sign in with a Slack password, which applies wherever SSO is not enforced.
slack_workspace_two_factor_required.risk: Where SSO is not required, a Slack password is the **only barrier to a fully searchable message history**, including any credential a colleague pasted into a channel. Slack account takeover is also a favoured route for internal phishing, because a message from a trusted colleague's real account bypasses the scepticism an external email would attract.

wui.description: Require two-factor authentication for all password-based sign-ins, preferring authenticator apps over SMS, and enforce the equivalent policy in your IdP where SSO is used.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Slack as a workspace owner or admin
2. Go to **Settings & administration > Workspace settings > Authentication**
3. Enable **Require two-factor authentication for everyone**
4. Notify members before enforcing, since those without 2FA are signed out until they enrol
5. Prefer an authenticator app over SMS, which is vulnerable to SIM swap
6. Where SSO is enforced, apply the equivalent requirement in the identity provider instead

slack_workspace_app_approval_required.title: Slack workspaces require admin approval before app installation
slack_workspace_app_approval_required.description: This check verifies that **app approval** is enabled and that app management is restricted to admins, so third-party integrations cannot be installed by any member without review.
slack_workspace_app_approval_required.risk: A Slack app authorised by an ordinary member can hold scopes that read **every message in every channel it is added to**, and that access continues silently long after whoever installed it has forgotten about it. Malicious and abandoned apps in the directory are a recurring problem, and without approval gating your review happens after the data has already left.

wui.description: Require admin approval for app installation, restrict app management to admins, and audit the apps already installed — an approval gate does not retroactively review them.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Slack as a workspace owner or admin
2. Go to **Settings & administration > Manage apps > App management settings**
3. Enable **Require App Approval**
4. Restrict app installation to admins
5. Review the apps already installed and restrict any that are unrecognised or no longer used
6. Maintain an allowlist of reviewed apps so approval does not become a bottleneck

slack_app_oauth_scopes_least_privilege.title: Slack apps do not hold workspace-wide message read scopes
slack_app_oauth_scopes_least_privilege.description: This check reports installed apps holding broad scopes such as `channels:history`, `groups:history`, `files:read` or any `admin.*` scope, which grant access far beyond a single channel's interaction.
slack_app_oauth_scopes_least_privilege.risk: A `history` scope lets an app read the **complete message archive of every conversation it can see**, not just messages that mention it, so one compromised vendor becomes a full export of your internal discussion. `admin.*` scopes go further still, allowing the app to change workspace settings and manage other apps — a self-sustaining foothold.

wui.description: Remove apps holding workspace-wide history or admin scopes unless clearly justified, scope message access to specific channels, and re-review scopes when apps update.

other.description:
1. Go to **Settings & administration > Manage apps**
2. Open each app and review its granted scopes
3. Remove apps holding history or admin scopes that they do not demonstrably need
4. Where an app must read messages, restrict it to specific channels rather than the workspace
5. Prefer apps that use Slack Connect or narrow event subscriptions over polling history
6. Re-review app scopes when an app updates, since new versions can request additional permissions

slack_channel_external_sharing_reviewed.title: Slack channels shared externally are private and actively used
slack_channel_external_sharing_reviewed.description: This check reports **externally shared** (Slack Connect) channels that are public within the workspace, and external channels left unarchived with no members, both of which extend a trust boundary beyond what anyone is actively managing.
slack_channel_external_sharing_reviewed.risk: An externally shared channel gives another organisation's members a **live view into your workspace**, and when the channel is also public internally, anyone who joins it — including a newly compromised account — is exposed to that external party. Forgotten Connect channels from ended engagements are the common case: the counterparty retains access long after the commercial relationship stops.

wui.description: Keep externally shared channels private, disconnect them when an engagement ends, restrict who may send Connect invitations, and add the review to vendor offboarding.

other.description:
1. Go to **Settings & administration > Manage organization > Channels** and filter to externally shared channels
2. Confirm each still corresponds to an active engagement
3. Convert externally shared channels to private so membership is deliberate
4. Archive or disconnect channels for finished engagements — disconnecting revokes the external party's access to history
5. Restrict who may create Slack Connect invitations to admins
6. Add the review to your vendor offboarding checklist

slack_workspace_retention_policy_configu.title: Slack workspaces configure message and file retention
slack_workspace_retention_policy_configu.description: This check verifies that the workspace sets an explicit **message and file retention** period rather than retaining everything indefinitely by default.
slack_workspace_retention_policy_configu.risk: Slack's default is to keep messages and files **forever**, so the workspace accumulates years of pasted credentials, customer data and confidential discussion that no policy ever authorised retaining. A single account compromise then exposes the organisation's entire history rather than its recent activity, and the archive becomes discoverable in litigation regardless of business need.

wui.description: Set explicit message and file retention matching your records policy, restrict per-channel overrides, and export to a governed archive where regulation requires longer retention.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Slack as a workspace owner
2. Go to **Settings & administration > Workspace settings > Message retention & deletion**
3. Set a retention period that matches your records policy — commonly 1 to 2 years for general channels
4. Set file retention separately; files are often the higher exposure
5. Decide whether channel owners may override the default, and restrict it if not
6. Where regulation requires longer retention, export to a governed archive rather than leaving data in Slack indefinitely

slack_workspace_audit_logs_accessible.title: Slack organizations have audit logs available for export
slack_workspace_audit_logs_accessible.description: This check verifies that the **Audit Logs API** is readable for the organization, indicating that administrative and access events can be exported to a SIEM.
slack_workspace_audit_logs_accessible.risk: Without audit log access there is **no record of app installations, permission changes, file downloads or Slack Connect invitations**. Those are exactly the events that distinguish an account compromise from normal use, so their absence means an intrusion is typically discovered only when its effects surface elsewhere.

wui.description: Enable the Audit Logs API, pull events into your SIEM on a schedule, and alert on app installations, scope expansions, bulk downloads and Slack Connect invitations.

other.description:
1. Confirm the organization is on a plan that includes the Audit Logs API
2. Create an app with the `auditlogs:read` scope and install it at the org level
3. Build or enable a scheduled pull of `/audit/v1/logs` into your SIEM
4. Alert on `app_installed`, `app_scopes_expanded`, `file_downloaded` in bulk, `user_channel_join` to sensitive channels and Slack Connect invitations
5. Retain the exported events for at least your investigation window

slack_workspace_enterprise_key_managemen.title: Slack Enterprise Grid organizations use enterprise key management
slack_workspace_enterprise_key_managemen.description: **Enterprise Key Management** encrypts Slack messages and files with a customer-managed key held in your own cloud KMS. This check reports Enterprise Grid organizations that have not enabled it; standalone workspaces where the feature is unavailable are skipped.
slack_workspace_enterprise_key_managemen.risk: With platform-managed keys only, you cannot **independently revoke access to your message history** — containment during a suspected platform incident depends entirely on the provider acting. Customer-managed keys also let you revoke access at channel or workspace granularity and give you the key-usage audit trail that regulated programmes expect.

wui.description: Enable Enterprise Key Management with a key in your own KMS, monitor key usage in your cloud audit log, and document a revocation runbook before you need it.

other.description:
1. Confirm the organization is on Enterprise Grid with the EKM add-on
2. Create a KMS key in your own cloud account
3. Grant Slack the minimum key usage permissions required
4. Enable EKM in the organization settings and select the channels or workspaces to cover
5. Enable key rotation and monitor key usage in your cloud audit log
6. Document the revocation runbook, including who is authorised to revoke and what it makes inaccessible

snowflake_user_mfa_enrolled.title: Snowflake human users are enrolled in multi-factor authentication
snowflake_user_mfa_enrolled.description: This check verifies that every enabled Snowflake user who can authenticate with a password is enrolled in **multi-factor authentication**. Service users authenticating by key pair are excluded, since they carry no password to phish.
snowflake_user_mfa_enrolled.risk: Snowflake accounts hold consolidated analytical copies of an organisation's most sensitive data, and a password-only login is directly usable from anywhere on the internet. Large-scale intrusions into Snowflake tenants have been driven almost entirely by **credential reuse against accounts without MFA**, using passwords harvested from unrelated infostealer infections rather than any flaw in the platform.

wui.description: Require MFA enrolment through an account-level authentication policy, and move every service user to key-pair authentication so the policy can be enforced without exempting automation.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Snowsight as ACCOUNTADMIN
2. Create an authentication policy with `MFA_ENROLLMENT = REQUIRED`
3. Apply it at the account level, exempting only service users that authenticate by key pair
4. Notify users, then enforce
5. Review `SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY` for password logins that predate enforcement and treat those credentials as exposed

terraform.description:
resource "snowflake_authentication_policy" "require_mfa" {
  database = "SECURITY"
  schema   = "POLICIES"
  name     = "REQUIRE_MFA"
  mfa_enrollment = "REQUIRED"
  client_types   = ["SNOWFLAKE_UI", "DRIVERS"]
}

snowflake_user_service_account_uses_key_.title: Snowflake service users authenticate with key pairs rather than passwords
snowflake_user_service_account_uses_key_.description: Snowflake users of type `SERVICE` or `LEGACY_SERVICE` cannot complete an interactive MFA challenge, so a password on such an account is a **single-factor credential**. This check verifies that service users have an RSA public key registered and no password set.
snowflake_user_service_account_uses_key_.risk: A service user's password is typically embedded in an **ETL configuration, CI variable or notebook**, where it is copied, logged and shared far beyond its intended scope, and it cannot be protected by MFA. Because these accounts commonly hold broad warehouse privileges, one leaked configuration file grants durable, non-attributable access to the data platform.

wui.description: Move every service user to key-pair authentication, remove its password, and rotate keys using the secondary key slot so rollover needs no downtime.

other.description:
1. Generate an RSA key pair and store the private key in your secrets manager
2. Register the public key with `ALTER USER <name> SET RSA_PUBLIC_KEY = '<key>'`
3. Update the client configuration to authenticate with the private key
4. Verify a successful key-pair login in `LOGIN_HISTORY`
5. Remove the password with `ALTER USER <name> UNSET PASSWORD`
6. Set `TYPE = SERVICE` so authentication policies can target these accounts distinctly
7. Rotate the key pair on a schedule using `RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_2` for zero-downtime rollover

snowflake_user_default_role_not_privileg.title: Snowflake users do not default to ACCOUNTADMIN or SECURITYADMIN
snowflake_user_default_role_not_privileg.description: A user's **default role** is assumed automatically on connection. This check reports enabled users whose default role is `ACCOUNTADMIN`, `SECURITYADMIN` or `ORGADMIN`, so privileged roles must be selected deliberately rather than inherited by every session.
snowflake_user_default_role_not_privileg.risk: When a session starts as ACCOUNTADMIN, every routine query, notebook and BI connection runs with **full account privileges**, and any SQL injection or compromised client immediately inherits them. Snowflake's own guidance is that ACCOUNTADMIN should be assumed explicitly for administrative work only, so a privileged default role removes the last barrier between an ordinary mistake and account-wide impact.

wui.description: Give every user a least-privilege functional default role, reserve ACCOUNTADMIN for explicit assumption by a small named group, and alert on its use.

other.description:
1. List users whose default role is privileged
2. Create or identify a least-privilege functional role for each user's day-to-day work
3. Set it with `ALTER USER <name> SET DEFAULT_ROLE = <functional_role>`
4. Keep ACCOUNTADMIN granted to a small named set of administrators who assume it explicitly with `USE ROLE`
5. Ensure every ACCOUNTADMIN holder is MFA-enrolled
6. Alert on ACCOUNTADMIN usage in `QUERY_HISTORY`

snowflake_user_no_stale_accounts.title: Snowflake has no enabled users that are dormant or never used
snowflake_user_no_stale_accounts.description: This check reports enabled Snowflake users that have never logged in, or whose last successful login predates the configured dormancy threshold (90 days by default).
snowflake_user_no_stale_accounts.risk: A dormant but enabled account is a **credential nobody is watching**: its password is rarely rotated, its owner may have left, and unusual activity on it raises no expectation of being noticed. Because Snowflake roles are typically granted at onboarding and rarely revisited, stale accounts often retain access to data the person or system no longer has any business reason to read.

wui.description: Disable then remove dormant accounts, and connect Snowflake to your IdP with SCIM so joiner-mover-leaver events deprovision users automatically instead of relying on periodic review.

other.description:
1. Run the dormancy query against `SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.USERS`
2. Confirm with the owning team whether each account is still needed
3. Disable rather than drop first, so any dependency surfaces safely
4. Drop accounts that remain unclaimed after the grace period
5. Connect Snowflake to your identity provider with SCIM so deprovisioning becomes automatic
6. Schedule the review as a recurring task

snowflake_account_network_policy_enforce.title: Snowflake accounts enforce an account-level network policy
snowflake_account_network_policy_enforce.description: An account-level **network policy** limits which IP addresses may connect to the Snowflake account. This check verifies that the `NETWORK_POLICY` account parameter is set rather than left empty.
snowflake_account_network_policy_enforce.risk: Without a network policy the account accepts authentication attempts from **any address on the internet**, so a credential harvested elsewhere is immediately usable with no further foothold required. Network scoping is the control that most reliably breaks that path, because it invalidates a stolen password even before authentication policy is considered.

wui.description: Attach a network policy at the account level covering only your corporate, VPN and data-pipeline egress ranges, and prefer PrivateLink for cloud-hosted clients.

other.description:
1. Collect the egress CIDR ranges of your offices, VPN, BI tools and ETL infrastructure
2. Create a network policy with those ranges in `ALLOWED_IP_LIST`
3. Verify your own address is included before applying, or you will lock yourself out
4. Apply it with `ALTER ACCOUNT SET NETWORK_POLICY = <name>`
5. For cloud-hosted clients, prefer private connectivity (PrivateLink) with a policy restricted to the private endpoint
6. Review `LOGIN_HISTORY` for connections from outside the intended ranges before enforcing

snowflake_account_sso_enabled.title: Snowflake accounts federate authentication through SSO
snowflake_account_sso_enabled.description: This check verifies that the account has a **SAML2 or External OAuth security integration** configured, so human access is governed by the corporate identity provider rather than by Snowflake-local passwords.
snowflake_account_sso_enabled.risk: Snowflake-local passwords sit outside the controls your identity provider applies — **no conditional access, no device posture, no central session revocation**, and no automatic disablement when someone leaves. During an incident, the inability to revoke access centrally materially extends the time an attacker keeps a working credential.

cli.description:
CREATE SECURITY INTEGRATION corporate_sso
  TYPE = SAML2
  ENABLED = TRUE
  SAML2_ISSUER = 'https://idp.example.com'
  SAML2_SSO_URL = 'https://idp.example.com/sso/saml'
  SAML2_PROVIDER = 'CUSTOM'
  SAML2_X509_CERT = '<certificate>';

wui.description: Federate human authentication through SAML2 or External OAuth, add SCIM for provisioning, then remove local passwords — keeping one monitored break-glass administrator.

other.description:
1. Register Snowflake as an application in your identity provider
2. Create a SAML2 (or External OAuth) security integration in Snowflake
3. Test federated login with a pilot user before broad rollout
4. Add a SCIM integration so user and role provisioning follows the IdP
5. Once federation is proven, remove Snowflake-local passwords from human users
6. Retain one break-glass local administrator with a stored, monitored credential

terraform.description:
resource "snowflake_saml_integration" "corporate_sso" {
  name           = "CORPORATE_SSO"
  enabled        = true
  saml2_issuer   = "https://idp.example.com"
  saml2_sso_url  = "https://idp.example.com/sso/saml"
  saml2_provider = "CUSTOM"
  saml2_x509_cert = var.idp_certificate
}

snowflake_account_periodic_rekeying_enab.title: Snowflake accounts enable periodic data rekeying
snowflake_account_periodic_rekeying_enab.description: With `PERIODIC_DATA_REKEYING` enabled, Snowflake re-encrypts data whose encryption key is older than one year with a fresh key. This check verifies that the account parameter is set to true.
snowflake_account_periodic_rekeying_enab.risk: Without rekeying, the same data encryption key protects a table for its entire lifetime, so the **window in which a single compromised key is useful is unbounded**. Periodic rekeying limits the blast radius of key compromise and satisfies the cryptoperiod expectations that appear in most data protection standards.

wui.description: Enable periodic data rekeying so encryption keys are rotated annually, and consider Tri-Secret Secure where you need the ability to revoke access with a customer-managed key.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Snowsight as ACCOUNTADMIN
2. Run `ALTER ACCOUNT SET PERIODIC_DATA_REKEYING = TRUE`
3. Note that rekeying consumes credits as it re-encrypts historical data; plan for the one-off cost
4. For stricter key control, additionally enable Tri-Secret Secure so a customer-managed key in your cloud KMS is required alongside Snowflake's key
5. Confirm the parameter with `SHOW PARAMETERS LIKE 'PERIODIC_DATA_REKEYING' IN ACCOUNT`

snowflake_account_external_stage_uses_st.title: Snowflake external stages use a storage integration rather than embedded credentials
snowflake_account_external_stage_uses_st.description: A **storage integration** lets Snowflake reach cloud object storage through a managed IAM trust relationship instead of credentials written into the stage definition. This check reports external stages with no storage integration attached.
snowflake_account_external_stage_uses_st.risk: An external stage created with inline credentials stores a **long-lived cloud access key inside the stage definition**, where it is visible to anyone who can run `DESC STAGE` and is copied into every clone, backup and DDL export. Those keys are typically over-permissioned on the bucket, so a Snowflake reader-level compromise escalates into direct access to the underlying data lake.

cli.description:
CREATE STORAGE INTEGRATION s3_data_lake
  TYPE = EXTERNAL_STAGE
  STORAGE_PROVIDER = 'S3'
  STORAGE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake-stage'
  ENABLED = TRUE
  STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS = ('s3://data-lake/curated/');
ALTER STAGE curated_stage SET STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_data_lake;

wui.description: Point every external stage at a storage integration scoped to the narrowest possible prefix, revoke any embedded access key, and set REQUIRE_STORAGE_INTEGRATION_FOR_STAGE_CREATION so the pattern cannot recur.

other.description:
1. Create a cloud IAM role trusted by your Snowflake account
2. Create a storage integration referencing that role, with `STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS` scoped to the specific prefix
3. Recreate or alter each external stage to use the integration
4. Remove the inline `CREDENTIALS = (...)` clause
5. Revoke the cloud access key that was embedded in the stage — treat it as compromised
6. Set `REQUIRE_STORAGE_INTEGRATION_FOR_STAGE_CREATION = TRUE` so new stages cannot reintroduce inline credentials

terraform.description:
resource "snowflake_storage_integration" "data_lake" {
  name                      = "S3_DATA_LAKE"
  type                      = "EXTERNAL_STAGE"
  storage_provider          = "S3"
  storage_aws_role_arn      = aws_iam_role.snowflake_stage.arn
  storage_allowed_locations = ["s3://data-lake/curated/"]
  enabled                   = true
}

snowflake_account_data_retention_time_co.title: Snowflake accounts configure a minimum Time Travel retention period
snowflake_account_data_retention_time_co.description: **Time Travel** retention determines how far back a table's prior state can be queried or restored. This check verifies that the account sets a retention period of at least one day, and reports where the minimum is left at zero.
snowflake_account_data_retention_time_co.risk: With retention at zero, a destructive statement — a mistaken `TRUNCATE`, or deliberate tampering by an attacker covering their tracks — is **immediately unrecoverable**, and there is no prior version to compare against when determining what was changed. Time Travel is often the only mechanism that can establish what a table contained before an incident.

cli.description:
ALTER ACCOUNT SET DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 7;
ALTER ACCOUNT SET MIN_DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 1;

wui.description: Set a Time Travel retention window that matches your recovery objective and enforce a floor with MIN_DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS so object owners cannot reduce it below policy.

other.description:
1. Sign in to Snowsight as ACCOUNTADMIN
2. Set `DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS` to your recovery objective (1 on Standard, up to 90 on Enterprise)
3. Set `MIN_DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS` so an object owner cannot lower retention below the floor
4. Increase retention specifically on databases holding regulated or business-critical data
5. Account for the storage cost of retained versions when choosing the window

snowflake_networkpolicy_no_broad_allowli.title: Snowflake network policies do not allow the entire internet
snowflake_networkpolicy_no_broad_allowli.description: This check inspects each network policy's `ALLOWED_IP_LIST` for entries that permit the whole address space (`0.0.0.0/0`, `::/0`) or an excessively wide range, which would make the policy ineffective.
snowflake_networkpolicy_no_broad_allowli.risk: A network policy containing `0.0.0.0/0` **satisfies configuration checks while enforcing nothing**, which is worse than having no policy at all because it creates the appearance of a control. These entries are usually added temporarily to unblock a client and then never removed, leaving the account open to authentication attempts from anywhere.

wui.description: Remove open ranges from the allowed IP list and replace them with the specific egress CIDRs of each client, preferring PrivateLink for workloads running in cloud accounts.

other.description:
1. Run `DESC NETWORK POLICY <name>` and review the allowed list
2. Replace `0.0.0.0/0` and other wide ranges with the specific CIDRs your clients use
3. Where a partner or SaaS tool needs access, use its documented static egress ranges rather than opening the policy
4. For cloud-hosted clients, move to PrivateLink and restrict the policy to the private endpoint
5. Re-test connectivity from each client after narrowing

terraformcloud_workspace_sensitive_varia.title: HCP Terraform workspace variables holding credentials are marked sensitive
terraformcloud_workspace_sensitive_varia.description: A **sensitive** workspace variable is write-only: its value cannot be read back through the API or UI and is redacted from run output. This check reports variables whose names indicate a credential but that are not marked sensitive.
terraformcloud_workspace_sensitive_varia.risk: A non-sensitive variable's value is **readable by every user with workspace read access and returned by the API**, and it appears in plan output where it is retained in run history indefinitely. Because these variables typically hold the cloud credentials Terraform provisions with, one exposed value grants the same access Terraform itself has — which is usually administrative.

wui.description: Mark every credential-bearing variable sensitive, rotate anything previously stored in the clear, and migrate to dynamic provider credentials so no static secret is stored.

other.description:
1. Open the workspace and go to **Variables**
2. For each credential variable, edit it and tick **Sensitive**
3. Rotate the credential — its value has been readable through the API and may appear in retained plan output
4. Move shared credentials into a **variable set** so they are managed in one place
5. Better still, replace static credentials with dynamic provider credentials so no long-lived secret is stored at all

terraform.description:
resource "tfe_variable" "aws_secret" {
  key          = "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"
  value        = var.aws_secret
  category     = "env"
  sensitive    = true
  workspace_id = tfe_workspace.prod.id
}

terraformcloud_workspace_dynamic_credent.title: HCP Terraform workspaces use dynamic provider credentials
terraformcloud_workspace_dynamic_credent.description: **Dynamic provider credentials** let a workspace exchange a signed workload identity token for short-lived cloud credentials at run time. This check reports workspaces still holding static cloud access keys as environment variables.
terraformcloud_workspace_dynamic_credent.risk: A static cloud access key stored in a Terraform workspace is a **long-lived credential with provisioning privileges** — typically broad enough to create IAM principals, which makes it a privilege escalation path into the whole cloud account. It never expires, exists in a system many engineers can read, and its compromise is not detectable from the cloud side, since the calls look like ordinary Terraform runs.

cli.description:
# Set the workspace to use dynamic credentials instead of static keys:
#   TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH = true
#   TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN  = arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/tfc-run
# then delete AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY.

wui.description: Move workspaces to dynamic provider credentials with a trust policy scoped to the specific workspace, then delete the static keys from Terraform and deactivate them in the cloud account.

other.description:
1. Create an OIDC identity provider in the cloud account trusting `app.terraform.io`
2. Create a role whose trust policy is scoped to the specific organization, project and workspace
3. Grant the role only the permissions that workspace's configuration actually needs
4. Set `TFC_<PROVIDER>_PROVIDER_AUTH` and the run role variable on the workspace
5. Run a plan to confirm authentication succeeds
6. Delete the static access key variables and **deactivate the key in the cloud account** — removing it from Terraform does not revoke it

terraformcloud_workspace_remote_state_no.title: HCP Terraform workspaces do not share remote state organization-wide
terraformcloud_workspace_remote_state_no.description: The `global-remote-state` setting allows **every workspace in the organization** to read a workspace's state. This check reports workspaces with global sharing enabled instead of an explicit consumer list.
terraformcloud_workspace_remote_state_no.risk: Terraform state contains the **full attribute set of every resource**, including generated passwords, private keys, connection strings and any provider output the configuration touched — regardless of whether the corresponding variable was marked sensitive. Sharing it organization-wide means anyone who can create a workspace can read the credentials of your production environment.

wui.description: Replace global remote state sharing with an explicit consumer list, and rotate any secret that appeared in state while it was organization-readable.

other.description:
1. Open the workspace and go to **Settings > General**
2. Set remote state sharing to **Share with specific workspaces**
3. List only the workspaces that genuinely consume this state
4. Prefer passing values through a data source or a variable set over remote state sharing where practical
5. Review the existing state for secrets, and rotate anything that was broadly readable
6. Restrict who can read state at the team level as well

terraformcloud_workspace_auto_apply_disa.title: HCP Terraform workspaces require manual apply approval
terraformcloud_workspace_auto_apply_disa.description: With **auto-apply** enabled, a workspace applies a successful plan without human review. This check reports workspaces where auto-apply is on, so approval is a deliberate exception rather than the default.
terraformcloud_workspace_auto_apply_disa.risk: Auto-apply removes the last review point between a merged configuration change and **live infrastructure**, so a malicious or mistaken commit reaches production without anyone reading the plan. Terraform plans also surface destructive actions — resource replacement and deletion — that a reviewer would catch; auto-apply executes them silently.

wui.description: Require manual apply on production workspaces, restrict apply permission to a named team, and add policy checks so risky changes are blocked rather than only reviewed.

other.description:
1. Open the workspace and go to **Settings > General**
2. Set **Apply Method** to `Manual apply`
3. Restrict apply permission to a specific team through **Team Access**
4. Add Sentinel or OPA policies to block high-risk changes automatically, so review effort concentrates on what matters
5. Where auto-apply is genuinely appropriate — a low-risk, non-production workspace — record the exception explicitly

terraformcloud_workspace_health_assessme.title: HCP Terraform workspaces enable health assessments and drift detection
terraformcloud_workspace_health_assessme.description: **Health assessments** periodically re-plan a workspace to detect drift between the configuration and the real infrastructure. This check reports workspaces with assessments disabled.
terraformcloud_workspace_health_assessme.risk: Without drift detection, an **out-of-band change to production goes unnoticed** until the next apply, which then silently reverts or compounds it. From a security standpoint drift is often the signal itself: a security group opened by hand, a policy loosened during an incident, or an attacker's modification all appear as drift, and detecting them at the next scheduled assessment is far faster than at the next release.

wui.description: Enable health assessments so drift is detected on a schedule, route notifications to the owning team, and treat unexplained drift on security-relevant resources as a potential incident.

other.description:
1. Open the workspace and go to **Settings > Health**
2. Enable **Health assessments**
3. Confirm the workspace's credentials permit a read-only plan on a schedule
4. Route drift notifications to the owning team, not just to the workspace page
5. Treat unexplained drift on security-relevant resources as a potential incident rather than a cleanup task
6. Note that assessments require a paid tier and a remote execution mode

terraformcloud_organization_sso_enforced.title: HCP Terraform organizations enforce SSO for collaborators
terraformcloud_organization_sso_enforced.description: The organization's **collaborator authentication policy** governs how members sign in. This check verifies that SAML SSO is enabled and set as the required policy rather than allowing password authentication.
terraformcloud_organization_sso_enforced.risk: HCP Terraform holds the credentials that **provision your entire cloud estate**, so an account there is effectively an administrative account for the infrastructure it manages. Without enforced SSO there is no conditional access and no central revocation, and a departed engineer's account keeps its apply permissions until someone remembers to remove it.

wui.description: Enforce SAML SSO for collaborators, map ownership to an IdP group, keep one monitored break-glass owner, and review team API tokens separately since they bypass SSO.

other.description:
1. In the organization settings, go to **SSO** and configure the SAML connection to your identity provider
2. Test sign-in with a pilot user
3. Set the **Authentication** policy to require SSO
4. Map the owners team to a SAML role so organization ownership follows the IdP group
5. Keep one documented break-glass owner account with a strong credential and monitoring
6. Review the team API tokens, which continue to work independently of SSO

terraformcloud_organization_two_factor_c.title: HCP Terraform organization members are two-factor conformant
terraformcloud_organization_two_factor_c.description: The `two-factor-conformant` attribute reports whether **every member** of the organization has two-factor authentication enabled. This check reports organizations with any non-conformant member.
terraformcloud_organization_two_factor_c.risk: A single member without two-factor authentication is enough to compromise the organization, because Terraform permissions are typically **broad by necessity** — the tooling must be able to create and destroy the resources it manages. An attacker holding one such account can read state containing production credentials and queue applies against live infrastructure.

wui.description: Bring every member into two-factor conformance or remove their access, and enforce the requirement in your IdP where SSO is used so it applies uniformly.

other.description:
1. List organization memberships and identify members without two-factor authentication
2. Ask them to enable it under **User Settings > Two-factor authentication**
3. Remove members who no longer need access rather than chasing enrolment
4. Where SSO is enforced, apply the requirement in the identity provider's conditional access policy so it covers everyone uniformly
5. Review team API tokens separately — they authenticate without a second factor

terraformcloud_organization_audit_trail_.title: HCP Terraform organizations have an accessible audit trail
terraformcloud_organization_audit_trail_.description: This check verifies that the organization's **audit trail** API is readable, so runs, variable changes, permission grants and token creation can be exported to a SIEM.
terraformcloud_organization_audit_trail_.risk: The Terraform audit trail is the record of **who changed the infrastructure and what credentials were touched**, and it is retained for a limited period. Without an export, a compromise of the Terraform organization cannot be reconstructed: you cannot establish which state files were read, which variables were altered, or when the attacker's team token was created.

wui.description: Export the organization audit trail to your SIEM on a schedule and alert on token creation, production variable changes, permission grants and workspace deletion.

other.description:
1. Confirm your tier includes audit trail access
2. Create an organization token with audit trail read permission
3. Build a scheduled pull of `/api/v2/organization/audit-trails` into your SIEM, or use the HCP audit log streaming integration
4. Alert on team token creation, variable changes on production workspaces, permission grants and workspace deletion
5. Retain exported records for at least your investigation window

vault_audit_device_enabled.title: Vault clusters have at least one audit device enabled
vault_audit_device_enabled.description: Vault **audit devices** record every request and response, including the requesting token's accessor. This check verifies that at least one audit device is enabled on the cluster.
vault_audit_device_enabled.risk: With no audit device, Vault keeps **no record of which secrets were read or by whom**, so a compromised token can drain the entire store leaving nothing to investigate. This is the single most consequential logging gap in a secrets platform: without it, an incident response cannot determine which credentials need rotating, forcing a rotation of everything.

cli.description:
vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault/audit.log
vault audit enable -path=syslog syslog tag="vault" facility="AUTH"
vault audit list -detailed

wui.description: Enable at least one audit device with log_raw disabled, ship the events to a SIEM outside the Vault administrators' control, and alert when audit events stop arriving.

other.description:
1. Enable a file audit device writing to a path with restrictive permissions
2. Ship the file to your SIEM with a log agent, or enable a syslog device in addition
3. Leave `hmac_accessor` at its default and `log_raw` disabled so secret values are not written in cleartext
4. Configure log rotation, and confirm Vault reopens the file afterwards with `vault audit`
5. Alert on the absence of audit events — a blocked audit device stops Vault from serving requests, which is by design

vault_audit_device_redundant.title: Vault clusters have more than one audit device enabled
vault_audit_device_redundant.description: Vault refuses to serve requests when an enabled audit device cannot write. This check verifies that at least two audit devices are enabled so a single failing sink does not take the cluster offline.
vault_audit_device_redundant.risk: A single audit device is both a logging and an **availability** dependency: if its disk fills or the syslog target becomes unreachable, Vault stops answering requests and every application depending on it for credentials fails. Operators under that pressure frequently disable auditing to restore service, which removes the record precisely when it matters most.

cli.description:
vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault/audit.log
vault audit enable -path=syslog syslog tag="vault" facility="AUTH"
vault audit enable -path=socket socket address="siem.example.com:9090" socket_type="tcp"

wui.description: Enable two audit devices with independent failure modes, monitor the audit volume's free space, and rehearse the blocked-audit-device response so nobody disables auditing under pressure.

other.description:
1. Enable a second audit device with a different failure mode — a local file plus syslog, for example
2. Monitor free space on the audit log volume and alert well before it fills
3. Configure log rotation with an agent that does not hold the file handle open
4. Test the failure path in a non-production cluster so the operational response is known
5. Never leave a socket device as the only sink; a network partition then blocks Vault entirely

vault_auth_no_active_root_tokens.title: Vault clusters have no outstanding root tokens
vault_auth_no_active_root_tokens.description: A Vault **root token** bypasses all policy enforcement. This check enumerates token accessors and reports any token carrying the `root` policy, which should exist only briefly during break-glass operations.
vault_auth_no_active_root_tokens.risk: A root token is **unrestricted and, unless explicitly created with a TTL, never expires**. Anyone holding one can read every secret, disable the audit devices that would record them doing so, and create further tokens for persistence. Root tokens generated during initial setup and never revoked are among the most common serious findings in a Vault deployment.

cli.description:
vault list auth/token/accessors
vault token lookup-accessor <accessor>
vault token revoke -accessor <accessor>

wui.description: Revoke all outstanding root tokens, generate one on demand through the quorum-based generate-root process when break-glass access is needed, and revoke it as soon as the operation completes.

other.description:
1. List token accessors and look up each one to identify those holding the root policy
2. Confirm no automation depends on them — automation should use an auth method, not a root token
3. Revoke each root token by accessor
4. When root access is genuinely needed, generate a temporary one with `vault operator generate-root` using the unseal key holders, and revoke it immediately afterwards
5. Ensure administrators authenticate through an identity-backed auth method with scoped policies for day-to-day work

vault_auth_token_ttl_bounded.title: Vault auth methods bound token lifetime
vault_auth_token_ttl_bounded.description: This check verifies that each auth method sets a **maximum lease TTL** within the configured bound (32 days by default), so tokens issued through it cannot be renewed indefinitely.
vault_auth_token_ttl_bounded.risk: A token with an unbounded maximum TTL can be **renewed forever**, so a credential stolen from a log, a container environment or a developer machine stays valid until someone notices and revokes it explicitly. Bounded lifetimes convert theft from a permanent compromise into a time-limited one, and force the legitimate consumer to re-authenticate through the identity source you actually control.

cli.description:
vault auth tune -default-lease-ttl=1h -max-lease-ttl=24h kubernetes/
vault read sys/auth/kubernetes/tune

wui.description: Tune each auth method with short default and bounded maximum lease TTLs, and confirm consuming applications re-authenticate cleanly before tightening the values.

other.description:
1. Review each auth method's tuning with `vault read sys/auth/<path>/tune`
2. Set `default_lease_ttl` to the shortest interval the consuming workload tolerates
3. Set `max_lease_ttl` so renewal cannot extend a token indefinitely
4. Prefer short-lived tokens obtained per workload run over long-lived ones held in configuration
5. Verify applications handle token renewal and re-authentication correctly before tightening

vault_auth_identity_backed_methods_enabl.title: Vault clusters authenticate through identity-backed methods
vault_auth_identity_backed_methods_enabl.description: This check verifies that the cluster enables at least one **identity-backed auth method** — OIDC, JWT, Kubernetes, AWS/Azure/GCP IAM, LDAP or cert — rather than relying solely on the built-in token method.
vault_auth_identity_backed_methods_enabl.risk: With only the token auth method available, every consumer holds a **static secret that was issued once and copied wherever it was needed**. There is no upstream identity to revoke, no attestation of what the caller actually is, and offboarding a person or decommissioning a workload leaves working tokens behind. Identity-backed methods let Vault verify the caller against a source of truth on every login.

cli.description:
vault auth enable oidc
vault auth enable kubernetes
vault auth list

wui.description: Enable identity-backed auth methods for both workloads and operators, bind roles narrowly to specific identities, and revoke static tokens once each consumer has migrated.

other.description:
1. Enable an auth method backed by your workload identity: Kubernetes for pods, JWT/OIDC for CI, cloud IAM for VMs
2. Enable OIDC against your corporate identity provider for human operators
3. Bind roles to specific service accounts, repositories or instance profiles rather than broad wildcards
