4. Migrate applications off static tokens one at a time, confirming each works before removing the old token
5. Revoke the static tokens once migration completes

vault_secret_engine_lease_ttl_bounded.title: Vault dynamic secret engines bound credential lease lifetime
vault_secret_engine_lease_ttl_bounded.description: This check verifies that dynamic secret engines — database, AWS, Azure, GCP, PKI, SSH and Consul — set a **maximum lease TTL**, so the credentials they issue expire rather than persisting indefinitely.
vault_secret_engine_lease_ttl_bounded.risk: The value of a dynamic secret engine is that credentials are **short-lived and revoked automatically**; without a bounded maximum lease TTL that property is lost and the engine simply becomes a generator of long-lived credentials scattered across your estate. Worse, each is a real database user or cloud principal, so an unbounded lease leaves durable access that no rotation of the Vault token will revoke.

cli.description:
vault secrets tune -default-lease-ttl=1h -max-lease-ttl=24h database/
vault read sys/mounts/database/tune

wui.description: Bound the maximum lease TTL on every dynamic secret engine, set shorter role-level TTLs where appropriate, and verify revocation actually removes the credential at the target system.

other.description:
1. Review each dynamic engine's tuning with `vault read sys/mounts/<path>/tune`
2. Set `max_lease_ttl` to the shortest period the consuming workload can operate within
3. Set role-level TTLs where they should be shorter than the mount default
4. Verify that revocation actually works — test that a revoked database credential is dropped at the target
5. Monitor the lease count; a growing backlog usually means consumers are not releasing leases

vault_system_listener_tls_enabled.title: Vault listeners require TLS
vault_system_listener_tls_enabled.description: This check reports Vault listeners configured with `tls_disable`, and confirms the cluster address itself uses HTTPS.
vault_system_listener_tls_enabled.risk: Vault tokens and secret values travel in the **request and response bodies**, so a listener without TLS publishes every credential the cluster serves to anyone on the network path. Because a captured token is immediately replayable, one intercepted request is enough to reach every secret that token's policy allows — the entire purpose of the system defeated at the transport layer.

cli.description:
# In the Vault server configuration:
#   listener "tcp" {
#     address       = "0.0.0.0:8200"
#     tls_cert_file = "/etc/vault/tls/vault.crt"
#     tls_key_file  = "/etc/vault/tls/vault.key"
#     tls_min_version = "tls12"
#   }
sudo systemctl restart vault

wui.description: Enable TLS on every listener with a minimum version of 1.2, remove tls_disable, and rotate all tokens and secrets that were previously served over plaintext.

other.description:
1. Provision a certificate for the Vault cluster's DNS name
2. Set `tls_cert_file` and `tls_key_file` on every listener and remove `tls_disable`
3. Set `tls_min_version = "tls12"` or higher
4. Restart Vault and confirm `VAULT_ADDR` uses `https://`
5. Enable `tls_require_and_verify_client_cert` where mutual TLS is practical
6. Rotate every token and secret that was served over a plaintext listener — treat them as intercepted

terraform.description:
# Vault Helm chart values
server:
  standalone:
    config: |
      listener "tcp" {
        address       = "0.0.0.0:8200"
        tls_cert_file = "/vault/userconfig/tls/tls.crt"
        tls_key_file  = "/vault/userconfig/tls/tls.key"
        tls_min_version = "tls12"
      }

vault_system_auto_unseal_configured.title: Vault clusters use auto-unseal or a quorum Shamir threshold
vault_system_auto_unseal_configured.description: This check verifies that the cluster uses an **auto-unseal seal** backed by a cloud KMS or HSM, or — where Shamir key sharing is used — that the unseal threshold is at least three of five shares.
vault_system_auto_unseal_configured.risk: With Shamir unsealing and a low threshold, **one or two key holders can unseal Vault alone**, removing the quorum control that protects the master key; and every restart requires humans to assemble, which pressures operators into storing shares together and defeating the split entirely. Auto-unseal moves the trust to a KMS key you can audit and revoke, and removes the temptation to hoard shares.

wui.description: Use KMS or HSM auto-unseal with recovery keys split 3-of-5 across separate holders, and tightly restrict and monitor the unseal key's policy since it is equivalent to the seal itself.

other.description:
1. Create a KMS key (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS) or provision an HSM
2. Add the corresponding `seal` stanza to the Vault configuration
3. Migrate the existing seal with `vault operator unseal -migrate`
4. Distribute the resulting recovery keys to separate holders using a threshold of at least 3 of 5
5. Store recovery key shares in physically separate locations — never together
6. Restrict and monitor the KMS key policy: whoever can use that key can unseal Vault

vault_system_not_sealed.title: Vault clusters are unsealed and serving requests
vault_system_not_sealed.description: A sealed Vault cannot decrypt its storage and refuses all requests. This check reports clusters found in a sealed state, and confirms high availability is enabled.
vault_system_not_sealed.risk: A sealed Vault is a **total outage for every application that depends on it** for database credentials, certificates and API keys, and the recovery path requires assembling unseal key holders under time pressure. Teams routinely respond by caching secrets locally or falling back to static credentials, which quietly undoes the controls Vault was deployed to provide.

cli.description:
vault status
vault operator unseal
# Prefer auto-unseal so restarts recover without human intervention.

wui.description: Restore the cluster to unsealed, configure auto-unseal so restarts recover unattended, run at least three nodes in HA, and alert on seal status transitions.

other.description:
1. Determine why the cluster is sealed — a restart, a crash, or a manual seal
2. Unseal it with the required key shares, or confirm the auto-unseal KMS key is reachable
3. Configure auto-unseal so restarts recover automatically
4. Run Vault in HA with at least three nodes, so a single node restart does not interrupt service
5. Alert on seal status changes and on nodes leaving the cluster
6. Verify applications retry gracefully rather than caching secrets when Vault is unavailable

project_firewall_enabled.title: Vercel projects have the firewall enabled
project_firewall_enabled.description: This check verifies that each project has the **Vercel Firewall** enabled, which is the prerequisite for custom rules, managed rulesets, IP blocking and rate limiting to take effect.
project_firewall_enabled.risk: With the firewall disabled, every request reaches the application's serverless functions directly, so **abusive traffic is billed and executed rather than dropped at the edge**. Application-layer attacks — credential stuffing against a login route, scraping, or a request flood — become both a security incident and an uncapped cost event, and the WAF rules configured at team level do nothing for that project.

wui.description: Enable the firewall on every project, turn on the relevant managed rulesets, rate-limit authentication routes, and verify legitimate traffic is unaffected before relying on it.

other.description:
1. Open the project in the Vercel dashboard
2. Go to **Settings > Firewall**
3. Enable the firewall for the project
4. Enable the **managed rulesets** appropriate to the application
5. Add rate limiting on authentication and other expensive routes
6. Review the firewall observability page after enabling to confirm legitimate traffic is not being blocked
7. Enable **Attack Challenge Mode** as a documented response for an active incident

project_bot_protection_enabled.title: Vercel projects enable bot protection
project_bot_protection_enabled.description: **BotID** distinguishes automated clients from real browsers at the edge, before a request reaches a function. This check reports projects with bot protection disabled.
project_bot_protection_enabled.risk: Without bot filtering, automated traffic reaches **the routes that cost the most to serve**: login endpoints for credential stuffing, signup forms for fake account creation, and any AI or database-backed route where each request has real compute cost. Because Vercel bills on execution, unfiltered bot traffic is simultaneously a security and a billing exposure, and it obscures genuine user metrics.

wui.description: Enable BotID and protect authentication, signup and compute-expensive routes, wiring in the client integration and pairing it with rate limiting.

other.description:
1. Open the project in the Vercel dashboard
2. Go to **Settings > Security** and enable **BotID**
3. Protect the specific routes that matter — authentication, signup, checkout, and any AI-backed endpoint
4. Add the client-side integration so classification has browser signals to work with
5. Verify legitimate integrations and monitoring probes are not being classified as bots
6. Combine with rate limiting rather than relying on bot detection alone

project_node_version_supported.title: Vercel projects run a supported Node.js version
project_node_version_supported.description: This check reports projects pinned to a Node.js version that has reached end of life and therefore no longer receives security patches from either the Node.js project or Vercel.
project_node_version_supported.risk: An end-of-life runtime accumulates **unpatched vulnerabilities in the JavaScript engine and the standard library**, including HTTP request parsing and TLS handling that process untrusted input on every request. Because the runtime sits underneath the application, no amount of application-level review addresses those flaws, and Vercel eventually stops building projects pinned to retired versions.

wui.description: Move projects to the current Node.js LTS release, align the engines field in package.json, and validate on a preview deployment before promoting.

other.description:
1. Open the project in the Vercel dashboard
2. Go to **Settings > General > Node.js Version**
3. Select the current LTS release
4. Update the `engines.node` field in `package.json` to match, so local and CI builds agree
5. Run the test suite against the new version before promoting to production
6. Deploy to a preview environment first and confirm behaviour, particularly around any native dependencies

project_secure_compute_configured.title: Vercel projects reaching private backends use Secure Compute
project_secure_compute_configured.description: **Secure Compute** places a project's functions in a dedicated VPC with static egress IPs, so a private backend can allowlist Vercel traffic precisely. This check reports projects with no Secure Compute configuration.
project_secure_compute_configured.risk: Without dedicated egress, functions leave through a **shared, rotating pool of addresses**, so any database or internal API they reach must either be internet-exposed or allowlist a broad range that other Vercel customers also use. Both outcomes weaken the network boundary around the backend, and the second means an allowlist entry does not actually identify your application.

wui.description: Assign projects that reach private backends to a Secure Compute network, restrict the backend allowlist to the resulting static egress IPs, and confirm preview environments are covered too.

other.description:
1. Confirm the team's plan includes Secure Compute
2. In the team settings, create a Secure Compute network in the region closest to the backend
3. Assign the project's production and preview environments to that network
4. Note the static egress IP addresses
5. Restrict the backend's firewall or database access list to those addresses and remove the broad ranges
6. Where a private connection is needed, peer the Secure Compute VPC with your own
7. Verify preview deployments still reach the backend — they use a separate egress range
